docs.title: Cost Analysis
docs.text:
This page estimates what a textbook costs when one DGX system generates it. It adds up the cost to buy the system, set it up, and run it, and spreads that cost over the books the system can produce. It then works out what a book-generation service would have to charge to keep a 20% profit margin.

Under the assumptions below, one unit costs about $8,300 a year to own and run. With the reference model, a whole textbook takes about 28 hours of machine time and costs about $53, so the service would have to charge about $66. Across the ten candidate models the price runs from about $40 to about $216.

An estimate built on one measured run

Only one model has finished one benchmark stage, and no model has generated a whole book on this hardware. Nobody has judged the quality of any output. Every time on this page except that one stage is calculated from assumptions. Treat the dollar figures as a model to adjust, not as a result.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text: The Primary Author set two of these assumptions: the three benchmark stages are 10% of the cost of a whole book, and the service keeps a 20% profit margin. Claude, the AI assistant that wrote this page, chose the others.

docs.title: Purchase and Setup
docs.text: Assumption Value Basis Hardware price $6,950 NVIDIA's list price for a 128 GB DGX Spark in October 2026. It was $3,999 at launch in October 2025 and $4,699 from February 2026. Partner systems sold for $7,000 to $9,000 Accessories $250 An uninterruptible power supply and network cabling. Assumed Service life 3 years, no resale value Assumed. The cost is spread evenly over the three years Setup labor 40 hours Assumed: 16 hours to connect, take the inventory, install the model server, and build the harness container, then 24 hours to test candidate models and choose one Labor rate $90 an hour Assumed, as a full cost with benefits for a technical employee

docs.title: Running
docs.text: Assumption Value Basis Share of hours spent generating 50% Assumed. The other half covers waiting for orders, failed and repeated runs, and maintenance Books in progress at once One per unit The evaluation ran one model and one session per unit Power while generating 150 W A published review measured 60 to 90 W in many model workloads and just under 200 W at most. 150 W is deliberately high. It was not measured at the wall on these units Power while idle 40 W The same review measured 40 to 45 W Electricity price $0.1385 per kWh The U.S. average commercial price for the 12 months ending July 2026 Operations labor 4 hours a month Assumed: updates, new models, and restarting runs that fail Network and space $20 a month Assumed share of an existing office's internet and floor space

docs.title: Workload
docs.text: Assumption Value Basis Book size 200 concepts, 13 chapters, 55,000 words of chapter text The published Algebra I book that the benchmark uses as its reference for scale Tokens generated in the three stages 200,000 The chapter text is about 73,000 tokens at 1.33 tokens per word. The rest is an allowance for the learning graph, the chapter outlines, reasoning, tool calls, and rewrites Turns in the three stages 280 55 measured in stage 1, 30 assumed for stage 2, and 15 assumed for each of 13 chapters in stage 3 Overhead per turn 15 seconds Assumed, for reading the new part of the prompt and running the tool. gemma4:26b read 3,000 prompt tokens a second Overhead per turn, qwen3.8:27b 90 seconds Measured: the server re-read the conversation on every turn, which added one to two minutes Share of the book in the three stages 10% The Primary Author's assumption. The learning graph, chapter design, and chapter content are one tenth of the cost. MicroSims, the glossary, the FAQ, quizzes, and references are the rest Profit margin 20% of the price The Primary Author's assumption

docs.title: Purchase, Setup, and Running Costs
docs.text:
Buying and setting up one unit takes $10,800 before the first book: $7,200 for the hardware and accessories, and $3,600 for 40 hours of setup labor.

Spread over three years and added to the running costs, one unit costs $8,275 a year.

Cost Calculation Per year Share Hardware ($6,950 + $250) ÷ 3 years $2,400 29% Setup 40 hours × $90 ÷ 3 years $1,200 15% Electricity 832 kWh × $0.1385 $115 1% Operations labor 4 hours × 12 months × $90 $4,320 52% Network and space $20 × 12 months $240 3% Total $8,275 100%

The electricity figure is 4,380 hours at 150 W plus 4,380 hours at 40 W, which is 832 kWh a year.

At 50% of the 8,760 hours in a year, the unit generates for 4,380 hours. Each generating hour therefore costs $8,275 ÷ 4,380, or $1.89.

People are the largest cost. Labor for setup and operations is two thirds of the total, and electricity is about one percent.

docs.title: Models, Sizes, and Speeds
docs.text:
The table lists the ten model candidates from the smallest download to the largest. Four speeds were measured in this evaluation. The other six models have not been run, so each takes the speed of the tested model it most resembles.

Model Parameters Download Generation speed Basis for the speed devstral-small-2:24b 24 billion 15 GB 34 tokens/s Assumed equal to gemma4:31b qwen3.8:27b 27 billion 17 GB 26 tokens/s Measured on the longest turn of its stage 1 run gemma4:26b 25.2 billion, 3.8 billion active 18 GB 108 tokens/s Measured: the midpoint of 86 to 130 muse-glimmer:30b 30 billion 18 GB 34 tokens/s Assumed equal to gemma4:31b granite4.2:30b about 30 billion, dense 18 GB 34 tokens/s Assumed equal to gemma4:31b gemma4:31b 30.7 billion, dense 20 GB 34 tokens/s Measured: the midpoint of 28 to 40 qwen3.6:35b 35 billion, about 3 billion active 24 GB 108 tokens/s Assumed equal to gemma4:26b nemotron-3.5-lightning:30b 30 billion, 3 billion active 25 GB 108 tokens/s Assumed equal to gemma4:26b gpt-oss:120b 117 billion, 5.1 billion active 65 GB 41 tokens/s Measured: the midpoint of 38 to 44 mistral-medium-3.5:128b 128 billion, dense 80 GB 8.5 tokens/s Assumed: one quarter of gemma4:31b, because it has four times the weights to read for each token

Three rules stand behind the assumed speeds.

  • A mixture-of-experts model of about 30 billion parameters, with 3 to 4 billion active, runs like gemma4:26b.
  • A model of 24 to 31 billion parameters with no published active count is treated as dense and runs like gemma4:31b.
  • A dense model's speed falls in proportion to the size of its weights.

These rules are rough. The second one predicts 34 tokens a second for qwen3.8:27b, and the measured figure was 26.

Download size has almost no effect on cost. Every model fits in 128 GB, and memory is paid for whether a model uses it or not. What a larger model costs is time.

docs.title: Time to Generate a Textbook
docs.text:
The time for the three benchmark stages has two parts: the time to generate the tokens, and the overhead of each turn.

three-stage time = 200,000 tokens ÷ generation speed
                 + 280 turns × overhead per turn

whole-book time  = three-stage time ÷ 10%

The unit costs the same for every hour it generates, so a tenth of the cost is a tenth of the machine time. A whole book takes ten times as long as the three stages.

The one measured stage checks the overhead figure. Stage 1 for qwen3.8:27b made 55 tool calls. At 90 seconds each that is 83 minutes, and one turn of reasoning took another 19 minutes. The sum is 102 minutes, which is the time the stage took.

Many of the models share a speed, so the ten models reduce to six cases.

Case Generating Turn overhead Three stages Whole book gemma4:26b, and by assumption qwen3.6:35b and nemotron-3.5-lightning:30b 31 minutes 70 minutes 1.7 hours 17 hours gpt-oss:120b 81 minutes 70 minutes 2.5 hours 25 hours gemma4:31b, and by assumption devstral-small-2:24b, muse-glimmer:30b, and granite4.2:30b 98 minutes 70 minutes 2.8 hours 28 hours qwen3.8:27b, if the re-reading is fixed 128 minutes 70 minutes 3.3 hours 33 hours mistral-medium-3.5:128b 392 minutes 70 minutes 7.7 hours 77 hours qwen3.8:27b, as measured 128 minutes 420 minutes 9.1 hours 91 hours

Two things stand out. For the fastest models, turn overhead is longer than generation, so a faster model saves less than its speed suggests. And the slowest case is not the largest model. It is a 27-billion-parameter model on a server that re-reads the conversation on every turn.

docs.title: Cost per Textbook and the Price at a 20% Margin
docs.text:
A book's cost is its machine time at $1.89 an hour. The price that leaves a 20% margin is the cost divided by 0.80, because the margin is a share of the price, not of the cost.

cost per book  = whole-book hours × $1.89
price per book = cost per book ÷ (1 − 0.20)
Case Whole book Books per year Cost per book Price at a 20% margin gemma4:26b, qwen3.6:35b, nemotron-3.5-lightning:30b 17 hours 260 $32 $40 gpt-oss:120b 25 hours 174 $48 $60 gemma4:31b, devstral-small-2:24b, muse-glimmer:30b, granite4.2:30b 28 hours 156 $53 $66 qwen3.8:27b, if the re-reading is fixed 33 hours 133 $62 $78 mistral-medium-3.5:128b 77 hours 57 $146 $182 qwen3.8:27b, as measured 91 hours 48 $173 $216

Books per year is 4,380 generating hours divided by the hours for one book.

The reference case on this page is gemma4:31b. Its speed was measured, it is near the middle of the four measured speeds, and it is the only model whose skill runs all ended with a site that builds. It has not finished a benchmark stage.

In the reference case one unit produces 156 books a year. At $66 each that is about $10,300 in revenue against $8,275 in cost, which leaves about $2,100 in profit. A 20% markup on cost is a different and lower number: it gives a price of $63 and a margin of 16.7%.

Of the $53, electricity is 58 cents.

docs.title: What Moves the Answer
docs.text:
Each row changes one assumption in the reference case and leaves the others alone.

Change Cost per book Price at a 20% margin Reference case $53 $66 Generating 75% of the time: 235 books a year $35 $44 Generating 25% of the time: 78 books a year $105 $132 Generating 10% of the time: 31 books a year $263 $329 No operations labor $25 $32 Operations labor of 8 hours a month $81 $101 Hardware at the launch price of $3,999 $47 $58 Hardware at $9,000 $57 $72 A five-year life for the hardware and setup $44 $55 The three stages are 20% of the book $26 $33 The three stages are 5% of the book $106 $132

Nearly all of the cost is fixed, so the cost of a book is close to the yearly cost divided by the number of books sold. A unit that sells 31 books a year has to charge five times what a unit that sells 156 does. Demand, labor, and the 10% share move the price far more than the hardware price does, and the electricity price hardly moves it at all.

Throughput is the other lever. This analysis has each unit generate one book at a time. A server that batches several sessions together could produce more books from the same hardware. vLLM is the candidate named in Design Choices, and it has not been tested.

docs.title: What the Price Leaves Out
docs.text:
• Human review. The price covers generation only. Ten hours of review by a subject expert at the same $90 an hour would add $900, seventeen times the cost of generating the book.
  • Stages that have not been run. The 10% share is an assumption about work no local model has attempted here. If a model cannot build working MicroSims, the other 90% of the book has no price at all.
  • The cost of selling. Marketing, customer support, payment fees, and taxes are not included.
  • Financing and sales tax on the hardware.
  • License terms. A service sells what the model writes. Several candidates state no license or attach conditions to commercial use, and the harness's terms for this use were not reviewed.
  • Supervision by a cloud model. In this evaluation a cloud assistant started and watched the runs. A service would replace it with scripts, and its cost is not counted.

This page does not compare the result with generating the same book in the cloud. The published Algebra I book was made with cloud models, and no token counts or timings were kept for it.

docs.title: Course Description: DGX Evaluation for Textbook Generation
docs.text:
Title: DGX Evaluation for Textbook Generation

Target Audience: Professional development and adult continuing education. The course is written for AI and machine-learning engineers, instructional technologists, technical authors, and IT infrastructure leads who must decide whether a local NVIDIA DGX system can replace or supplement cloud AI services for generating interactive intelligent textbooks.

Prerequisites:

  • Comfort with a Linux or macOS command line: navigating directories, editing files, running commands, and using SSH
  • Basic Python: reading a script, running it, and installing a package
  • Basic git and GitHub: clone, commit, push
  • Hands-on experience with at least one generative AI chat or coding assistant
  • No prior experience with GPU administration, model serving, or model training is required

docs.title: Course Overview
docs.text:
Intelligent textbooks are usually generated by cloud-hosted frontier models driven by agent skills. This course asks an empirical question: can a single NVIDIA DGX system running an open-weight small language model (SLM) generate the same interactive intelligent textbook, end to end, without sending a token to the cloud? The course teaches how to answer that question with measurements instead of opinions. The benchmark workload is the ibook-skills skill chain, which turns a course description into a learning graph, chapters, MicroSims, a glossary, an FAQ, and quizzes.

Students work through the full setup in the order a real evaluation requires. They reach the DGX over Tailscale, verify the hardware with Python probes, build a reproducible conda environment, choose and install an open-weight model and an inference server, and install an AI agent harness that executes skills against the local model. Each step ends with an explicit test, so a failure is caught where it happens and not three layers later. Students then run the textbook pipeline as a benchmark and score the results against a cloud-generated baseline of the same book.

The course does not assume a specific DGX model. The DGX family spans x86_64 and aarch64 CPUs, single and multiple GPUs, and both dedicated GPU memory and unified memory, so the hardware probes run first and every later step branches on what they report. The same procedure applies to any DGX system a reader has access to.

The course opens with a detailed case for and against SLMs. It compares local models with cloud services and agentic frameworks such as Anthropic Claude, OpenAI ChatGPT, Google Antigravity, and Devin, and it keeps three terms separate throughout: cost is what you pay to own and operate hardware, price is what a provider charges you for a service, and quality is how good the generated textbook is. The final deliverable is an evidence-based evaluation report that recommends a local, cloud, or hybrid workflow.

An evaluation report is meant to be shared, and the raw material behind it is not safe to share. Probe reports, command output, logs, and screenshots carry addresses, hostnames, account names, and identifiers that make the tested machine easier to find and reach. The course therefore treats sanitization as a required step before anything is published.

docs.title: Software Stack Under Evaluation
docs.text: Layer Role in the evaluation Examples covered Remote access Reach the DGX from a laptop Tailscale, Tailscale SSH, MagicDNS Operating system Host OS, GPU driver, compute libraries DGX OS, NVIDIA driver, CUDA Environment Isolated, reproducible Python Miniforge, conda, pip Hardware probes Verify what the machine really has psutil, nvidia-smi, NVML Python bindings, PyTorch Model Open-weight SLM that does the generation Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral, and Phi families Inference server Loads the model and exposes a local API Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM Agent harness Runs the agent loop and executes skills Claude Code against a local endpoint, OpenCode, Codex CLI, Goose Skills The benchmark workload ibook-skills Site build Turns generated Markdown into the book MkDocs Material Sanitization Keeps device details out of published results Redaction script, placeholder conventions, a secret scanner such as gitleaks

docs.title: Main Topics Covered
docs.text:
1. Intelligent textbooks and the generation pipeline. The five levels of intelligent textbooks, learning graphs, MicroSims, MkDocs Material, and the ordered ibook-skills skill chain used as the benchmark workload.
  2. Small language models. What separates an SLM from a frontier LLM: parameter count, context window, open weights, licenses, model families, model cards, and the capabilities textbook generation demands (long-form writing, structured output, tool calling, and code generation).
  3. Local SLMs versus cloud LLM services. Pros and cons of running a model on owned hardware compared with Claude, ChatGPT, Google Antigravity, and Devin: privacy, data sovereignty, rate limits, availability, vendor lock-in, version pinning, and operational burden.
  4. Cost, price, and quality tradeoffs. Capital cost, depreciation, electricity, and administration time; per-token, subscription, and per-seat pricing; total cost of ownership; cost per chapter; break-even volume; and quality-adjusted cost.
  5. NVIDIA DGX hardware architecture. The DGX product family treated model-agnostically: CPU architecture (x86_64 and aarch64), system RAM, GPU configuration, dedicated GPU memory versus unified memory, storage, power, thermals, DGX OS, the NVIDIA driver, and CUDA, and how each variation changes the setup steps that follow.
  6. Secure remote access with Tailscale. Mesh VPN concepts, WireGuard, tailnets, installing Tailscale on the laptop and the DGX, authentication, MagicDNS, Tailscale SSH, access control lists, key expiry, connectivity tests, and sharing a local web preview or model endpoint across the tailnet.
  7. Reproducible Python environments with conda. Miniforge, creating and activating environments, pinning the Python version, conda versus pip, environment.yml, requirements.txt, architecture-specific wheels, CUDA-enabled PyTorch, and rebuilding an environment from its specification.
  8. Python hardware probes. Scripts that report CPU model, core count, and architecture; system RAM; storage capacity and read speed; GPU count and model; driver and CUDA versions; total and free GPU memory; temperature; and power draw, all written to a machine-readable report.
  9. Model sizing and model fit. Parameters, numeric precision, bytes per weight, quantization levels, file formats (GGUF and safetensors), size on disk, context and KV-cache memory, safety headroom, and a calculator that predicts whether a model will fit before it is downloaded.
  10. Selecting and installing an open-weight model. Selection criteria, the Hugging Face Hub, license review, downloading, checksum verification, storage management, and shortlisting candidates.
  11. Inference servers. Installing and configuring a local runtime, GPU offload, OpenAI-compatible API endpoints, and a first-prompt smoke test from both curl and a Python client.
  12. AI agent harnesses and skills. The agent loop, tool calling, file editing, shell execution, permissions, context management, the Agent Skills SKILL.md format, connecting a harness to a local endpoint, installing ibook-skills, and verifying that a skill runs.
  13. Optimizing SLM performance. Quantization tradeoffs, context length, batch size, concurrency, prompt caching, sampling parameters, tokens per second, time to first token, GPU utilization monitoring, and thermal throttling.
  14. Objective evaluation methodology. Framing the question, controlled variables, cloud baselines, fixed inputs, repeated runs, metric selection, scoring rubrics, logging, sources of bias such as LLM-as-judge scoring, and blind human review.
  15. Running the textbook benchmark and reporting. An end-to-end generation run, per-stage metrics (skill completion rate, tool-call success rate, build success, structural validity, throughput, wall-clock time, energy, and cost per chapter), comparison with the baseline, and a written recommendation.
  16. Sanitizing evaluation artifacts before publication. The details that make a device easier to find, reach, or log in to: IP addresses, hostnames, tailnet names, usernames, passwords, keys, tokens, hardware identifiers, and access configuration. Redacting probe reports, command output, logs, and screenshots; placeholder conventions and documentation address ranges; scanning for secrets before a commit; and why a later commit does not remove data from git history.

docs.title: Topics Not Covered
docs.text:
• Training and fine-tuning. The course evaluates inference only. Training a model from scratch, full fine-tuning, and LoRA adapters are out of scope.
  • Transformer internals. Deep-learning mathematics is limited to what is needed to estimate memory use and throughput.
  • Cluster-scale infrastructure. Multi-node clusters, Kubernetes, Slurm, and DGX SuperPOD deployments are not covered.
  • Non-NVIDIA accelerators. Apple Silicon, AMD, and Intel hardware appear only as brief comparison points.
  • Non-text generation. Image, audio, and video models for cover art or narration are not evaluated.
  • Retrieval systems. Retrieval-augmented generation, vector databases, and production chatbots are out of scope.
  • Enterprise security and compliance. Security coverage stops at Tailscale access control, basic host hygiene, and sanitizing published artifacts.
  • Textbook pedagogy. How to design a good textbook is covered by other books in this series. Here the pipeline is the workload, not the subject.
  • Cloud service tutorials. Cloud services appear as comparison baselines. The course does not teach how to use each one in depth.
  • Procurement. Purchasing negotiation and vendor selection are not covered beyond the inputs the cost model needs.

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text: After completing this course, students will be able to:

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
Retrieving, recognizing, and recalling relevant knowledge from long-term memory.

  • Define small language model, open-weight model, quantization, context window, token, inference, and agent harness.
  • List the DGX hardware components that determine inference capacity: CPU, system RAM, GPU, GPU memory, and storage.
  • Recall the stages of the ibook-skills textbook generation pipeline in order.
  • Name the Tailscale commands that join a tailnet, show device status, and test connectivity.
  • Identify the conda commands that create, activate, list, export, and remove an environment.
  • List common quantization levels and model file formats.
  • State the definitions of cost, price, and quality as used in this course.
  • Recognize the cloud services and agentic frameworks used as comparison baselines: Claude, ChatGPT, Google Antigravity, and Devin.
  • List the categories of device-identifying detail that must never appear in a published artifact.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
Constructing meaning from instructional messages, including oral, written, and graphic communication.

  • Explain the reasons to prefer a local SLM over a cloud LLM service and the reasons not to.
  • Describe how parameter count and quantization determine a model's memory footprint.
  • Explain the difference between the cost of owning hardware and the price of a cloud service, and how each relates to output quality.
  • Describe how Tailscale builds an encrypted peer-to-peer mesh, and distinguish its coordination plane from its data plane.
  • Explain why an isolated conda environment makes an evaluation reproducible.
  • Summarize how an agent harness loads a skill, plans steps, and calls tools.
  • Explain the difference between dedicated GPU memory and unified memory and why it changes the model-fit calculation.
  • Interpret the output of nvidia-smi.
  • Explain why deleting sensitive data in a later commit does not remove it from git history or from an already published site.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
Carrying out or using a procedure in a given situation.

  • Install and configure Tailscale on a laptop and a DGX, then connect over SSH using a MagicDNS name.
  • Create a conda environment with a pinned Python version, install the required libraries, and record the result in environment.yml.
  • Write and run Python probes that report CPU, system RAM, storage, GPU configuration, GPU memory, driver version, and CUDA version.
  • Calculate whether a model at a given quantization and context length fits in the available GPU memory.
  • Download an open-weight model, serve it from a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and send a first test prompt.
  • Install an agent harness, connect it to the local endpoint, install ibook-skills, and execute a skill.
  • Measure tokens per second, time to first token, GPU utilization, memory use, and power draw during a generation run.
  • Preview the generated textbook from a laptop across the tailnet.
  • Redact a probe report, a log excerpt, and a terminal screenshot using placeholders, then scan the result for secrets before committing it.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
Breaking material into constituent parts and determining how the parts relate to one another and to an overall structure or purpose.

  • Compare candidate open-weight models by license, size, context window, tool-calling reliability, and writing quality.
  • Diagnose a failed run by distinguishing out-of-memory errors, context overflow, malformed tool calls, and harness misconfiguration in the logs.
  • Break down the wall-clock time of a generation run into model loading, prompt processing, token generation, and tool execution.
  • Compare quantization levels by their effect on memory, speed, and output quality.
  • Differentiate the pipeline stages by their sensitivity to model capability: learning graph, chapter prose, MicroSim code, and quizzes.
  • Separate fixed costs from variable costs and identify the generation volume at which local hardware breaks even with cloud pricing.
  • Trace which data leaves the machine in each configuration, including inference traffic, Tailscale coordination metadata, and package downloads.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
Making judgments based on criteria and standards through checking and critiquing.

  • Judge whether a given DGX configuration is sufficient for end-to-end textbook generation, citing probe and benchmark evidence.
  • Assess generated chapters, learning graphs, and MicroSims against a rubric and against a cloud-generated baseline.
  • Critique an evaluation design for bias, uncontrolled variables, too few repetitions, and unfair comparisons.
  • Justify a choice of model, quantization level, inference server, and agent harness using measured results.
  • Weigh cost, price, and quality to recommend a local, cloud, or hybrid workflow.
  • Assess the security of a remote-access setup built on Tailscale.
  • Review an evaluation report and its supporting files for leaked device details and judge whether it is safe to publish.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
Putting elements together to form a coherent or functional whole; reorganizing elements into a new pattern or structure.

  • Design a hardware probe suite that produces a machine-readable DGX configuration report with identifying fields redacted by default.
  • Build a model-fit calculator that takes parameter count, quantization, and context length and returns a fit verdict with headroom.
  • Construct an environment specification and install script that rebuilds the full software stack on a fresh DGX.
  • Develop a benchmark runner that executes the pipeline stages and logs metrics for each one.
  • Develop a cost model that compares the local cost per textbook with cloud pricing for the same book.
  • Compose an evaluation report that states the question, method, results, limitations, and recommendation.
  • Capstone project: Conduct a complete objective evaluation of a DGX system. Probe the hardware, select and install the software stack, generate a small intelligent textbook end to end with ibook-skills on the local GPU, compare it with a cloud-generated baseline of the same book, sanitize every artifact, and publish the report with a recommendation.

docs.title: Design Choices
docs.text:
This page records the design decisions behind the testing configuration. For each one it gives the choice, the options weighed against it, and the reason.

Three parties made these decisions: the Primary Author; the Administrator, who runs the DGX systems; and Claude, the AI assistant that built and ran the tests under the Primary Author's direction. The page says who decided each one, because a choice made by a person with a goal and a choice made by an assistant filling a gap deserve different scrutiny.

Some of these choices did not hold up. They are marked where they appear and collected in the last section.

docs.title: Who Decided What
docs.text: Decision Decided by Tailscale for remote access The Administrator, who delegated the choice to their own Claude assistant Python and Unix shell scripts for automation The Primary Author A dedicated dgx conda environment on the laptop The Primary Author Start testing before Docker access existed The Primary Author Algebra I as the benchmark course The Primary Author Three pipeline stages in the benchmark, and no more The Primary Author Fix the skill's faulty example before the comparison runs The Primary Author Run the harness in a Docker container on the DGX The Primary Author, on Claude's recommendation Only a local model may generate benchmark content The Primary Author Everything else on this page Claude

docs.title: Remote Access: Tailscale
docs.text:
Decided by: The Administrator, through their own Claude assistant.

This evaluation did not weigh the alternatives and does not know the reasoning behind the choice. What the choice gave the evaluation is clear: the laptop reaches both DGX systems across two home routers, and the evaluation never had to ask for a change to either router.

The choices Claude made inside that decision were about the laptop.

Option Assessment conda-forge tailscale and tailscaled packages Chosen. The Primary Author asked for the tools in a conda environment, and these are the open-source client and daemon The Tailscale macOS application Simpler to run, but it lives outside the conda environment the Primary Author asked for Homebrew Same software, but again outside the conda environment

The cost is that the daemon must be started by hand, with sudo, in every session.

docs.title: Automation: Python and Unix Shell
docs.text:
Decided by: The Primary Author.

Every test, probe, and runner is a Python or shell script. Claude made three choices inside that decision.

Choice Alternative considered Why Standard library only for Python that runs on the DGX Packages such as requests, psutil, and NVML bindings The scripts run on a fresh machine with no installs and no administrator rights. The cost is parsing nvidia-smi text for GPU readings Pipe read-only scripts over SSH Copy files to the DGX first An inventory can run before anything is installed or written there Run long jobs inside tmux nohup, or a user-level system service A dropped SSH session does not stop a download or a run. The cost is that nothing restarts after a reboot

docs.title: Login: SSH Keys
docs.text:
Decided by: Claude proposed it, and the Primary Author created and installed the key.

Option Assessment An Ed25519 key with no passphrase Chosen. Scripts and the assistant can log in unattended Password login Cannot be automated, and the assistant does not enter passwords A key with a passphrase, held by an agent Safer if the laptop is stolen, at the price of more setup Tailscale SSH Needs a configuration change on the DGX, which is the Administrator's to make

The cost is that the private key file alone is enough to reach the DGX.

docs.title: Model Server: Ollama
docs.text:
Decided by: Claude.

Option Assessment Ollama Chosen. It installs from one archive into a home directory, has the widest ready-made model library, and offers an API that Claude Code can use directly llama.cpp built from source The compiler and CMake were present, so it was possible. It would have meant a build step and manual model downloads before the first measurement vLLM Better throughput under concurrent load. The usual route on this hardware is a container, and the account had no Docker access when the choice was made

vLLM remains the candidate for a second pass on whichever model wins.

Ollama had a cost that appeared later. With one model, the server re-read almost the whole conversation on every turn, which added one to two minutes per turn. The cause was not identified.

docs.title: Installing Without Administrator Rights
docs.text:
Decided by: The Primary Author directed that testing start before Docker access existed. Claude chose the method.

Option Assessment Official release archive, unpacked into the home directory Chosen. No privileges, a checksum to verify, a pinned version, and one directory to delete to undo it Ollama's install script Needs sudo and creates a system service on a machine that belongs to someone else Ask the Administrator to install it Correct for a permanent setup, and it would have blocked the first measurements

The server listens on the DGX's own loopback interface only. Exposing it on the tailnet would have been convenient, and it would have changed which services the Administrator's machine offers. The laptop reaches it through SSH instead.

docs.title: Candidate Models
docs.text:
Decided by: Claude.

The criteria came from the workload. A model had to support tool calling, offer a context window of at least 64,000 tokens, fit in memory with room for that context, and come from a publisher that could be identified, under terms that could be checked.

Model Size on disk Why it was included qwen3.8:27b 17 GB The newest Qwen release, built for agent work gemma4:26b 18 GB A mixture-of-experts model with about 4 billion active parameters, expected to be fast gemma4:31b 20 GB The dense counterpart from the same family, for a direct comparison gpt-oss:120b 65 GB The largest model that still runs at a usable speed on one unit

docs.title: Why qwen3.8:27b
docs.text:
Four things put it on the list.

  • It is aimed at this workload. Its publisher describes it as improved for long-running agent tasks, for planning, for handling feedback from tools, and for compatibility with agent harnesses. That is a description of running a skill.
  • Its family has the tool-calling record. A mid-2026 survey reported Qwen models holding most of the top places on a public function-calling leaderboard. A harness is useless with a model that writes malformed tool calls.
  • It fits with room to spare. At 17 GB it leaves most of the 128 GB free for a long context, and it declares a 256,000-token window. An 8-bit version at 30 GB exists for a later quality comparison.
  • It is current and widely used. It was the newest Qwen release in the model library, with several million downloads, so the server's support for it was likely to be well exercised.

Two things were not known when it was chosen. Its library page did not say whether it is a dense or a mixture-of-experts model. Its license was reported as Apache 2.0 by secondary sources only, and that still needs checking against the license file.

It then followed every formatting rule in the model tests, wrote the most careful reports in the harness, and was by far the slowest model there.

docs.title: Models Left Out
docs.text: Option Why not, for now qwen3.5:122b At 81 GB it was the largest download, and gpt-oss:120b already covered the large tier Models whose publisher or license could not be identified A result cannot be recommended to readers who cannot check the terms Models that need both units combined The course does not cover multi-machine serving

docs.title: Quantization and Reasoning
docs.text: Each model ran at its default 4-bit quantization. That keeps downloads small and speed high, and it leaves an 8-bit retest for the winner, since memory is not the constraint. The model tests ran with reasoning turned off to bound their run time. The harness runs used each model's default, and that difference mattered: see the last section.

docs.title: Two Layers of Testing
docs.text:
Decided by: Claude.

A model is tested alone first, on five short tasks, and only then inside the harness.

Option Assessment Model alone, then harness Chosen. A model that cannot keep a blank line before a list fails in seconds, not after an hour Go straight to the pipeline Every failure would be slow, and would mix model faults with harness faults Rely on published leaderboards They do not test this book's rules, such as how a MicroSim attaches its canvas

The first versions of three checks were too strict and failed correct output. Each was fixed and the saved output was scored again.

docs.title: Harness: Claude Code
docs.text:
Decided by: Claude chose it over the alternatives. The Primary Author then confirmed it, with the condition that only a local model generates.

Option Assessment Claude Code Chosen. The published books were generated with it and the skills were written for it, so the model becomes the only thing that changes OpenCode Open source with a lighter prompt. A good second harness for telling a model failure from a harness mismatch Codex CLI, Goose Both implement Agent Skills. Neither matched the way the comparison books were made A cloud model plans and the local model writes Offered to the Primary Author as a hybrid. He chose the local harness, because the benchmark tests whether a local harness can execute the skills

The cost is that Claude Code's own instructions and tool definitions run to about 19,000 tokens and were written for Claude models. A local model that struggles may be struggling with the harness.

docs.title: Where the Harness Runs
docs.text:
Decided by: The Primary Author chose the container, on Claude's recommendation.

Option Assessment A Docker container on the DGX Chosen. The agent can run any command and can write only to its run directory On the laptop, through an SSH port forward Used for the first runs. It has no sandbox, so the agent was allowed no shell commands, and most skills need them Directly on the DGX No isolation from the Administrator's system. The assistant's own permission checks also refused to run an installer there

Claude made the choices inside the container: a pinned harness version, a non-root user whose files belong to the account that started the run, the skills mounted read-only, a placeholder credential, and the harness's optional network features turned off.

One of those choices is a known weakness. The container shares the host's network so that it can reach the model server. It is a filesystem sandbox, not a network sandbox.

docs.title: Context Length
docs.text:
Decided by: Claude. This choice did not hold up.

Option Assessment 64,000 tokens The minimum the model server's own guidance recommends for this harness 128,000 tokens Used for the first harness runs, without incident 256,000 tokens Chosen for the container runs. The harness assumes a window near 200,000 tokens, and a smaller one is silently truncated

With one model loaded and idle at this setting, its machine showed 66 GiB in use. A few minutes into that model's first long run, the machine stopped responding entirely and needed the Administrator. Memory exhaustion is the leading suspect and was not confirmed.

docs.title: Benchmark Definition
docs.text:
Decided by: The Primary Author chose the course and the scope. Claude chose the mechanics.

The Primary Author set the benchmark as Algebra I, limited to three skills: the learning graph, the chapter structure, and the chapter content.

Choice Alternative considered Why A fixed template and one fixed prompt per stage Interactive runs Every model must start from identical input Prompts carry a standing answer to approval questions Answering by hand Nobody is present during a run, and a paused run measures nothing Each stage starts from a copy of the previous stage's output One long session for all stages Each stage gets its own timing and token counts, and its input is preserved Run output is kept outside the repository Committing results as they arrive Raw output holds local paths and has not been sanitized The published book is a reference for scale only Treating it as the baseline It was made with earlier skills, and no timings or token counts were kept

docs.title: Scoring
docs.text:
Decided by: Claude.

Option Assessment Structural checks by script Chosen for now. A program can verify that a graph has 200 concepts and no cycles A language model as judge It brings its own biases, and it would send the generated text to a cloud service Human review against a rubric The right test of quality. It has not been done yet

A structural pass does not mean the content is good. No quality judgment has been made.

docs.title: Choices That Did Not Hold Up
docs.text:
• The 256,000-token context. It is the suspected cause of a machine freezing. A memory watchdog now runs before any model does.
  • Long runs on both units at once. When one unit froze, there was no idle machine to observe from, so the cause could not be seen as it happened.
  • Testing with reasoning off, then running with it on. The model tests predicted speeds that the harness runs did not match. One model spent nineteen minutes on a single turn, nearly all of it reasoning.
  • Dropping a model before the skill was fixed. The fastest model was set aside partly for broken navigation files. Those came from a faulty example in the skill, which has since been corrected. That model has not been retested.

docs.title: Evaluation Status
docs.text:
Last updated October 10, 2026, at 11:30 AM. Stages 2 and 3 are running, one model at a time. Model Results holds what each model produced.

Model Name Params Disk Space Used Learning Graph Book Structure Chapters Generated Automated Quality Score Human Quality Score qwen3.8:27b 27 B 17 GB ✅ — — — — gemma4:31b 30.7 B 20 GB ✅ — — — — muse-glimmer:30b 30 B 18 GB ❌ — — — — qwen3.6:35b 35 B 22 GB ✅ ✅ ✅ — — gemma4:26b 25.2 B 18 GB ✅ ✅ 10 of 14 — — nemotron-3.5-lightning:30b 30 B 25 GB ✅ — — — — mistral-medium-3.5:128b 128 B 160 GB ❌ — — — — gpt-oss:120b 117 B 65 GB ✅ — — — — devstral-small-2:24b 24 B 30 GB ❌ — — — — granite4.2:30b 30 B 17 GB ❌ — — — —

Six of the ten models have produced a learning graph. Two of them have been through all three stages: qwen3.6:35b wrote all eleven of its chapters, and gemma4:26b wrote ten of its fourteen. No quality score exists yet.

docs.title: How to Read the Table
docs.text:
• ✅ Done. The stage ran to the end and produced its output.
  • ❌ Not done. The stage was tried and failed, or could not be run.
  • A count, such as 10 of 14. The stage ended with only that many chapters written.
  • — Not started.

A green check records that a stage finished. It says nothing about how good the output is. The six learning graphs differ in quality, and First-Round Results lists what was wrong with each.

Four models have no learning graph, each for a different reason:

  • muse-glimmer:30b lost the task after a few steps.
  • mistral-medium-3.5:128b was not run. With the model loaded, no usable context length leaves enough memory free.
  • devstral-small-2:24b wrote its tool call as text, so nothing ran.
  • granite4.2:30b was stopped at the 150-minute limit with only the concept list written.

gemma4:26b ran once for each of its fourteen chapters and wrote ten of them. In three runs the skill's own check found that the chapter depended on concepts placed in later chapters, and the model stopped as the skill requires. That traces back to the chapter structure the same model designed in stage 2. In one run the model ended without writing anything.

docs.title: What Each Column Means
docs.text:
• Params. The total number of parameters, in billions, as the publisher states it. Model Candidates also gives the number active for each token, for the models that use only part of their parameters at a time.
  • Disk Space Used. The space the model takes on the unit used for the first round. Two models, mistral-medium-3.5:128b and devstral-small-2:24b, are on disk in two variants, the standard one and one in llama.cpp format, so each takes twice its download size. Together the ten models take about 397 GB.
  • Learning Graph. Stage 1. The model runs the learning-graph-generator skill on the Algebra I course description. It is done when the run ends on its own and leaves a learning graph as both a CSV file and a JSON file.
  • Book Structure. Stage 2. The model runs the book-chapter-generator skill to design the chapters from its own learning graph.
  • Chapters Generated. Stage 3. The model runs the chapter-content-generator skill once for each chapter. A chapter counts as written when its placeholder is gone and it has at least 1,000 words.
  • Automated Quality Score. A score a program computes from the output. No score has been defined yet. Each model's section in Model Results has a learning graph quality report and a page of chapter metrics, but they have not been combined into one number.
  • Human Quality Score. A person's judgment of whether the content is correct and worth reading. Nobody has reviewed any output yet.

docs.title: What Is Left
docs.text:
• Stages 2 and 3. Four of the six models with a learning graph still have to run them. The run of gemma4:31b was cut short when the second DGX unit stopped responding a few minutes in, so that model has no stage 2 result yet.
  • Repeated runs. Every test so far has been run once, so nobody knows whether a model gives a comparable result the second time.
  • Scoring. The automated score has to be defined, and a person has to review the output.
  • A cloud baseline. The same book has not yet been generated by a cloud service for comparison.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
This page records the setup steps this evaluation actually performed, in the order they were done. By the end, a laptop can open a shell on the DGX with no password prompt, and you know what hardware and software the DGX has.

Every step ends with a test. Run the test before moving on, so a failure shows up at the step that caused it.

Placeholders, not real values

This site is public, so every address, hostname, and login on this page is a placeholder: 100.x.y.z, <dgx-host>, and <user>. Substitute the values your administrator gives you, and never copy your real ones into a file you plan to publish.

docs.title: What You Need
docs.text:
• A laptop with Miniforge installed. These steps were run on macOS, and they are the same on Linux.
  • A user account on the DGX, created by its administrator.
  • An invitation to the administrator's tailnet, or a share of the DGX into your own tailnet.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the dgx Conda Environment
docs.text:
The tools for reaching the DGX live in their own conda environment named dgx. Keeping them separate from the environment that builds this book means neither one can break the other.

Tailscale comes from conda-forge as two packages. tailscale is the command-line client, and tailscaled is the daemon the client talks to. The client does nothing without the daemon, so install both, at the same version.

conda create -n dgx -c conda-forge tailscale tailscaled
conda activate dgx

Activate the environment in every new terminal before you use these tools.

Test: both commands print the same version number.

tailscale version
tailscaled --version

docs.title: Step 2: Start the Daemon and Join the Tailnet
docs.text:
The daemon creates a network interface, which requires administrator rights on the laptop. sudo discards the conda PATH, so give it the full path to the binary. Run this in its own terminal tab and leave it running.

sudo "$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/tailscaled"

In a second tab, with dgx activated, join the tailnet.

tailscale up

The command prints a login URL. Open it and sign in with the account the administrator invited. Signing in with a different account joins a different tailnet, and the DGX will not appear.

Test: the DGX is listed next to your laptop.

tailscale status

100.x.y.z   <laptop-name>   <you>@     macOS   -
100.x.y.z   <dgx-host>      <admin>@   linux   -

docs.title: Step 3: Log In Once with Your Password
docs.text:
Connect with ordinary SSH, using the DGX's tailnet address. Linux login names are case-sensitive, so type yours exactly as the administrator created it.

ssh <user>@100.x.y.z

The first connection asks you to accept the DGX's host key. Compare the fingerprint it shows with the one your administrator reports before you answer yes. Then enter your password.

Test: you see the DGX login banner and a shell prompt on the DGX. Type exit to return to the laptop.

You do not need tailscale set --ssh on the laptop

That command turns on the Tailscale SSH server on the machine where it runs. It belongs on the DGX, and only if the administrator chooses Tailscale SSH. A DGX that accepts ordinary OpenSSH logins over the tailnet, as this one does, needs nothing extra on either side.

docs.title: Step 4: Switch to Key-Based Login
docs.text:
Scripts, benchmark runners, and AI agents cannot type a password. An SSH key lets them log in unattended. Create one on the laptop, then install its public half on the DGX.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519

ssh-copy-id <user>@100.x.y.z

ssh-copy-id asks for your password one last time. If you are evaluating more than one DGX, repeat it for each address.

Test: the command below prints the DGX's hostname without prompting. BatchMode makes SSH fail instead of asking for a password, which is exactly what an unattended script needs.

ssh -o BatchMode=yes <user>@100.x.y.z hostname

A key with no passphrase is a password in a file

Leaving the passphrase empty is what allows unattended logins, and it also means the private key file alone is enough to reach the DGX. Keep ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 on the laptop, never commit it, and tell the administrator that you installed a key on their machine.

docs.title: Step 5: Take a Read-Only Inventory
docs.text:
Before installing anything, find out what the DGX already has. These commands change nothing and need no administrator rights.

ssh <user>@100.x.y.z '
  grep -E "^(NAME|VERSION)=" /etc/os-release
  uname -srm
  lscpu | grep -E "^(Architecture|CPU\(s\)|Model name)"
  free -h
  df -h /
  nvidia-smi
  docker --version
  python3 --version
  id -nG
'

Some system files contain identifiers

On DGX OS, /etc/dgx-release includes the unit's serial number. Filter it out with grep -v SERIAL /etc/dgx-release, and read any captured output before you save or share it.

The two units in this evaluation reported identical configurations:

Component Result System DGX Spark-class desktop, aarch64 Operating system DGX OS 7.4 on Ubuntu 24.04, Linux kernel 6.17 CPU 20 Arm cores: 10 Cortex-X925 and 10 Cortex-A725 Memory 128 GB unified memory, shared by the CPU and the GPU Storage 1 TB NVMe SSD, about 780 GB free GPU NVIDIA GB10, Blackwell architecture, 6,144 CUDA cores GPU software NVIDIA driver 580, CUDA 13.0 Containers Docker 29.1 with NVIDIA Container Toolkit 1.18 Python 3.12, with pip and venv Build tools gcc, cmake, git, curl Model runtimes None installed

The inventory commands do not report the GPU's core count. The 6,144 figure comes from NVIDIA's published DGX Spark hardware overview, and it is the one row in this table that was looked up, not measured.

On this system nvidia-smi reports GPU memory as Not Supported. The GPU has no memory of its own: it shares the system's unified memory with the CPU. Read memory use from free -h on a unified-memory system, not from nvidia-smi.

Test: nvidia-smi lists a GPU, and you can state the memory, free disk space, and CUDA version without guessing.

docs.title: Step 6: Ask for Docker Access
docs.text:
The inventory's last line, id -nG, lists the groups your account belongs to. At first this account was in no group but its own, so every Docker command failed with permission denied. Only the administrator can change that, with one command on each DGX:

sudo usermod -aG docker <user>

Membership in the docker group is equivalent to administrator access on that machine, so this is the administrator's decision to make. The change applies to new logins.

Test: docker appears in your groups, and Docker answers without an error.

ssh <user>@100.x.y.z 'id -nG; docker ps'

docs.title: Where This Leaves You
docs.text: The laptop reaches the DGX over an encrypted tailnet, logs in without a password, and can run containers. The DGX has a GPU, CUDA, and plenty of free disk, and no model or inference server yet. Choosing and installing those is the next step of the evaluation.

docs.title: Model Candidates
docs.text:
These are the ten open-weight models most worth testing for textbook generation on this hardware: one DGX unit with 128 GB of unified memory. They are listed in the order they were chosen for evaluation, before any results.

Model Parameters Main strength qwen3.8:27b 27 billion Built for long agent tasks; produced the cleanest learning graph, and took the longest gemma4:31b 30.7 billion, dense The most consistent rule-follower in the tests run so far muse-glimmer:30b 30 billion Top instruction-following and tool-use scores in its publisher's own comparison qwen3.6:35b 35 billion, about 3 billion active Agentic coding at mixture-of-experts speed, with reasoning carried across turns gemma4:26b 25.2 billion, 3.8 billion active The fastest model tested, three times quicker than its dense sibling nemotron-3.5-lightning:30b 30 billion, 3 billion active Designed for always-on agents, with a one-million-token context window mistral-medium-3.5:128b 128 billion, dense The largest dense model that fits, promoted for instruction and system-prompt adherence gpt-oss:120b 117 billion, 5.1 billion active The largest model that still runs fast on one unit devstral-small-2:24b 24 billion A coding-agent model with a 384,000-token window in the smallest download granite4.2:30b about 30 billion, dense Structured output and tool calling under a plain Apache 2.0 license

The benchmark tests two abilities above all others. The first is following a detailed skill: a SKILL.md file that can run past a thousand lines, with reference documents, templates, and scripts beside it that the model must find and use at the right step. The second is tool calling: reading files, writing files, and running commands through the harness, correctly, dozens of times in one session.

The order was set before testing: the four models with early results first, then the models whose publishers make claims closest to those two abilities. All ten have since been through a first round on one unit, and each section ends with what happened. A first round is one run of each test, so every result here is provisional. Claims attributed to a publisher come from that publisher's own page as of October 2026 and have not been checked.

docs.title: 1. qwen3.8:27b
docs.text:
This model produced the cleanest result of the first benchmark stage, the learning graph for Algebra I. Its graph had exactly 200 concepts and 299 dependencies with no cycles and no duplicate labels, every expected file was present, the JSON matched the CSV, and the resulting site passed a strict build. It made 55 tool calls and one failed.

Its publisher describes it as improved for long-running agent work, planning, and handling feedback from tools, which is a description of running a skill. In the model-only tests it followed every formatting rule.

The reason to keep evaluating it is its cost in time. That stage took 102 minutes, where the five other models that finished took between 6 and 22. The server re-read almost the whole conversation on every turn, and one turn ran for nineteen minutes, nearly all of it reasoning. Both need investigating before the longer stages.

Download: 17 GB. Context window: 256,000 tokens. License: reported as Apache 2.0, not yet verified. Status: tested through stage 1.

docs.title: 2. gemma4:31b
docs.text:
No other model has been as consistent. It passed every rule in the model-only tests, twice, and every one of its four analyzer smoke runs ended with a correct result and a site that builds. It is a dense model, so every parameter takes part in every token, and it still generated 28 to 40 tokens per second.

Its publisher gives it built-in function calling and a 256,000-token window. In one published comparison it scored within a point of the leader on an instruction-following benchmark.

Its first attempt at the learning graph was lost when a machine froze, at a context setting that is now treated as unsafe. The second attempt, at a smaller context, finished in 21 minutes with a 200-concept graph, no cycles, and no duplicate labels. It left out two things the skill asks for: the concept taxonomy page and the navigation entries. Eight of its 50 tool calls failed.

Download: 20 GB. Context window: 256,000 tokens. License: Apache 2.0. Status: tested through stage 1.

docs.title: 3. muse-glimmer:30b
docs.text:
This model is aimed at exactly what the benchmark measures. Its publisher, Meta, describes it as built for local agents that run unattended, and stresses recovery: a model that diagnoses a failed step and retries instead of stopping. A long skill run with nobody watching needs that.

Meta's published comparison puts it first among three similar-sized models on an instruction-following benchmark and on a tool-use benchmark, and first on a long-context test at 128,000 tokens. The same table shows it behind qwen3.6:27b on several coding benchmarks, so the claim is specific to following instructions and using tools.

It also accepts images, which matters for reviewing MicroSim screenshots.

First-round result. It did not complete either harness test. After a few steps it lost the task and answered with a greeting. The cause looks like context: its first prompt took 35,000 tokens where the other models took 17,000 to 21,000, and within eight turns it was at 120,000, the edge of its window. In the model-only test it ran at 13 tokens per second and returned invalid JSON on the structured-output task.

Download: 18 GB. Context window: 128,000 tokens. License: Apache 2.0. Status: tested; failed in the harness.

docs.title: 4. qwen3.6:35b
docs.text:
This is the release before qwen3.8, in a larger mixture-of-experts form. A mixture-of-experts model uses only a few billion parameters for each token, and on this hardware that was worth a threefold speed gain in the one direct comparison made so far.

Its publisher highlights agentic coding and a new option to keep reasoning from earlier turns, which should help on a skill with many steps. If qwen3.8:27b stays slow, this model is the natural test of whether the same family can do the work faster.

The parameter split is taken from a chart name on its page and is not stated in the text.

First-round result. It was the best combination of speed and correctness. It ran at 83 to 105 tokens per second, passed the analyzer smoke test in 65 seconds, and finished the learning graph in 22 minutes with every file present, the navigation updated, and a site that builds. The graph is looser than the one from qwen3.8:27b: 19 concepts have no prerequisite, where that model had 2, and five labels run past the length limit. Its conversation peaked at 135,000 tokens, the second largest of any run.

Download: 22 GB. Context window: 256,000 tokens. License: not stated on its page. Status: tested through stage 1.

docs.title: 5. gemma4:26b
docs.text:
This is the fastest model tested: 86 to 130 tokens per second, and it read a 30,000-token prompt in ten seconds. It finished the skill smoke test in about a minute, where others took three to eleven.

It was set aside for two reasons, and one of them no longer holds. Its skill runs produced a navigation file that would not build, but that error was copied from a faulty example in the skill, which has since been corrected. The other reason stands: in the model-only tests it twice broke two rules, omitting the blank line before a list and writing a p5.js call that fails when run.

Retested against the corrected skill, it passed the analyzer smoke test in 57 seconds, and it finished the learning graph in under six minutes. That graph has a serious flaw: 40 of its 200 concept labels are duplicates. It also left out the index page and the navigation entries. A model this fast can afford a second attempt at a step, but something has to notice that one is needed.

Download: 18 GB. Context window: 256,000 tokens. License: Apache 2.0. Status: tested through stage 1.

docs.title: 6. nemotron-3.5-lightning:30b
docs.text:
This model comes from NVIDIA, which also makes the hardware. Its publisher describes it as the execution layer for always-on agents and claims four times the throughput of comparable open models. With 3 billion active parameters, high speed on this machine is plausible.

Its context window is one million tokens on the main download. A skill with many reference files can use a long window, though on unified memory a long context competes directly with everything else.

It accepts text only, so it cannot review screenshots. Its page states no license.

First-round result. It was as fast as claimed, at 84 to 105 tokens per second, and it finished the learning graph in 18 minutes. It got there the long way: 140 tool calls, nearly three times as many as any other model, and a conversation that peaked at 147,000 tokens. The graph has 199 concepts, one short of the 200 asked for, and the navigation was not updated. In the model-only test it broke four formatting rules, and its analyzer report left out the score in the frontmatter.

Download: 25 GB. Context window: 1,000,000 tokens. License: not stated on its page. Status: tested through stage 1.

docs.title: 7. mistral-medium-3.5:128b
docs.text:
This is the test of whether size helps. It is a dense model more than four times larger than gemma4:31b, and its publisher names instruction following and system-prompt adherence as headline strengths. A harness works by giving the model a long system prompt, so that claim bears directly on the benchmark. It also supports function calling, JSON output, and image input.

Expect it to be slow. A dense model reads all of its weights for every token, and this one is 80 GB. It also leaves little room: after the weights, less than 50 GB remain for the context and the system, which probably rules out the largest context settings.

Its license allows commercial use with exceptions for companies with large revenue, which should be read before relying on it.

First-round result. It loaded and ran, at 3 tokens per second. It used 88 GiB of memory at a 32,000-token context, so no context of 64,000 tokens or more would fit, and the harness tests were not run. On one unit of this hardware it is not a usable choice.

Download: 80 GB. Context window: 256,000 tokens. License: modified MIT. Status: tested; not usable on one unit.

docs.title: 8. gpt-oss:120b
docs.text:
This is the largest model that still ran at a usable speed: 38 to 44 tokens per second from 117 billion parameters, because only about 5 billion are active for each token. Its publisher released it with function calling, structured output, and adjustable reasoning effort.

Its results here were mixed, and that is the reason to test it further. In one of two skill runs it printed a tool call as plain text and stopped after a single turn. In the model-only tests it twice returned the wrong value from a 24,000-token prompt. A model that misreads a long prompt is a poor fit for long skills, but two runs are not enough to settle it.

It used 69 GB of memory at a modest context, which leaves less room than the smaller models have.

First-round result. It finished the learning graph in 17 minutes, and all 28 of its tool calls succeeded. Every file was present and the navigation was updated. The graph itself is thin: 180 dependencies for 200 concepts, with 19 concepts connected to nothing. In the analyzer smoke test it wrote its navigation entries into the wrong part of the site configuration, and the site no longer built. It also returned the wrong value from the long prompt for a third time.

Download: 65 GB. Context window: 128,000 tokens. License: Apache 2.0. Status: tested through stage 1.

docs.title: 9. devstral-small-2:24b
docs.text:
This model was built to drive software-engineering agents: exploring a set of files, editing several of them, and calling tools along the way. A skill run is the same kind of work, with Markdown where the code would be.

It has a 384,000-token context window, the second largest on the list, in the smallest download. Its publisher reports 65.8% on a widely used software-engineering benchmark.

The open question is prose. Nothing on its page speaks to long-form writing, and a textbook is mostly prose. It is most likely to earn a place on the code that MicroSims need.

First-round result. It did no work in either harness test. Both times it wrote its first tool call as plain text, the harness saw no tool call, and the run ended after one turn. In the model-only test it ran at 15 tokens per second and worked the example at the wrong precision.

Download: 15 GB. Context window: 384,000 tokens. License: Apache 2.0. Status: tested; failed in the harness.

docs.title: 10. granite4.2:30b
docs.text:
This model is the conservative choice. Its publisher, IBM, lists tool calling, general instruction following, structured JSON output, and reasoning that can be switched on or off for each request. The learning-graph stage depends on exact structured output, and the benchmark has already shown how much time uncontrolled reasoning can cost.

Its license is Apache 2.0 with no added conditions, and its page describes governance and compliance checks on its training data. For a reader who must justify a model choice to an employer, those points can matter more than a benchmark score.

Its page gives no benchmark results, and its context window is among the smallest here.

First-round result. It was too slow to finish. It ran at 12 tokens per second, took eleven minutes over the analyzer smoke test, and was stopped at the 150-minute limit on the learning graph, having reached only the concept list. Its analyzer report was written, but the navigation was not updated.

Download: 17 GB. Context window: 128,000 tokens. License: Apache 2.0. Status: tested; too slow to finish.

docs.title: Other Qualities That Matter for a Textbook
docs.text:
Following a skill and calling tools decide whether a run finishes. These qualities decide whether the result is worth reading.

  • Long-form writing at a set reading level. A course description names its audience. Chapters for grade 9 and chapters for engineers need different sentences, and a model has to hold that level across tens of thousands of words.
  • Faithfulness to the course description. The description lists what the course covers and what it excludes. A model that drifts outside those limits produces a different book.
  • Dependency reasoning. A learning graph orders 200 concepts so that each comes after the ones it depends on. That is a reasoning task, and an error in it carries into every chapter.
  • Exact structured output. The pipeline passes CSV, JSON, and YAML between stages. One malformed file stops the next stage.
  • Markdown that builds. A missing blank line before a list, or a wrong indent in a navigation file, breaks the site. Most of the failed skill runs in this evaluation failed this way.
  • Code that runs. MicroSims are JavaScript programs. Code that looks right and fails in the browser is worse than no simulation.
  • Mathematical notation. A mathematics or science book needs correct formulas in the notation the site renders.
  • Vision. Checking a MicroSim's layout means looking at a screenshot. Only models that accept images can do that step.
  • Speed in a long session. Generation speed is half the story. A harness resends a growing conversation on every turn, so the speed of reading a prompt, and whether the server reuses what it has already read, can dominate.
  • Memory left for context. On unified memory, a long context takes memory from the same pool as the weights. A smaller model with a long context can need more memory than a larger model with a short one.
  • Control over reasoning. Reasoning can improve a hard step and waste minutes on an easy one. A model whose reasoning can be limited is easier to budget.
  • Repeatability. Two runs of the same stage should give comparable results. Scores that differ from run to run make a model hard to depend on.
  • License. A recommendation is only useful if readers are allowed to follow it, and if they can publish what the model writes.

docs.title: Models Left Off the List
docs.text:
• laguna-s-2.1 has 118 billion parameters and a strong published score on a terminal-agent benchmark. Its page gives two different download sizes, 75 GB and 96 GB, and at the larger one there is too little memory left for a long context.
  • qwen3.5:122b is the largest Qwen model that fits. It is older than qwen3.8, and gpt-oss:120b already covers the large mixture-of-experts tier.
  • qwen3-coder:30b was a strong coding-agent model with a 256,000-token window. It is about a year old, and newer Qwen releases have replaced it.
  • nemotron3:33b is aimed at understanding video, audio, and documents, which this benchmark does not use.
  • Models that need more than one unit, and models offered only as a cloud service, are outside what this evaluation tests.

docs.title: Testing Architecture
docs.text:
This page shows how the evaluation was wired: one laptop, two home networks, the internet between them, and two DGX systems. Step through the diagram to see which machine does each job.

Run the Testing Architecture MicroSim Fullscreen

Placeholders, not real values

The diagram leaves out every address, hostname, and login, and it calls the machines "DGX unit A" and "DGX unit B". A published architecture diagram should show how the parts connect, never how to reach them.

docs.title: Three Roles, Three Places
docs.text:
The evaluation separates three jobs that are easy to confuse.

Role What fills it Where it runs Orchestrator A Claude Code session using a cloud model The laptop Harness Claude Code as the agent loop, in a Docker container Each DGX Model An open-weight model served by Ollama Each DGX GPU

The orchestrator starts runs, watches them, and scores the output. The harness loads a skill, sends prompts to the model, and runs the tools the model asks for. The model generates every token of the textbook.

docs.title: Inside Each DGX
docs.text:
Both units have the same hardware. The disks hold different models.

Component DGX unit A DGX unit B CPU 20 Arm cores 20 Arm cores GPU NVIDIA GB10, 6,144 CUDA cores NVIDIA GB10, 6,144 CUDA cores Memory 128 GB unified, shared by CPU and GPU 128 GB unified, shared by CPU and GPU Disk 1 TB NVMe 1 TB NVMe Models on disk qwen3.8:27b (17 GB), gpt-oss:120b (65 GB) gemma4:26b (18 GB), gemma4:31b (20 GB)

The GPU has no memory of its own. Ollama loads a model from disk into unified memory, and the GPU works on it there. Model weights and the conversation context compete for the same 128 GB that the CPU and every other program use.

A 200 Gb/s link joins the two units. The evaluation did not combine them: each unit ran its own model independently.

docs.title: What Crosses Each Boundary
docs.text:
The reason to run a model locally is to control where data goes. This table lists what each outside party could see.

Party What it sees When Tailscale coordination server Machine identities, public keys, and addresses When a machine joins or reconnects Home routers and Tailscale relay Encrypted WireGuard packets Whenever the laptop talks to a DGX Model registry Requests for model files Once, at download Software sources Requests for the container image and installer Once, when the container was built Claude API The orchestrator's commands and everything it reads back Throughout Nobody outside the DGX Generation prompts and generated tokens During the generation loop, once the harness ran on the DGX

Two rows need care. First, the orchestrator is a cloud model. Whatever it reads to monitor or score a run, including generated text, goes to the Claude API. The generation loop is local; the supervision of it was not.

Second, the harness was configured to send its model requests only to Ollama on the same machine, with a placeholder credential and its optional network features turned off. That configuration was not confirmed with a packet capture.

docs.title: Two Arrangements of the Harness
docs.text:
The harness ran in two places during the evaluation. The last step of the diagram shows the earlier one.

  • First runs: harness on the laptop. Claude Code ran on the laptop and reached Ollama through an SSH port forward inside the tunnel. Prompts and tokens crossed the tailnet, encrypted, on every turn.
  • Later runs: harness on the DGX. Claude Code moved into a Docker container on each DGX. The harness and the model then talked over the machine's own loopback interface, and a run kept going with the laptop disconnected.

The container also limits what the agent can change. Inside it the agent may run any command, and the only places it can write are its own run directory and its transcript folder.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text:
This is the list of chapters in DGX Evaluation for Textbook Generation. Each chapter has its own folder under docs/chapters/ with a two-digit numeric prefix (for example, 01-introduction/).

Chapters are added by the book-chapter-generator skill once the learning graph is complete; their content is filled in by the chapter-content-generator skill.

docs.title: Learning Graph
docs.text:
The learning graph captures how concepts in DGX Evaluation for Textbook Generation depend on each other. It is a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) — every concept has a path back to one or more foundational concepts that have no prerequisites.

Once the learning-graph-generator skill runs, this section will be populated with:

  • Course Description Assessment — quality review of course-description.md
  • Concept Enumeration — the ~200 concepts the book will cover
  • Concept Taxonomy — concepts grouped into 8–12 categories
  • Graph Quality Analysis — DAG structure, foundational and terminal nodes
  • Taxonomy Distribution — concept count per taxonomy category

Use the book-installer skill (option 23) to add an interactive graph viewer once learning-graph.json exists.

docs.title: Overall Score
docs.text:
100 / 100 — Excellent. Ready for learning graph generation.

The description was written against this rubric in the same session, so a full score is expected and says only that every required element is present. The open decisions listed under Gap Analysis are not measured by the rubric and matter more than the score.

Descriptive Context 5 5 Five-paragraph overview plus a software-stack table. Total 100 100

docs.title: Gap Analysis
docs.text:
No rubric element scored below full points.

Decided: the course is DGX-model-agnostic. The author confirmed on 2026-10-09 that no specific DGX model is named. The description states this in the overview and in the hardware topic. The consequence for downstream content is that the conda, probe, and model-fit chapters must cover both x86_64 and aarch64 CPUs and both dedicated GPU memory and unified memory, with the probe report deciding which branch a reader follows.

Added: sanitization before publication. On 2026-10-09 the author asked for a sanitization topic, because the book is public and the tested DGX is a real machine. Topic 16 and one outcome at each of the Remember, Understand, Apply, and Evaluate levels cover it. The probe-suite outcome now redacts identifying fields by default, and the capstone sanitizes every artifact before publishing.

Three decisions are still open. None of them blocks concept enumeration, but each one changes specific chapters.

  1. The model and harness lists are candidates, not selections. The software-stack table names model families and four agent harnesses as examples. Whether each harness loads the ibook-skills skills unmodified against a local endpoint has not been tested and is itself part of the evaluation.
  2. The cloud baseline is not fixed. Four cloud services are named for the pros-and-cons discussion. The benchmark needs one specific model and harness as the quality reference.
  3. The benchmark book is not chosen. The capstone generates "a small intelligent textbook". The subject and size of that book determine run time and cost per chapter.

docs.title: Improvement Suggestions
docs.text:
Listed in order of impact on downstream content.

  1. Pick the cloud baseline (one model, one harness) and add it to the Objective evaluation methodology topic.
  2. Choose the benchmark book and record its subject, target concept count, and chapter count.
  3. After the first probe run, replace the model-family examples with the shortlisted models that fit the measured GPU memory.

docs.title: Concept Generation Readiness
docs.text:
The description has enough breadth and depth to generate well over 200 concepts. The estimate below counts the distinct terms, tools, commands, metrics, and procedures each topic names or implies.

The Bloom's Taxonomy outcomes cover all six levels with concrete artifacts at the Create level (probe suite, model-fit calculator, install script, benchmark runner, cost model, and evaluation report), so the concept list should include procedures and deliverables as well as definitions.
