docs.title: What the Columns Mean
docs.text:
• Written. The chapter's placeholder is gone and it has at least 1,000 words. A chapter marked No is still the outline from stage 2.
  • Words. Every word in the chapter file after its frontmatter, including tables and diagram specifications.
  • Diagrams. The number of #### Diagram headings. Each one is a specification for a diagram or MicroSim to be built later.
  • Reading grade. The Flesch-Kincaid grade level: the United States school grade at which a reader should follow the text. Algebra I is usually taught in grade 9.
  • Reading ease. The Flesch reading-ease score. Higher is easier; 60 to 70 is plain English.
  • Words per sentence. The average sentence length.
  • Lists that will not render. Lists with no blank line before them, which the site shows as a run-on paragraph.
  • Links removed. Links to pages that do not exist. They were removed from this copy so that the site builds, and their text was kept. The chapter list page had 14 more.

The three reading measures come from analyze-reading-levels.py in the book-installer skill, which uses the textstat package. It strips formatting first, but tables and diagram specifications still count as prose, so a chapter with many of them scores as harder than its sentences are. The whole-book figure is the average of the written chapters. Chapters that were not written have no reading measures.

docs.title: Algebra I
docs.text: Course Title: Algebra I Target Audience: Junior High or High School Students (Grades 8–10) Prerequisites: Successful completion of Pre-Algebra or equivalent foundational mathematics course, including proficiency in arithmetic operations, fractions, decimals, ratios, and basic geometry.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
Algebra I is a foundational mathematics course designed to transition students from arithmetic reasoning to abstract algebraic thinking. This course introduces variables, functions, and relationships among quantities, emphasizing the ability to represent real-world situations using mathematical models. Students will develop fluency in manipulating algebraic expressions, solving equations and inequalities, analyzing patterns, and interpreting data.

Algebra I serves as the gateway to higher-level mathematics such as Geometry, Algebra II, Trigonometry, and Calculus. Students will explore both symbolic and graphical representations of relationships and will use technology and reasoning to analyze linear, quadratic, and exponential functions. The course encourages mathematical communication, critical thinking, and problem-solving, aligning with the Common Core State Standards for Mathematics (CCSSM) and the National Council of Teachers of Mathematics (NCTM) recommendations.

docs.title: Intended Audience
docs.text: This course is intended for students who are beginning formal study in algebra, typically in Grades 8 through 10. It provides essential preparation for college- and career-readiness by building the quantitative reasoning skills required in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) disciplines.

docs.title: 1. Algebra Foundations
docs.text:
• Properties of operations and order of operations
  • Writing, expanding, and factoring algebraic expressions
  • Evaluating expressions with variables and exponents

docs.title: 2. Exponents and Radicals
docs.text:
• Integer and rational exponents
  • Laws of exponents
  • Simplifying and interpreting exponential expressions

docs.title: 3. Linear Equations and Inequalities
docs.text:
• Solving one-step, two-step, and multi-step equations
  • Literal equations and formulas
  • Solving and graphing linear inequalities and absolute value equations

docs.title: 4. Functions and Relations
docs.text:
• Understanding the function concept
  • Function notation, domain, and range
  • Interpreting graphs and tables
  • Piecewise and step functions

docs.title: 5. Linear Relationships
docs.text:
• Slope and rate of change
  • Writing linear equations in multiple forms (slope-intercept, point-slope, standard)
  • Graphing lines and modeling linear relationships
  • Solving and interpreting systems of linear equations and inequalities

docs.title: 6. Polynomials and Factoring
docs.text:
• Adding, subtracting, and multiplying polynomials
  • Factoring by GCF, trinomials, and difference of squares
  • Using factoring to solve quadratic equations

docs.title: 7. Quadratic and Exponential Functions
docs.text:
• Graphing quadratic functions and identifying vertex and axis of symmetry
  • Solving quadratics by factoring, square roots, completing the square, and the quadratic formula
  • Modeling real-world data using quadratic and exponential functions

docs.title: 8. Statistics and Data Analysis
docs.text:
• Creating and interpreting data displays and scatterplots
  • Analyzing correlation and line of best fit
  • Comparing linear and exponential models
  • Arithmetic and geometric sequences

docs.title: Concepts Not Included
docs.text:
• Calculus
  • Integrals
  • Derivatives

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text: After this course, students will be able to:

docs.title: Remembering
docs.text:
• Recall and apply key algebraic properties (commutative, associative, distributive)
  • Identify the components of expressions, equations, and inequalities
  • Recognize linear, quadratic, and exponential forms

docs.title: Understanding
docs.text:
• Explain the meaning of variables, constants, coefficients, and exponents
  • Describe relationships between graphical, tabular, and symbolic representations
  • Interpret slope and intercepts in context of real-world problems

docs.title: Applying
docs.text:
• Solve linear, quadratic, and exponential equations using multiple methods
  • Model real-world problems with algebraic equations and functions
  • Apply rules of exponents and factoring in simplifying expressions

docs.title: Analyzing
docs.text:
• Compare characteristics of linear, quadratic, and exponential functions
  • Decompose complex expressions into simpler components
  • Analyze the effects of changing parameters on graphs of functions

docs.title: Evaluating
docs.text:
• Justify solutions to equations and systems through substitution and verification
  • Evaluate the appropriateness of mathematical models in context
  • Critically assess data to determine correlation and causation

docs.title: Creating
docs.text:
• Construct new equations or inequalities to represent unfamiliar problems
  • Design and interpret linear and quadratic models from real data
  • Integrate algebraic methods to solve multi-step, multi-concept problems

docs.title: Alignment to Common Core Domains
docs.text: Domain Description A-SSE (Seeing Structure in Expressions) Interpret, simplify, and factor expressions A-APR (Arithmetic with Polynomials) Perform operations on polynomials A-CED (Creating Equations) Create and solve equations and inequalities to model real situations A-REI (Reasoning with Equations and Inequalities) Understand and solve equations and systems logically F-IF (Interpreting Functions) Understand functions and their representations F-BF (Building Functions) Write, transform, and compose functions F-LE (Linear, Quadratic, and Exponential Models) Model growth and decay phenomena S-ID (Statistics and Probability) Analyze data using scatterplots, correlation, and regression

docs.title: Course Outcomes Summary
docs.text:
By the end of Algebra I, students will be able to:

  • Translate real-world scenarios into algebraic representations.
  • Use graphs, tables, and equations to model and analyze data.
  • Solve and interpret linear, quadratic, and exponential equations and inequalities.
  • Reason quantitatively, verify solutions, and communicate mathematical thinking clearly.
  • Build confidence and curiosity for further study in mathematics and STEM disciplines.

Standards Alignment: Aligned with the Common Core State Standards for Mathematics (CCSSM), High School Algebra and Functions Domains.

docs.title: Algebra Foundations
docs.text: To begin our journey into algebra, we must first understand the language used to describe mathematical relationships. In arithmetic, we work with concrete numbers: \( 5 + 3 = 8 \). However, real-world situations are often more complex. We might know that a taxi charges a flat fee plus a rate per mile, but we don't know exactly how many miles a passenger will travel. Algebra allows us to use symbols to represent these unknown quantities, creating a mathematical "template" that can be applied to any specific case.

docs.title: Variables, Constants, and Coefficients
docs.text:
In algebra, we use symbols to represent numbers that can change or are not yet known. These symbols are called variables. For example, in the expression \( 3x + 5 \), the letter \( x \) is a variable. It acts as a placeholder for any value we choose to plug into the expression.

A constant is a value that does not change. In the same expression, the number \( 5 \) is a constant because its value remains fixed regardless of what \( x \) is. Constants provide the fixed points or starting values in our mathematical models.

When a number is multiplied by a variable, it is called a coefficient. In the term \( 3x \), the number \( 3 \) is the coefficient of \( x \). It tells us how many "copies" of the variable we have. For instance, if \( x \) represents the number of apples, \( 3x \) represents three times that number of apples.

docs.title: Diagram: Anatomy of an Algebraic Expression
docs.text:
Anatomy of an Expression

Type: diagram sim-id: algebraic-expression-anatomy Library: mermaid Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: describe Learning Objective: The learner will describe the role of variables, constants, and coefficients in a given algebraic expression.

Prerequisites: None

Evidence of Mastery: The learner can correctly label the variable, constant, and coefficient in a new expression like \( -7y + 12 \).

Misconceptions: Confusing a coefficient with a constant, or thinking a variable must always be \( x \).

Instructional Rationale: Visualizing the components of an expression helps anchor the abstract terminology to a concrete structure.

Content: - Expression: \( 3x + 5 \) - Coefficient: \( 3 \) - Variable: \( x \) - Constant: \( 5 \) - Term: \( 3x \) and \( 5 \)

Provenance: Illustrative

Rules: A term is separated from others by addition or subtraction.

Learner Activity: 1. Observe the diagram of \( 3x + 5 \). 2. Identify the parts. 3. Apply the identification to a new expression.

Feedback: If the learner identifies \( 5 \) as a coefficient, explain that \( 5 \) is not attached to a variable.

Starting State: An image showing \( 3x + 5 \) with arrows pointing to its parts.

Chapter Anchors: variables, constants, coefficients, terms, expressions

docs.title: Terms and Expressions
docs.text:
An expression is a mathematical phrase that combines numbers, variables, and operation symbols (like \( +, -, \times, \div \)). For example, \( 4y - 7 \) is an expression. It represents a value, but it does not state an equality or inequality.

Within an expression, individual parts separated by addition or subtraction are called terms. For example, in the expression \( 2x + 9y - 4 \), there are three terms: \( 2x \), \( 9y \), and \( -4 \). Terms can be single numbers, single variables, or a combination of both.

docs.title: Evaluating Expressions
docs.text:
Evaluating an expression means finding its numerical value by replacing the variables with specific numbers. This is a fundamental skill in algebra, allowing us to move from a general rule to a specific result.

Worked Example: Evaluating an Expression

Let's evaluate the expression \( 5x - 3 \) for \( x = 4 \).

  1. Substitute the value of the variable: Replace \( x \) with \( 4 \). [ 5(4) - 3 ]
  2. Simplify using the order of operations: [ 20 - 3 ] [ 17 ]

So, when \( x = 4 \), the value of the expression is \( 17 \).

docs.title: Order of Operations
docs.text:
When an expression contains multiple operations, we must follow a specific order to ensure everyone reaches the same result. Without a standardized order, an expression like \( 2 + 3 \times 4 \) could be interpreted as \( 20 \) (if adding first) or \( 14 \) (if multiplying first). To prevent this ambiguity, we use the order of operations, often remembered by the mnemonic PEMDAS.

  1. Parentheses: Perform operations inside parentheses or brackets first.
  2. Exponents: Calculate powers and roots.
  3. Multiplication and Division: Perform these from left to right.
  4. Addition and Subtraction: Perform these from left to right.

docs.title: Worked Example: Applying PEMDAS
docs.text:
Evaluate the expression: \( 10 + (6 - 2)^2 \div 2 \)

  1. Parentheses: Solve inside the parentheses first. [ (6 - 2) = 4 ] The expression becomes: \( 10 + 4^2 \div 2 \)
  2. Exponents: Calculate the power. [ 4^2 = 16 ] The expression becomes: \( 10 + 16 \div 2 \)
  3. Division: Perform the division. [ 16 \div 2 = 8 ] The expression becomes: \( 10 + 8 \)
  4. Addition: Final step. [ 10 + 8 = 18 ]

The final result is \( 18 \).

docs.title: Algebraic Reasoning
docs.text: Algebraic reasoning involves using mathematical properties to manipulate and simplify expressions. These properties are the rules of the "game," allowing us to rewrite expressions in more useful forms without changing their underlying value.

docs.title: The Distributive Property
docs.text:
One of the most important tools in algebra is the distributive property. It states that multiplying a sum by a number is the same as multiplying each addend by that number and then adding the products. This property is essential for expanding expressions and solving equations.

Formally: \( a(b + c) = ab + ac \)

Worked Example: Using the Distributive Property

Simplify the expression: \( 3(2x + 5) \)

  1. Distribute the \( 3 \) to the first term: \( 3 \times 2x = 6x \).
  2. Distribute the \( 3 \) to the second term: \( 3 \times 5 = 15 \).
  3. Combine the results: \( 6x + 15 \).

The simplified expression is \( 6x + 15 \).

docs.title: Exponents
docs.text:
An exponent represents how many times a number, called the base, is used as a factor in a multiplication. Exponents provide a powerful way to express very large or very small numbers concisely.

For example, in \( 5^3 \): - \( 5 \) is the base. - \( 3 \) is the exponent (or power).

This is shorthand for \( 5 \times 5 \times 5 \), which equals \( 125 \). If the exponent were 1, it would just be \( 5 \). If it were 0, it would be 1 (for any non-zero base).

docs.title: Rules of Exponents
docs.text: Exponents follow specific laws that allow us to simplify complex expressions involving powers. These laws are foundational for higher-level math like calculus.

docs.title: Diagram: Visualizing Exponents
docs.text:
Visualizing Exponents

Type: diagram sim-id: exponent-visual-growth Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: describe Learning Objective: The learner will describe the relationship between the base and the exponent through a visual growth model.

Prerequisites: Algebra Foundations

Evidence of Mastery: The learner correctly predicts whether changing the exponent from 2 to 3 will increase or decrease the growth rate in a multiple-choice question.

Misconceptions: Thinking \( 5^3 \) means \( 5 \times 3 \).

Instructional Rationale: A visual representation of repeated multiplication helps differentiate between linear and exponential scaling.

Content: - Base: 2 - Exponent: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 - Visual: A growing area or number of dots.

Provenance: Synthetic

Rules: - Base \( b > 0 \) - Exponent \( n \) increases by 1 each step.

Learner Activity: 1. Observe the growth of the visual element. 2. Change the base from 2 to 3. 3. Notice the difference in speed of growth.

Feedback: If the learner expects linear growth, show the mathematical difference between \( 2n \) and \( 2^n \).

Starting State: A small square representing \( 2^1 \).

Chapter Anchors: base, exponent, power

docs.title: Worked Example: Simplifying with Exponent Laws
docs.text:
Simplify: \( (x^3)(x^4) \)

According to the Product Rule of Exponents, when multiplying terms with the same base, you add the exponents: \( x^a \cdot x^b = x^{a+b} \).

  1. Identify the base: The base is \( x \).
  2. Add the exponents: \( 3 + 4 = 7 \).
  3. Result: \( x^7 \).

docs.title: Linear Inequalities
docs.text: An inequality is a mathematical statement that compares two values, indicating if one is greater than, less than, or equal to another. Unlike equations, which describe a specific point of balance, inequalities describe a range of possibilities. We use symbols like \( < \) (less than), \( > \) (greater than), \( \leq \) (less than or equal to), and \( \geq \) (greater than or equal to).

docs.title: Solving Inequalities
docs.text:
Solving an inequality is very similar to solving an equation, with one critical difference: when you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, you must reverse the inequality sign. This is because multiplying by a negative number flips the order of numbers on the number line.

Worked Example: Solving a Two-Step Inequality

Solve: \( 2x - 4 > 6 \)

  1. Add 4 to both sides to isolate the term with \( x \): [ 2x > 10 ]
  2. Divide by 2 on both sides: [ x > 5 ]

The solution is all numbers greater than 5.

docs.title: Absolute Value Equations
docs.text:
The absolute value of a number, denoted by \( |x| \), is its distance from zero on a number line. Because distance is never negative, the absolute value is always zero or positive. For example, \( |-5| = 5 \) and \( |5| = 5 \).

An absolute value equation asks us to find the values that satisfy a certain distance. Because a distance can be in either direction, these equations often have two solutions.

Example: To solve \( |x| = 3 \), we look for numbers that are exactly 3 units away from zero. Those numbers are \( 3 \) and \( -3 \).

docs.title: Function Concept
docs.text:
A function is a special relationship where each input (often called \( x \)) is associated with exactly one output (often called \( f(x) \) or \( y \)).

Think of a function like a machine: you put something in, the machine performs a specific rule, and it spits out exactly one result. If you put in the same input twice, you must get the same output both times.

docs.title: Domain and Range
docs.text:
To fully describe a function, we need to know what numbers it can accept and what numbers it can produce.

  • The domain is the set of all possible input values. It's like the "menu" of things you can feed the function.
  • The range is the set of all possible output values. It's the collection of all results the function can produce.

docs.title: Diagram: The Function Machine
docs.text:
Function Machine Mapping

Type: diagram sim-id: function-mapping-diagram Library: mermaid Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: describe Learning Objective: The learner will describe the relationship between input, output, domain, and range using a mapping diagram.

Prerequisites: Algebra Foundations

Evidence of Mastery: The learner can identify the domain and range from a provided mapping diagram.

Misconceptions: Thinking an input can have two different outputs.

Instructional Rationale: Mapping diagrams are the standard way to visualize the one-to-one or many-to-one nature of functions.

Content: - Set A (Domain/Input) - Set B (Range/Output) - Mapping arrows

Provenance: Illustrative

Rules: Each element in Set A must have exactly one arrow pointing to an element in Set B.

Learner Activity: 1. Observe the arrows connecting inputs to outputs. 2. Identify which elements belong to the domain. 3. Identify which elements belong to the range.

Feedback: If the learner identifies an input with two outputs, explain that this violates the definition of a function.

Starting State: A mapping diagram with 3 inputs and 2 outputs.

Chapter Anchors: function, input, output, domain, range

docs.title: Worked Example: Evaluating a Function
docs.text:
Given the function \( f(x) = 2x + 1 \), find \( f(3) \).

  1. Substitute \( 3 \) for \( x \): [ f(3) = 2(3) + 1 ]
  2. Simplify: [ f(3) = 6 + 1 = 7 ]

So, \( f(3) = 7 \).

docs.title: Piecewise Functions
docs.text:
A piecewise function is a function that is defined by different rules for different parts of its domain. Instead of one single formula, it uses a collection of formulas, each applied only to a certain interval of \( x \).

For example, a function might use one formula if \( x \) is negative and a different formula if \( x \) is positive. This allows us to model more complex, real-world behaviors that change abruptly.

docs.title: Systems of Linear Equations
docs.text:
A system of linear equations consists of two or more equations with the same set of variables. The solution to the system is the set of values that makes all equations in the system true at the same time.

Graphically, if you draw the lines for both equations, the solution is the point where the lines intersect.

docs.title: Worked Example: Solving by Substitution
docs.text:
Solve the system: 1) \( y = 2x \) 2) \( x + y = 9 \)

  1. Substitute the first equation into the second: Since \( y = 2x \), replace \( y \) in the second equation with \( 2x \). [ x + (2x) = 9 ]
  2. Solve for \( x \): [ 3x = 9 ] [ x = 3 ]
  3. Find \( y \) by substituting \( x = 3 \) back into the first equation: [ y = 2(3) = 6 ]

The solution is \( (3, 6) \).

docs.title: Linear Inequalities Systems
docs.text: A system of linear inequalities is a set of two or more inequalities. Unlike a system of equations, which usually has a single point as a solution, a system of inequalities has an entire region of solutions. This region is the area on a graph where the shaded areas of all inequalities overlap.

docs.title: Factoring Quadratic Equations
docs.text:
Factoring is the process of breaking down an expression into a product of simpler expressions. For a quadratic equation like \( x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0 \), factoring means finding two expressions that multiply to give the quadratic.

In this case, \( (x - 2)(x - 3) = 0 \). This tells us that the original equation is true if either \( x - 2 = 0 \) or \( x - 3 = 0 \), which leads to the solutions \( x = 2 \) or \( x = 3 \).

docs.title: Solving by Square Roots
docs.text:
If an equation is in the form \( x^2 = a \), we can solve it by taking the square root of both sides. Because squaring a negative number also results in a positive number, we must account for both possibilities.

Example: To solve \( x^2 = 16 \), take the square root of both sides: [ x = \pm \sqrt{16} ] [ x = 4 \text{ or } x = -4 ]

docs.title: Comparing Function Models
docs.text: As we progress, we will learn to compare different types of mathematical models. For instance, a linear model grows at a constant rate, resulting in a straight line on a graph. In contrast, an exponential model grows by a constant percentage, creating a curve that becomes progressively steeper. Being able to distinguish between these models is crucial for making accurate predictions in science and economics.

docs.title: Arithmetic Sequences
docs.text:
An arithmetic sequence is a list of numbers where the difference between any two consecutive terms is constant. This constant difference is called the common difference.

Example: \( 2, 5, 8, 11, \dots \) Here, the common difference is \( 3 \).

docs.title: Worked Example: Finding a Term
docs.text:
Find the 10th term of the sequence \( 5, 9, 13, 17, \dots \)

  1. Identify the first term (\( a_1 \)): \( a_1 = 5 \)
  2. Identify the common difference (\( d \)): \( d = 4 \)
  3. Use the formula \( a_n = a_1 + (n-1)d \): [ a_{10} = 5 + (10-1)4 ] [ a_{10} = 5 + 9(4) ] [ a_{10} = 5 + 36 = 41 ]

The 10th term is \( 41 \).

docs.title: Arithmetic Means
docs.text: Arithmetic means are the terms that sit between two given numbers in an arithmetic sequence. For example, in the sequence \( 2, 4, 6, 8 \), the numbers \( 4 \) and \( 6 \) are the arithmetic means between \( 2 \) and \( 8 \).

docs.title: Detailed Content
docs.text: To master algebra, we must first master its language. Before we can solve complex problems, we need to understand how to represent ideas and how those ideas behave under different operations.

docs.title: Symbolic Representation
docs.text:
In algebra, we don't just use numbers; we use symbols to represent patterns and relationships. Symbolic representation is the practice of using letters, numbers, and operators to express mathematical ideas concisely. Instead of writing "the sum of a number and five," we use the much simpler \( x + 5 \). This allows us to work with general rules that apply to any number.

Worked Example: Translating Phrases to Symbols

Let's practice translating verbal descriptions into symbolic forms:

  1. "Five less than a number \( n\)"

    • The phrase "less than" indicates subtraction.
    • "A number \( n \)" is our variable.
    • Symbolic form: \( n - 5 \)

  2. "The product of three and a number \( y \)"

    • "Product" indicates multiplication.
    • Symbolic form: \( 3y \)

  3. "A number \( z \) squared, increased by ten"

    • "Squared" means an exponent of 2.
    • "Increased by" indicates addition.
    • Symbolic form: \( z^2 + 10 \)

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
At the heart of symbolic representation are variables. A variable is a symbol (usually a letter like \( x, y, \) or \( n \)) that acts as a placeholder for a value that can change or is currently unknown.

When we say \( x = 5 \), we are assigning a specific value to that variable. When we say "for any value of \( x \)," we are treating it as a dynamic placeholder. Variables allow us to write formulas, such as the area of a circle, \( A = \pi r^2 \), where \( r \) can be any radius.

Worked Example: Evaluating a Variable

If we have the expression \( 7x - 3 \) and we are told that \( x = 4 \), we can find the value of the expression by substituting the variable with the given number.

  1. Substitute \( 4 \) for \( x \): [ 7(4) - 3 ]
  2. Multiply: [ 28 - 3 ]
  3. Subtract: [ 25 ]

So, when \( x = 4 \), the expression \( 7x - 3 \) equals \( 25 \).

docs.title: Power of an Exponent
docs.text:
When we multiply a number by itself multiple times, we use exponents to simplify the notation. In the expression \( b^n \), \( b \) is the base (the number being multiplied) and \( n \) is the exponent (the number of times the base is used as a factor).

For example, \( 2^4 \) means \( 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 \), which equals \( 16 \).

Worked Example: Applying the Power Rule

Consider the expression \( (x^3)^2 \). According to the power of a power rule, when you raise a power to another power, you multiply the exponents: \( (a^m)^n = a^{m \cdot n} \).

  1. Identify the exponents: \( 3 \) and \( 2 \).
  2. Multiply them: \( 3 \times 2 = 6 \).
  3. Result: \( x^6 \).

docs.title: Cube Roots
docs.text:
If exponents allow us to grow numbers quickly, roots allow us to work backward. A cube root is the value that, when multiplied by itself three times, gives the original number. We denote this as \( \sqrt[3]{x} \).

For example, the cube root of \( 27 \) is \( 3 \) because \( 3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27 \).

Worked Example: Finding Cube Roots

Find the value of \( \sqrt[3]{-125} \).

  1. Recognize the sign: Since we are dealing with an odd root (a cube root), we can have a negative result from a negative input.
  2. Find the base: What number multiplied by itself three times is \( 125 \)? Since \( 5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125 \), the base is \( 5 \).
  3. Apply the sign: Because the input was \( -125 \), the result is \( -5 \).

Checking our work: \( (-5) \times (-5) \times (-5) = 25 \times (-5) = -125 \).

docs.title: Two-Step Equations
docs.text:
An equation is a mathematical statement that two expressions are equal, indicated by an equals sign (\( = \)). A two-step equation is an equation that requires two distinct inverse operations to isolate the variable.

To solve these, we follow the principle of performing the same operation on both sides of the equation to maintain balance, typically undoing addition or subtraction first, and then undoing multiplication or division.

Worked Example: Solving \( 3x + 7 = 22 \)

  1. Step 1: Undo addition. Subtract \( 7 \) from both sides: [ 3x + 7 - 7 = 22 - 7 ] [ 3x = 15 ]
  2. Step 2: Undo multiplication. Divide both sides by \( 3 \): [ \frac{3x}{3} = \frac{15}{3} ] [ x = 5 ]

docs.title: Diagram: The Balance of an Equation
docs.text:
Solving Two-Step Equations

Type: diagram sim-id: two-step-equation-solver Library: mermaid Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: solve Learning Objective: The learner will solve a two-step equation by following the correct sequence of inverse operations.

Prerequisites: Variables, Algebraic Expressions

Evidence of Mastery: The learner can correctly identify whether to add/subtract or multiply/divide first in a given equation and reaches the correct solution.

Misconceptions: Attempting to multiply before undoing addition, or only performing the operation on one side of the equation.

Instructional Rationale: A flow diagram reinforces the algorithmic nature of solving equations and highlights the "balance" required.

Content: - Start: Equation \( ax + b = c \) - Step 1: Subtract \( b \) from both sides - Intermediate: \( ax = c - b \) - Step 2: Divide by \( a \) - End: \( x = (c - b)/a \)

Provenance: Illustrative

Rules: - Maintain equality by doing the same to both sides. - Undo addition/subtraction before multiplication/division.

Learner Activity: 1. Observe the flow of operations. 2. Apply the steps to a new equation. 3. Verify the result by substituting back.

Feedback: If the learner tries to divide first, show how the constant term would also need to be divided, making it more complex.

Starting State: An equation \( 3x + 7 = 22 \).

Chapter Anchors: two-step equations, inverse operations, balance

docs.title: Absolute Value Equations
docs.text:
The absolute value of a number, denoted by \( |x| \), represents its distance from zero on a number line. Because distance is always non-negative, \( |x| \) is always \( \geq 0 \). An absolute value equation is an equation where the variable is inside absolute value bars.

Solving these requires considering two cases: one where the expression inside the bars is positive, and one where it is negative.

Definition: To solve \( |A| = B \), you must solve both \( A = B \) and \( A = -B \).

docs.title: Multi-Step Inequalities
docs.text:
An inequality describes a relationship where one expression is greater than, less than, or not equal to another. A multi-step inequality requires multiple operations to isolate the variable, similar to two-step equations.

The most important rule to remember is: If you multiply or divide both sides of an inequality by a negative number, you must reverse the inequality sign.

For example, if \( -2x < 10 \), dividing by \( -2 \) gives \( x > -5 \).

docs.title: Domain of a Function
docs.text:
As we saw in Chapter 2, a function is a rule that assigns each input to exactly one output. The domain of a function is the complete set of all possible input values (the \( x \)-values) for which the function is defined and produces a real number output.

In many real-world functions, the domain is restricted. For instance, if a function models the height of a ball over time, the domain cannot include negative time.

Worked Example: Finding the Domain

Consider the function \( f(x) = \frac{10}{x - 3} \).

We need to find which values of \( x \) would make this function "break." In mathematics, dividing by zero is undefined. Therefore, the denominator cannot be zero.

  1. Set the denominator to zero: [ x - 3 = 0 ]
  2. Solve for \( x \): [ x = 3 ]
  3. Identify the restriction: Since \( x = 3 \) makes the denominator zero, it cannot be in the domain.
  4. State the domain: The domain is all real numbers except \( x = 3 \).

docs.title: Rate of Change
docs.text:
The rate of change describes how one quantity changes in relation to another. In the context of linear functions, the rate of change is constant and is known as the slope. It tells us how much the output \( y \) changes for every one-unit increase in the input \( x \).

Worked Example: Calculating Slope from Two Points

If a car travels from position \( y = 10 \) miles to position \( y = 50 \) miles in \( x = 4 \) hours, what is its rate of change?

  1. Identify the points: \( (x_1, y_1) = (0, 10) \) and \( (x_2, y_2) = (4, 50) \).
  2. Use the slope formula: \( m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} \).
  3. Substitute and calculate: [ m = \frac{50 - 10}{4 - 0} = \frac{40}{4} = 10 ]

The rate of change is \( 10 \) miles per hour.

docs.title: Scatterplots
docs.text:
In science and social studies, we often collect data from many different observations. A scatterplot is a graph where each data point is plotted as a single dot representing two variables. Scatterplots are powerful tools for identifying patterns, such as trends or correlations, in a set of data.

Worked Example: Interpreting a Scatterplot

Imagine a scatterplot showing the relationship between "Hours Studied" (x-axis) and "Test Score" (y-axis). If the dots generally move from the bottom-left to the top-right, we can infer a positive relationship: as study time increases, test scores also tend to increase.

docs.title: Piecewise Functions
docs.text:
Most real-world relationships don't follow a single, smooth rule. A piecewise function is a function that is defined by different rules (sub-functions) for different intervals of the input.

For example, a cellular data plan might cost a flat fee of \( \$30 \) for up to 5GB of data, but then charge an additional \( \$10 \) for every extra GB used. This change in pricing rule creates a "break" or a change in the function's behavior at the 5GB mark.

docs.title: Elimination Method
docs.text:
When we have a system of linear equations, we are looking for the point where both equations are true. The elimination method is a technique used to solve these systems by adding or subtracting the equations to "eliminate" one of the variables.

Worked Example: Solving by Elimination

Solve the system: 1) \( 2x + y = 10 \) 2) \( 3x - y = 5 \)

  1. Align the variables: The equations are already aligned.
  2. Add the equations: Notice that \( y \) and \( -y \) will cancel out if we add the two equations together. [ (2x + y) + (3x - y) = 10 + 5 ] [ 5x = 15 ]
  3. Solve for \( x \): [ x = 3 ]
  4. Substitute back to find \( y \): Use the first equation. [ 2(3) + y = 10 ] [ 6 + y = 10 ] [ y = 4 ]

The solution is \( (3, 4) \).

docs.title: Exponential Growth
docs.text:
While linear functions change by a constant amount, exponential functions change by a constant percentage or ratio. This leads to exponential growth, where the quantity increases more and more rapidly as time goes on.

A classic example is compound interest in a bank account or the spread of a virus in a population.

Worked Example: Calculating Exponential Growth

A population of bacteria starts with 100 cells and doubles every hour. How many cells will there be after 4 hours?

  1. Identify the initial amount (\( a \)): \( a = 100 \).
  2. Identify the growth factor (\( b \)): Since it doubles, \( b = 2 \).
  3. Identify the time (\( x \)): \( x = 4 \).
  4. Apply the formula \( y = a \cdot b^x \): [ y = 100 \cdot 2^4 ] [ y = 100 \cdot 16 = 1600 ]

After 4 hours, there will be 1,600 bacteria.

docs.title: Geometric Sequences
docs.text:
A sequence is an ordered list of numbers. In a geometric sequence, each term is found by multiplying the previous term by a fixed, non-zero number called the common ratio (\( r \)).

Example: \( 3, 6, 12, 24, \dots \) Here, the common ratio is \( 2 \).

docs.title: Geometric Mean
docs.text:
The geometric mean is a specific type of average used for sets of numbers that are being multiplied or grow exponentially. Unlike the arithmetic mean (which adds numbers), the geometric mean is found by multiplying the numbers together and then taking the \( n \)-th root.

For two numbers \( a \) and \( b \), the geometric mean is \( \sqrt{a \cdot b} \).

Worked Example: Finding the Geometric Mean

Find the geometric mean of \( 4 \) and \( 16 \).

  1. Multiply the numbers: \( 4 \times 16 = 64 \).
  2. Take the square root (since there are two numbers): \( \sqrt{64} = 8 \).

The geometric mean is \( 8 \). Note that \( 8 \) is the middle term in the geometric sequence \( 4, 8, 16 \).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: In this chapter, we have expanded our algebraic toolkit. We learned how to express ideas symbolically, how to handle the power of exponents, and how to solve both linear and absolute value equations. We explored the diverse behavior of functions, from the steady climb of linear rates of change to the explosive speed of exponential growth. Finally, we saw how sequences and means help us understand patterns of growth. These tools form the foundation for the advanced mathematical modeling you will encounter in higher-level courses.

This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Algebra Foundations and Basic Operations

docs.title: Building Blocks: Constants and Coefficients
docs.text: To work effectively with algebra, we must first understand the different types of numbers that make up mathematical expressions. These are the fundamental units from which all complex equations and functions are constructed.

docs.title: Constants
docs.text:
A constant is a value that does not change. In an algebraic expression, constants provide a fixed reference point. Unlike variables, which can take on many different values, a constant remains exactly what it is throughout any calculation.

Constants can appear in many different forms. They might be simple integers like \( 5 \) or \( -12 \), or they might be fractions like \( \frac{3}{4} \). They can also be irrational numbers that have infinite, non-repeating decimals, such as \( \pi \) (approximately \( 3.14159 \)) or \( \sqrt{2} \). No matter how much the rest of the expression changes, the constant is "constant."

Worked Example: Identifying Constants

Let's examine three different expressions to find the constants:

  1. Expression: \( 7x + 5 \)
  2. Here, \( x \) is the variable.

  3. The number \( 5 \) is the constant because its value is always five.

  4. Expression: \( y - \frac{2}{3} \)

  5. The variable is \( y \).

  6. The constant is \( -\frac{2}{3} \).

  7. Expression: \( 4a^2 + \pi \)

  8. The variable is \( a \).
  9. The constant is \( \pi \).

docs.title: Coefficients
docs.text:
A coefficient is a numerical or constant quantity placed before and multiplying a variable in an algebraic expression. It tells us "how many" of the variable we have.

The coefficient essentially acts as a multiplier. In the term \( 6x \), the number \( 6 \) is the coefficient of \( x \). This tells us that we are taking the value of \( x \) and multiplying it by six.

It is important to remember two special cases: 1. The Invisible One: When a variable appears alone, such as \( y \), its coefficient is implicitly \( 1 \). Similarly, \( -z \) has a coefficient of \( -1 \). 2. Fractional Coefficients: A coefficient can be a fraction, such as \( \frac{1}{2}x \), meaning we are taking half of the value of \( x \).

Worked Example: Finding Coefficients

Identify the coefficients in the following expressions:

  1. \( -12m \)
  2. The coefficient is \( -12 \).
  3. \( \frac{5}{8}k \)
  4. The coefficient is \( \frac{5}{8} \).
  5. \( w + 10 \)
  6. The coefficient of \( w \) is \( 1 \).
  7. \( -p \)
  8. The coefficient of \( p \) is \( -1 \).

docs.title: Exponents and Roots
docs.text: Once we understand the building blocks, we can explore how numbers can be scaled and transformed using exponents and roots. These operations allow us to express very large or very small quantities efficiently.

docs.title: Integer Exponents
docs.text:
An exponent (also called a power) indicates how many times a base is multiplied by itself. When we use integer exponents, we are dealing with whole numbers (positive, negative, or zero) as our powers.

The expression \( b^n \) tells us to take the base \( b \) and multiply it by itself \( n \) times.

The Rules of Exponents:

  1. Positive Exponents: If \( n > 0 \), then \( b^n \) is \( b \) multiplied by itself \( n \) times.
  2. Example: \( 3^4 = 3 \times 3 \times 3 \times 3 = 81 \)
  3. Zero Exponent: If \( n = 0 \) and \( b \neq 0 \), then \( b^0 = 1 \). This rule is vital for simplifying complex expressions.
  4. Example: \( 525^0 = 1 \)
  5. Negative Exponents: If \( n < 0 \), then \( b^n = \frac{1}{b^{-n}} \). A negative exponent indicates the reciprocal of the base raised to the positive version of that exponent. It is a way of saying "divide by the base this many times."
  6. Example: \( 2^{-3} = \frac{1}{2^3} = \frac{1}{8} \)

Worked Example: Calculating with Integer Exponents

Solve the following:

  1. \( 10^3 \)
  2. \( 10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1,000 \)
  3. \( ( \frac{2}{3} )^0 \)
  4. Any non-zero number to the power of zero is \( 1 \).
  5. \( 6^{-2} \)
  6. \( \frac{1}{6^2} = \frac{1}{36} \)

docs.title: Exponential Decay
docs.text:
Exponential decay is a process where a quantity decreases at a rate proportional to its current value. This often results in the quantity getting smaller and smaller, approaching zero but never quite reaching it. In algebra, we model this using a base between 0 and 1.

The "decay factor" is the base of the exponent. If a quantity decreases by \( 20\% \), the decay factor is \( 1 - 0.20 = 0.80 \).

Worked Example: Modeling Decay

Imagine you have \( 500 \) mg of a substance in a lab, and it decays by \( 15\% \) every hour. This means \( 85\% \) (or \( 0.85 \)) remains each hour.

The amount remaining after \( t \) hours can be modeled by: [ A(t) = 500(0.85)^t ]

  • After 1 hour: \( 500(0.85)^1 = 425 \) mg
  • After 2 hours: \( 500(0.85)^2 = 361.25 \) mg

docs.title: nth Roots
docs.text:
The nth root of a number is a value that, when multiplied by itself \( n \) times, equals the original number. This is the inverse operation of raising a number to the \( n^{th} \) power.

Worked Example: Finding Roots

  1. Square Root (\( n=2 \)): \( \sqrt{144} = 12 \) (since \( 12 \times 12 = 144 \))
  2. Cube Root (\( n=3 \)): \( \sqrt[3]{125} = 5 \) (since \( 5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125 \))
  3. Fifth Root (\( n=5 \)): \( \sqrt[5]{32} = 2 \) (since \( 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 32 \))

docs.title: Patterns and Statistics
docs.text: Beyond individual numbers, algebra helps us describe patterns in numbers and summarize large sets of data.

docs.title: Common Ratio
docs.text:
In a geometric sequence, a common ratio is the constant factor used to get from one term to the next. You can find it by dividing any term by the term before it.

Example: In the sequence \( 5, 15, 45, 135, \dots \), the common ratio is \( 3 \) because \( 15/5 = 3 \) and \( 45/15 = 3 \).

docs.title: Arithmetic Mean
docs.text:
The arithmetic mean (often simply called the "average") is a single value that represents the "center" of a set of numbers. To find it, add all the numbers in a set together and divide the sum by the total count of numbers in that set.

Example: The mean of \( 12, 15, \) and \( 21 \) is \( \frac{12+15+21}{3} = \frac{48}{3} = 16 \).

docs.title: Data Displays and Graphical Representation
docs.text: When we collect data, we use data displays to make patterns visible. A graphical representation is a visual way to show relationships, such as plotting points on a coordinate plane or using a chart.

docs.title: Functions and Linear Relationships
docs.text: Functions and linear equations allow us to model relationships between changing quantities.

docs.title: Slope-Intercept Form
docs.text:
A linear equation can be written in the slope-intercept form: [ y = mx + b ]

Where: - \( m \) is the slope, representing the "rise over run" (the rate of change). - \( b \) is the y-intercept, the point where the line crosses the vertical y-axis.

Worked Example: Graphing from an Equation

For the equation \( y = -\frac{2}{3}x + 5 \): 1. The y-intercept is \( 5 \), so start at the point \( (0, 5) \). 2. The slope is \( -\frac{2}{3} \), meaning "down 2, right 3". Move from \( (0, 5) \) to \( (3, 3) \).

docs.title: Range of a Function
docs.text:
When we talk about a function, we focus on two sets of values: the inputs (domain) and the outputs (range). The range is the set of all possible output values.

Example: For the function \( f(x) = |x| \), the range is all non-negative numbers (\( y \geq 0 \)) because an absolute value can never be negative.

docs.title: Step Functions
docs.text:
A step function is a piecewise function that consists of constant segments, creating a staircase-like appearance on a graph. These functions are useful for modeling things that change in discrete jumps, like postage rates or parking garage fees.

Example: If a parking garage charges $5 for the first hour and $10 for the second hour, the cost "jumps" at the one-hour mark.

docs.title: Equations and Systems
docs.text: Finally, we use algebra to solve for unknown values in complex situations.

docs.title: Multi-Step Equations
docs.text:
A multi-step equation is an equation that requires several algebraic operations (like combining like terms, using the distributive property, or moving variables) to isolate the variable.

To solve these, you must follow the "Golden Rule of Algebra": Whatever you do to one side of the equation, you must do to the other. This maintains the equality.

The Process of Solving:

  1. Simplify: Use the distributive property to remove parentheses and combine like terms on each side.
  2. Isolate the Variable Term: Use addition or subtraction to move all terms containing the variable to one side and all constant terms to the other.
  3. Solve for the Variable: Use multiplication or division to get the variable by itself.
  4. Verify: Plug your answer back into the original equation to ensure it works.

Worked Example: A Complex Multi-Step Equation

Solve for \( x \): [ 4(x - 3) + 2x = 2(x + 5) ]

  1. Simplify (Distribute): [ 4x - 12 + 2x = 2x + 10 ]
  2. Simplify (Combine Like Terms on the left): [ 6x - 12 = 2x + 10 ]
  3. Isolate (Subtract \( 2x \) from both sides): [ 4x - 12 = 10 ]
  4. Isolate (Add \( 12 \) to both sides): [ 4x = 22 ]
  5. Solve (Divide by 4): [ x = \frac{22}{4} = 5.5 ]

Equation Balance Simulator

Misconceptions: Performing an operation on only one side; incorrect sign when moving terms.

Instructional Rationale: A visual balance model makes the abstract concept of equality concrete.

Provenance: Synthetic

Learner Activity: 1. Observe the initial equation on the scale. 2. Choose an operation (e.g., "Subtract 5"). 3. Observe the scale adjusting. 4. Repeat until the variable is isolated.

Feedback: - Correct: "Balanced! The solution is \( x = \dots \)" - Incorrect: "The scale is unbalanced! Remember to do the same to both sides."

Starting State: An equation like \( 2x + 4 = 10 \).

docs.title: Graphing Inequalities
docs.text:
An inequality is a mathematical statement that compares two expressions, showing if one is less than, greater than, or not equal to the other. Graphing inequalities involves shading a region on a coordinate plane that represents all the possible solutions.

Definition: Graphing an inequality is the process of representing the set of all points that make an inequality true on a graph.

If the inequality is \( y > x \), we use a dashed line for the boundary. If it is \( y \geq x \), we use a solid line.

docs.title: Graphing Systems
docs.text:
A system of equations is a set of two or more equations that you deal with at the same time. The solution to the system is the point (or region) where the graphs of the equations overlap.

Worked Example: Finding the Intersection

Consider the system: 1. \( y = 2x - 1 \) 2. \( y = -x + 5 \)

  1. Graph the first line: Start at \( (0, -1) \) and use a slope of \( 2 \) (up 2, right 1).
  2. Graph the second line: Start at \( (0, 5) \) and use a slope of \( -1 \) (down 1, right 1).
  3. Find the intersection: The two lines cross at the point \( (2, 3) \).
  4. Solution: The solution to the system is the coordinate \( (2, 3) \).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from: - Chapter 1: Algebra Foundations and Basic Operations - Chapter 2: Algebraic Expressions and Functions - Chapter 4: Exponents and Mathematical Constants

In this chapter, we will move beyond basic arithmetic and begin to explore the structure of algebraic expressions. We will learn how to manipulate variables using the laws of exponents, how to describe complex relationships with polynomials, and how to use these tools to model real-world phenomena like growth and decay.

docs.title: Terms in an Expression
docs.text:
Before we can perform complex algebra, we must understand the fundamental building blocks of any algebraic expression. An algebraic expression is a mathematical phrase that can contain numbers, variables, and operation symbols.

The basic unit of an expression is called a term. A term can be a single number (called a constant), a single variable, or a combination of numbers and variables multiplied together. For example, in the expression \( 4x^2 - 3y + 7 \), the terms are \( 4x^2 \), \( -3y \), and \( 7 \). Note that the sign (positive or negative) is attached to the term.

docs.title: Worked Example: Identifying Terms
docs.text:
Consider the expression: [ 5a + 2b - 9 ]

  1. The first term is \( 5a \), which consists of the coefficient \( 5 \) and the variable \( a \).
  2. The second term is \( 2b \), consisting of the coefficient \( 2 \) and the variable \( b \).
  3. The third term is \( -9 \), which is a constant term.

Each of these terms is separated by an addition or subtraction sign.

docs.title: Combining Like Terms
docs.text:
Once we can identify individual terms, we can begin to simplify expressions by combining like terms.

Two or more terms are considered like terms if they have the exact same variables raised to the exact same exponents. The coefficients (the numbers in front of the variables) do not need to be the same. For instance, \( 7x^2 \) and \( -2x^2 \) are like terms, but \( 7x^2 \) and \( 7x \) are not, because the exponents are different.

docs.title: Worked Example: Simplifying an Expression
docs.text:
Simplify the following expression: [ 8x + 5y - 3x + 2y + 4 ]

Step 1: Group the like terms. [ (8x - 3x) + (5y + 2y) + 4 ]

Step 2: Combine the coefficients of the like terms. [ (8 - 3)x + (5 + 2)y + 4 ] [ 5x + 7y + 4 ]

The simplified expression is \( 5x + 7y + 4 \).

docs.title: Polynomials
docs.text:
We can now expand our view to a special class of expressions called polynomials. A polynomial is a mathematical expression made up of one or more terms, where each term consists of a coefficient multiplied by a variable raised to a non-negative integer power.

Polynomials are classified by the number of terms they contain: - Monomial: A polynomial with exactly one term (e.g., \( 5x^3 \)). - Binomial: A polynomial with exactly two terms (e.g., \( 2x + 3 \)). - Trinomial: A polynomial with exactly three terms (e.g., \( x^2 - 4x + 4 \)).

The degree of a polynomial is the highest exponent found in any of its terms. For example, in the polynomial \( 4x^3 - 2x + 7 \), the degree is 3.

docs.title: Worked Example: Adding Polynomials
docs.text:
When adding polynomials, we follow the same process as combining like terms.

Simplify: \( (3x^2 + 5x - 4) + (x^2 - 2x + 7) \)

Step 1: Remove the parentheses. [ 3x^2 + 5x - 4 + x^2 - 2x + 7 ]

Step 2: Group the like terms. [ (3x^2 + x^2) + (5x - 2x) + (-4 + 7) ]

Step 3: Combine the coefficients. [ 4x^2 + 3x + 3 ]

The sum is \( 4x^2 + 3x + 3 \).

docs.title: Product Rule of Exponents
docs.text:
When we multiply two powers that have the same base, we can simplify the result using the Product Rule of Exponents.

The rule states that for any non-zero base \( x \) and any exponents \( a \) and \( b \): [ x^a \cdot x^b = x^{a+b} ]

Essentially, when you multiply terms with the same base, you keep the base and add the exponents.

docs.title: Worked Example: Applying the Product Rule
docs.text:
Simplify: \( y^4 \cdot y^7 \)

Step 1: Identify the base and the exponents. Base: \( y \) Exponents: \( 4 \) and \( 7 \)

Step 2: Apply the rule by adding the exponents. [ y^{4+7} ] [ y^{11} ]

The simplified result is \( y^{11} \).

docs.title: Exponential Base
docs.text:
In an exponential expression, the base is the number that is being multiplied by itself multiple times. The number of times it is multiplied is known as the exponent.

For example, in the expression \( 5^3 \), the number 5 is the base, and 3 is the exponent. This means \( 5^3 = 5 \cdot 5 \cdot 5 = 125 \).

docs.title: Worked Example: Identifying the Base
docs.text:
Identify the base and exponent in the following expression: [ 10^6 ]

  • Base: 10
  • Exponent: 6

The expression represents 10 multiplied by itself 6 times.

docs.title: Rational Exponents
docs.text:
Sometimes, we encounter exponents that are not whole numbers. These are called rational exponents. A rational exponent is a fraction, and it represents a combination of a power and a root.

The rule for rational exponents is: [ x^{m/n} = \sqrt[n]{x^m} ]

In this notation, \( n \) is the index of the root, and \( m \) is the power.

docs.title: Worked Example: Simplifying a Rational Exponent
docs.text:
Simplify: \( 27^{2/3} \)

Step 1: Rewrite the expression using the radical form. [ \sqrt[3]{27^2} \quad \text{or} \quad (\sqrt[3]{27})^2 ]

Step 2: Calculate the cube root first (it is usually easier). The cube root of 27 is 3 (because \( 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 = 27 \)). [ (3)^2 ]

Step 3: Square the result. [ 3^2 = 9 ]

The simplified value of \( 27^{2/3} \) is 9.

docs.title: Simplifying Radicals
docs.text:
To work with roots more efficiently, we often need to simplify radicals. Simplifying a radical means rewriting it so that the number under the radical sign (the radicand) has no perfect power factors.

For example, \( \sqrt{12} \) can be simplified because 12 has a perfect square factor, 4.

docs.title: Worked Example: Simplifying a Square Root
docs.text:
Simplify: \( \sqrt{50} \)

Step 1: Find the largest perfect square factor of 50. The factors of 50 are 1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50. The largest perfect square is 25.

Step 2: Rewrite the radical as a product. [ \sqrt{25 \cdot 2} ]

Step 3: Apply the product rule for radicals. [ \sqrt{25} \cdot \sqrt{2} ] [ 5\sqrt{2} ]

The simplified form is \( 5\sqrt{2} \).

docs.title: Linear Inequalities
docs.text:
While equations tell us when two expressions are equal, linear inequalities tell us when one expression is greater than, less than, or equal to another.

A linear inequality uses one of the following symbols: - \( > \) : greater than - \( < \) : less than - \( \ge \) : greater than or equal to - \( \le \) : less than or equal to

docs.title: Example: A Simple Inequality
docs.text: The expression \( x + 5 > 10 \) means that the value of \( x \) plus 5 must be strictly larger than 10. Solving this, we find \( x > 5 \).

docs.title: Input and Output
docs.text:
In algebra, we often study how one quantity changes in response to another. This is the core of the concept of a function.

A function is a relationship where every input (the independent variable, often \( x \)) produces exactly one output (the dependent variable, often \( y \) or \( f(x) \)).

docs.title: Worked Example: Evaluating a Function
docs.text:
Given the function: [ f(x) = 3x - 2 ]

Find the output when the input is 4.

Step 1: Substitute the input value into the function. [ f(4) = 3(4) - 2 ]

Step 2: Perform the arithmetic. [ f(4) = 12 - 2 ] [ f(4) = 10 ]

When the input is 4, the output is 10.

docs.title: Point-Slope Form
docs.text:
When we want to write the equation of a straight line, there are several ways to do it. One of the most useful forms is the point-slope form.

The point-slope form of a linear equation is: [ y - y_1 = m(x - x_1) ]

Where: - \( m \) is the slope of the line. - \( (x_1, y_1) \) is a specific point on the line.

This form is particularly helpful when you know one point on the line and how steep the line is.

docs.title: Worked Example: Writing an Equation
docs.text:
Find the equation of the line that passes through the point (2, 5) and has a slope of 3.

Step 1: Identify the given values. \( m = 3 \) \( x_1 = 2 \) \( y_1 = 5 \)

Step 2: Substitute these into the point-slope formula. [ y - 5 = 3(x - 2) ]

The equation in point-slope form is \( y - 5 = 3(x - 2) \).

docs.title: Systems of Equations
docs.text: Sometimes, we need to find a value that satisfies two or more equations at the same time. This is known as a system of equations. The solution to the system is the point (or points) where the graphs of the equations intersect.

docs.title: Example: A Simple System
docs.text:
Consider this system: [ y = x + 1 ] [ y = 2x - 1 ]

To solve this, we can find where the two lines meet. By setting them equal to each other (\( x + 1 = 2x - 1 \)), we find that \( x = 2 \). Plugging \( x = 2 \) back into either equation gives \( y = 3 \). So the solution is the point (2, 3).

docs.title: Tabular Representation
docs.text: A tabular representation is a way to show the relationship between variables using a table. Each row in the table represents a pair of input and output values. This is a great way to organize data before graphing it or finding a mathematical model.

docs.title: Worked Example: Creating a Table
docs.text:
Create a table for the function \( f(x) = 2x + 3 \) for the inputs \( x = -1, 0, 1, 2 \).

Step 1: Calculate the output for each input. - For \( x = -1 \): \( f(-1) = 2(-1) + 3 = 1 \) - For \( x = 0 \): \( f(0) = 2(0) + 3 = 3 \) - For \( x = 1 \): \( f(1) = 2(1) + 3 = 5 \) - For \( x = 2 \): \( f(2) = 2(2) + 3 = 7 \)

Step 2: Organize into a table.

Input (\( x \)) Output (\( f(x) \)) -1 1 0 3 1 5 2 7

docs.title: Correlation
docs.text:
In statistics, we often look for patterns in how two variables change together. This relationship is called correlation.

If one variable increases as the other increases, they have a positive correlation. If one increases as the other decreases, they have a negative correlation. If there is no apparent pattern, they have no correlation.

docs.title: Worked Example: Identifying Correlation
docs.text:
Imagine you collect data on the number of hours spent studying and the test scores achieved by a group of students.

  • If students who study more tend to have higher scores, this is a positive correlation.
  • If students who study more tend to have lower scores (which is unlikely!), this would be a negative correlation.
  • If there is no relationship between study time and score, it is no correlation.

docs.title: Arithmetic Sequences
docs.text: A pattern of numbers can often be described using a mathematical sequence. An arithmetic sequence is a special kind of sequence where the difference between any two consecutive terms is always the same. This constant difference is called the common difference.

docs.title: Worked Example: Identifying an Arithmetic Sequence
docs.text:
Consider the following sequence: [ 5, 12, 19, 26, 33, \dots ]

Step 1: Find the difference between consecutive terms. - \( 12 - 5 = 7 \) - \( 19 - 12 = 7 \) - \( 26 - 9 = 7 \)

Step 2: Check if the difference is constant. Since the difference is always 7, this is an arithmetic sequence with a common difference of 7.

docs.title: Summary of Key Takeaways
docs.text: In this chapter, we have: - Learned to identify and manipulate terms and polynomials. - Explored the powerful laws of exponents, including the product rule and rational exponents. - Seen how linear relationships can be described using point-slope form and inequalities. - Started to explore how data can be modeled using tables, correlation, and sequences.

You will bridge the gap between integer exponents and radicals, explore polynomial operations, and deepen your understanding of functions and data relationships.

docs.title: Evaluating Expressions
docs.text:
In the study of algebra, variables serve as placeholders for numerical values that can change. To find the specific value of an algebraic expression, we perform a process called evaluation. This is a fundamental skill used by scientists and engineers to model real-world phenomena where specific conditions are known.

To evaluate an expression, you substitute the given numerical values for each variable and then simplify the resulting numerical expression by following the standard order of operations—often remembered by the acronym PEMDAS (Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication and Division, Addition and Subtraction). Precision is critical; even a small error in substitution or order can lead to an incorrect result.

Before we perform a complex calculation, let's review the systematic approach in the table below.

Step Action Description 1 Substitute Replace every variable with its given numerical value, using parentheses to maintain correct signs. 2 Simplify Exponents Calculate any terms raised to a power. 3 Multiply/Divide Perform all multiplication and division from left to right. 4 Add/Subtract Perform all addition and subtraction from left to right to find the final value.

docs.title: Worked Example: Multi-Step Evaluation
docs.text:
Suppose we are asked to evaluate the following expression: [ 5x^2 - 3(y + 4) + \frac{z}{2} ] when \( x = 3 \), \( y = -2 \), and \( z = 10 \).

  1. Substitute the values: We carefully place our numbers into the expression, using parentheses for the substitution of \( y \). [ 5(3)^2 - 3(-2 + 4) + \frac{10}{2} ]
  2. Simplify within parentheses: First, address the expression inside the parentheses. [ 5(3)^2 - 3(2) + \frac{10}{2} ]
  3. Evaluate exponents: Calculate the square of 3. [ 5(9) - 3(2) + \frac{10}{2} ]
  4. Perform multiplication and division: Execute these operations from left to right. [ 45 - 6 + 5 ]
  5. Final addition and subtraction: Combine the remaining terms. [ 39 + 5 = 44 ]

The evaluated value of the expression is \( 44 \).

docs.title: Power of a Power Rule
docs.text:
Exponents indicate how many times a base is multiplied by itself. While we are often familiar with single exponents, we frequently encounter situations where an entire power is raised to another exponent. This requires the application of the Power of a Power Rule.

The Power of a Power Rule states that to simplify an expression where a power is raised to another power, you must multiply the exponents together. Formally, for any non-zero base \( a \): [ (a^m)^n = a^{m \cdot n} ]

This rule is a logical consequence of the definition of exponents. For instance, if we consider \((x^2)^3\), we are essentially saying that \( x^2 \) is multiplied by itself three times: \((x^2) \cdot (x^2) \cdot (x^2)\). Since each \( x^2 \) represents \( x \cdot x \), the total product is \( x \cdot x \cdot x \cdot x \cdot x \cdot x \), which is \( x^6 \). Note that \( 2 \times 3 = 6 \).

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Problem: Simplify the expression \((w^4)^5\).

  1. Identify the exponents: The inner exponent is \( 4 \) and the outer exponent is \( 5 \).
  2. Apply the rule: According to the Power of a Power Rule, we multiply these exponents. [ w^{4 \cdot 5} ]
  3. Calculate the product: [ w^{20} ]

The simplified result is \( w^{20} \).

docs.title: Radical Expressions
docs.text:
In previous chapters, we focused on integer exponents. However, algebra also requires us to work with roots, which can be represented using radical expressions. A radical expression is any expression that contains a radical symbol (\(\sqrt{}\)).

A radical can be expressed in two mathematically equivalent ways: using the radical symbol or using a rational exponent. A radical with an index \( n \) and a radicand \( a \) is written as: [ \sqrt[n]{a} ] This is equivalent to the rational exponent form: [ a^{1/n} ]

The number \( n \) is called the index, which indicates the degree of the root. The value inside the radical, \( a \), is called the radicand. When the index is \( 2 \), it is a square root, and the index is typically omitted. When the index is \( 3 \), it is a cube root. For example, \(\sqrt[3]{27}\) or \( 27^{1/3} \) is equal to \( 3 \).

docs.title: Laws of Radicals
docs.text:
To simplify complex radical expressions, mathematicians use a set of rules known as the Laws of Radicals. These laws allow us to decompose radicals into simpler components, making it easier to perform arithmetic operations.

The two most fundamental laws are:

  1. The Product Law: This law states that the radical of a product is equal to the product of the individual radicals. [ \sqrt[n]{ab} = \sqrt[n]{a} \cdot \sqrt[n]{b} ]
  2. The Quotient Law: This law states that the radical of a quotient is equal to the quotient of the individual radicals. [ \sqrt[n]{\frac{a}{b}} = \frac{\sqrt[n]{a}}{\sqrt[n]{b}} \quad (\text{where } b \neq 0) ]

These laws are essential for simplifying expressions like \(\sqrt{50}\), which can be broken down into \(\sqrt{25 \cdot 2}\), and then further simplified to \(5\sqrt{2}\) using the Product Law.

docs.title: Exponential Functions
docs.text:
While integer exponents describe repeated multiplication, exponential functions describe a relationship where the input variable itself resides in the exponent. This results in a function that grows or decays at an ever-increasing or ever-decreasing rate.

An exponential function is defined by the general form: [ f(x) = ab^x ] In this definition, the components are as follows: - \( a \): The initial value or \( y\)-intercept, representing the value of the function when \( x = 0 \). - \( b \): The base or growth factor, which determines the rate of change. - \( x \): The exponent, which is the independent variable.

For the function to be considered exponential, we must have \( a \neq 0 \) and \( b > 0 \). Furthermore, the value of \( b \) determines the behavior: if \( b > 1 \), the function exhibits exponential growth; if \( 0 < b < 1 \), the function exhibits exponential decay.

Instructional Rationale: Visualizing the rapid rise of growth and the slow descent of decay provides an intuitive understanding of the function's behavior. docs.title: Binomials
docs.text:
In the study of polynomials, we categorize expressions based on the number of terms they contain. A binomial is a specific type of polynomial that consists of exactly two terms. These terms are typically joined by addition or subtraction. Examples of binomials include \( x + 5 \), \( 3y^2 - 10 \), or \( a - b \).

The complexity of binomials increases when we perform operations such as multiplication. When multiplying two binomials, we are essentially determining the product of two algebraic quantities. A helpful way to visualize this is through the geometric concept of area. If you have a rectangle with sides of length \( (x + a) \) and \( (x + b) \), the total area of that rectangle is the product of the two binomials.

To ensure that every term in the first binomial is multiplied by every term in the second, we use the FOIL method. FOIL is a mnemonic device that stands for First, Outer, Inner, and Last.

docs.title: Worked Example: The FOIL Method
docs.text:
Let's multiply the binomials \( (2x + 3)(x - 5) \).

  1. First: Multiply the first term of each binomial. [ 2x \cdot x = 2x^2 ]
  2. Outer: Multiply the outermost terms. [ 2x \cdot (-5) = -10x ]
  3. Inner: Multiply the innermost terms. [ 3 \cdot x = 3x ]
  4. Last: Multiply the last term of each binomial. [ 3 \cdot (-5) = -15 ]
  5. Combine Like Terms: Finally, combine the terms that have the same variable and exponent. [ 2x^2 - 10x + 3x - 15 ] [ 2x^2 - 7x - 15 ]

The final product is \( 2x^2 - 7x - 15 \).

docs.title: Factoring Trinomials
docs.text:
Factoring is the algebraic process of breaking an expression down into a product of simpler expressions. It is the inverse of multiplication. If multiplying binomials results in a trinomial, then factoring a trinomial means finding the original binomial "building blocks." A trinomial is a polynomial that contains exactly three terms, such as \( x^2 + 7x + 12 \).

We will focus on factoring trinomials in the form \( x^2 + bx + c \), where the leading coefficient is \( 1 \). To factor these successfully, you must find two numbers that satisfy two specific conditions simultaneously: 1. The product of the two numbers must equal the constant term \( c \). 2. The sum of the two numbers must equal the coefficient of the middle term \( b \).

This process is closely related to the concept of finding the "roots" or "zeros" of a function, as the values that make the binomials zero are the same values that make the trinomial zero.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Problem: Factor the trinomial \( x^2 - 5x + 6 \).

  1. Identify the target values: Here, the constant term \( c \) is \( 6 \) and the middle coefficient \( b \) is \( -5 \).
  2. Find the pair: We need two numbers that multiply to \( 6 \) and add to \( -5 \). Let's list the integer factors of \( 6 \):
    • \( 1 \times 6 = 6 \quad (\text{Sum: } 7) \)
    • \( 2 \times 3 = 6 \quad (\text{Sum: } 5) \)
    • \( (-1) \times (-6) = 6 \quad (\text{Sum: } -7) \)
    • \( (-2) \times (-3) = 6 \quad (\text{Sum: } -5) \)
  3. Select the correct pair: The pair \( (-2) \) and \( (-3) \) satisfies both conditions.
  4. Write the factors: Place these numbers into the two binomial factors. [ (x - 2)(x - 3) ]

The factored form is \( (x - 2)(x - 3) \).

docs.title: Quadratic Functions
docs.text:
A quadratic function is a polynomial function of degree two, meaning the highest power of the variable is \( 2 \). These functions are central to algebra because they model a wide variety of real-world phenomena, such as the trajectory of a projectile or the area of a shape. The standard form of a quadratic function is: [ f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c ] where \( a, b, \) and \( c \) are constants and \( a \neq 0 \).

The graph of a quadratic function is a unique, symmetrical curve known as a parabola. The direction in which the parabola opens is determined by the leading coefficient \( a \). If \( a > 0 \), the parabola opens upward, meaning it has a lowest point called the vertex. If \( a < 0 \), the parabola opens downward, meaning it has a highest point (a maximum) at the vertex.

docs.title: Worked Example: Analyzing a Quadratic
docs.text:
Consider the function \( f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3 \).

  1. Identify the degree: The highest exponent is \( 2 \), so it is a quadratic function.
  2. Determine the direction: Since \( a = 1 \) (positive), the parabola opens upward.
  3. Find the y-intercept: The y-intercept is the point where the graph crosses the y-axis, found by setting \( x = 0 \). [ f(0) = 0^2 - 4(0) + 3 = 3 ] The y-intercept is \( (0, 3) \).
  4. Find the vertex (Conceptual): The vertex is the "turning point" of the parabola. For this function, the vertex is located at \( (2, -1) \).

docs.title: Diagram: A coordinate plane showing a parabola opening upward, with the vertex labeled at the lowest point and the y-intercept marked.
Variables on Both Sides
docs.text:
In many algebraic equations, the variable does not appear on only one side of the equals sign. When we encounter equations with variables on both sides, our objective is to isolate the variable by moving all terms containing it to one side of the equation.

To solve these equations, we use the properties of equality—adding, subtracting, multiplying, or dividing both sides by the same value—to "collect" the variable terms on one side and the constant terms on the other. Think of the equation as a balanced scale; whatever operation you perform on one side, you must perform on the other to maintain the balance.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Problem: Solve \( 5x - 4 = 2x + 11 \).

  1. Collect variable terms: We want to move all \( x \) terms to the left side. We can do this by subtracting \( 2x \) from both sides. [ 5x - 2x - 4 = 2x - 2x + 11 ] [ 3x - 4 = 11 ]
  2. Isolate the variable term: Now, move the constant \( -4 \) to the right side by adding \( 4 \) to both sides. [ 3x - 4 + 4 = 11 + 4 ] [ 3x = 15 ]
  3. Solve for \( x \): Divide both sides by the coefficient \( 3 \) to find the final value. [ \frac{3x}{3} = \frac{15}{3} ] [ x = 5 ]

The solution is \( x = 5 \).

docs.title: Elimination Method
docs.text:
When we have a system of linear equations (a set of two or more equations with the same variables), we can use several methods to find the point where the lines intersect. One of the most powerful and efficient techniques is the elimination method.

The elimination method involves adding or subtracting the entire equations to "eliminate" one of the variables. This works most effectively when the coefficients of one variable in the two equations are additive opposites (for example, \( 3y \) and \( -3y \)). Once one variable is eliminated, you are left with a simple one-variable equation that can be solved easily.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Problem: Solve the following system: [ \begin{cases} 2x + y = 10 \ x - y = 2 \end{cases} ]

  1. Observe the coefficients: Notice that the \( y \) terms have coefficients of \( 1 \) and \( -1 \). They are already additive opposites.
  2. Add the equations: Adding the two equations together will eliminate the \( y \) variable. [ (2x + x) + (y - y) = (10 + 2) ] [ 3x = 12 ]
  3. Solve for the remaining variable: [ x = 4 ]
  4. Substitute to find the second variable: Now, plug \( x = 4 \) back into either of the original equations to find \( y \). Using the second equation: [ 4 - y = 2 ] [ -y = -2 \implies y = 2 ]

The solution to the system is the ordered pair \( (4, 2) \).

docs.title: Graphing Linear Equations
docs.text:
A linear equation represents a relationship where the change in one variable is constant, resulting in a straight line on a coordinate plane. To visualize this relationship, we use graphing.

The most common and efficient way to graph a line is by using its slope-intercept form: [ y = mx + b ] In this equation, the parameters have specific meanings: - \( m \) is the slope, which represents the rate of change or the "steepness" of the line. - \( b \) is the y-intercept, which is the point where the line crosses the y-axis.

In real-world contexts, the slope can represent a rate, such as speed (miles per hour) or cost (dollars per item), while the y-intercept represents a starting value.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Problem: Graph the line represented by \( y = \frac{2}{3}x - 1 \).

  1. Identify the y-intercept: The value of \( b \) is \( -1 \). Start by plotting the point \( (0, -1) \) on the y-axis.
  2. Use the slope to find a second point: The slope \( m \) is \( \frac{2}{3} \). Since slope is defined as "rise over run":
    • Rise: Move up \( 2 \) units from your starting point.
    • Run: Move right \( 3 \) units.
  3. Plot the second point: From \( (0, -1) \), moving up 2 and right 3 lands you at \( (3, 1) \).
  4. Draw the line: Use a straight edge to connect the points \( (0, -1) \) and \( (3, 1) \).

docs.title: Diagram: A coordinate plane showing the line \( y = \frac{2}{3}x - 1 \) passing through \( (0, -1) \) and \( (3, 1) \).
Dependent Variable
docs.text:
In any mathematical or scientific function, we study how one quantity changes in response to another. To describe this relationship, we distinguish between the independent variable and the dependent variable.

The independent variable is the input of the function. It is the factor that is controlled or changed. In most algebraic functions, this is represented by \( x \).

The dependent variable is the output of the function. Its value "depends" on the value chosen for the independent variable. It is the result of the function's operation and is typically represented by \( y \) or \( f(x) \).

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Imagine a scenario where a plumber charges a flat service fee of \( \$50 \) plus \( \$75 \) for every hour worked. This relationship can be modeled by the function: [ C(h) = 75h + 50 ] where \( C \) is the total cost and \( h \) is the number of hours.

  • The independent variable is \( h \) (the number of hours), because the number of hours is the factor we are observing or controlling.
  • The dependent variable is \( C \) (the total cost), because the final amount of money charged is entirely determined by how many hours were worked.

In a scientific experiment, if you were testing how sunlight affects plant growth, the amount of sunlight would be the independent variable, and the height of the plant would be the dependent variable.

docs.title: Negative Correlation
docs.text:
When we analyze data, we look for patterns that describe how two variables relate to one another. A correlation is a statistical measure that describes the strength and direction of a relationship between two variables.

A negative correlation occurs when the two variables move in opposite directions. This means that as the value of one variable increases, the value of the other variable tends to decrease. This relationship is visually represented in a scatterplot as a cluster of points that follows a downward-sloping trend.

docs.title: Worked Example
docs.text:
Consider a study observing the relationship between the number of hours spent playing video games and the number of hours spent studying for exams.

If the data shows that students who play more video games tend to study less, this is a negative correlation.

  • Variable 1 (Increasing): Hours of Gaming
  • Variable 2 (Decreasing): Hours of Studying

While correlation does not necessarily imply that gaming causes less studying (there could be other factors involved), it clearly shows an inverse relationship in the collected data.

Instructional Rationale: Interactive scatterplots allow students to see how the density and direction of points define the type of correlation.
