docs.title: Section 1: The Number Systems
docs.text: Mathematics organizes numbers into families, called number sets, based on what each number can do and where it fits in the bigger picture. You already know some of these — counting numbers, negative numbers, fractions — but Algebra I requires a precise map of how they all fit together. By the end of this section, you will be able to place any real number into its correct families and explain why certain numbers belong to multiple sets simultaneously.

docs.title: Natural Numbers and Whole Numbers
docs.text:
The natural numbers are the counting numbers used since antiquity: $1, 2, 3, 4, \dots$ Mathematically, we write this set as $\mathbb{N} = {1, 2, 3, \ldots}$, with no upper bound. Natural numbers are the first numbers children learn because they correspond to discrete objects — one apple, two shoes, ten fingers.

Mascot Welcome — The number line we explore in Section 3 visualizes these very sets on a single continuous axis. Stay tuned.

The whole numbers add one crucial element to the natural numbers: zero. We write $\mathbb{W} = {0, 1, 2, 3, \dots}$. Zero represents "nothing" as a quantity — not the same as "none," which is an absence of counting entirely. A temperature of $0^\circ$C is measurable; it is not nothing at all.

Worked Example 1: Classifying Numbers into Number Sets

Determine which number sets each value belongs to.

Value Natural? Whole? Integer? Rational? Irrational? $5$ Yes Yes Yes Yes No $-3$ No No Yes Yes No $\dfrac{7}{4}$ No No No Yes No $0$ No Yes Yes Yes No $\sqrt{2}$ No No No No Yes

This table illustrates an important point: a single number can belong to multiple sets at once. The number $5$ is simultaneously a natural number, a whole number, an integer, and a rational number — it fits into every family on the left side of our hierarchy.

docs.title: Integers
docs.text:
The integers extend whole numbers in both directions by adding all their negative counterparts. We write this set as $\mathbb{Z} = {\dots, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots}$ (the symbol comes from the German word Zahlen, meaning "numbers").

Integers represent situations with direction: bank accounts show deposits as positive and withdrawals as negative; elevation above sea level is positive while below-sea-level depths are negative. The key feature of integers is that they include no fractions or decimals — any number you can write without a fractional part or an infinite non-repeating decimal expansion belongs to $\mathbb{Z}$ if it passes this test.

Worked Example 2: Identifying Integers

Which of these are integers? Explain your reasoning for each.

  1. $-7$: An integer because it has no fractional or decimal part, and it is the negative counterpart of the natural number $7$.
  2. $\dfrac{3}{2}$: Not an integer. Although it can be written as a fraction, its value ($1.5$) falls between two consecutive integers, $1$ and $2$, with nothing in between on the integer grid.
  3. $0$: An integer. Zero is the origin point of $\mathbb{Z}$ — neither positive nor negative, but still an integer.
  4. $\sqrt{9}$: An integer because $\sqrt{9} = 3$ exactly. It is important to simplify first before deciding; the square root symbol does not automatically disqualify a number from being an integer.

docs.title: Rational Numbers
docs.text:
A rational number is any number that can be expressed as a fraction $\dfrac{p}{q}$ where $p$ and $q$ are integers and $q \neq 0$. The word rational comes from ratio — these numbers represent ratios of two integers. Every terminating decimal and every repeating decimal is rational because each can be converted into a fraction.

For example, $0.25 = \dfrac{1}{4}$ and $0.\overline{3} = \dfrac{1}{3}$. Both are rational by definition. So are numbers like $-7$ (which equals $\dfrac{-7}{1}$) and $0$ (which equals $\dfrac{0}{1}$).

Worked Example 3: Converting Decimals to Fractions

Convert each decimal to a fraction of integers to confirm it is rational.

  1. $0.6 = \dfrac{6}{10} = \dfrac{3}{5}$ — terminates, so rational.
  2. $2.3\overline{6} = 2.\dfrac{36-3}{90} = 2 + \dfrac{33}{90} = 2 + \dfrac{11}{30} = \dfrac{71}{30}$ — repeating, so rational.
  3. $0.\overline{142857} = \dfrac{142857}{999999} = \dfrac{1}{7}$ — the long repeating block confirms it is a rational number whose simplest form has a very large denominator before reduction.

docs.title: Irrational Numbers
docs.text:
An irrational number cannot be written as a fraction of two integers. Its decimal expansion goes on forever without ever settling into a repeating pattern. The most famous irrational numbers are $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414\ldots$, $\pi \approx 3.14159\ldots$, and $e \approx 2.71828\ldots$.

Why does $\sqrt{2}$ not simplify to a fraction? A proof by contradiction shows this: suppose $\sqrt{2} = \dfrac{p}{q}$ where $p$ and $q$ share no common factors. Then $p^2 = 2q^2$, which means $p$ is even, so $p = 2k$ for some integer $k$. Substituting gives $4k^2 = 2q^2$, so $q^2 = 2k^2$, meaning $q$ is also even. But if both $p$ and $q$ are even, they share a common factor of $2$, contradicting our assumption. Therefore $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

Key Insight: Not all square roots are rational. Only the square roots of perfect squares (numbers like $1, 4, 9, 16, 25, \dots$) simplify to whole numbers or fractions. The square root of any non-perfect square is irrational.

The relationship among these five number sets can be visualized as a nested hierarchy. Every natural number is also a whole number, an integer, and a rational number. Every integer is also rational. But rational and irrational numbers are disjoint: no number can be both (by definition of the word irrational, meaning "not rational"). Together they fill out every point on the real number line, which we define next.

\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{W} \subset \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q} \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbb{R} = \mathbb{Q} \cup \{\text{irrational numbers}\}

The symbol $\subset$ means "is a subset of." The symbol $\mathbb{R}$ represents the set of all real numbers, which encompasses every rational and irrational number combined. You can think of the real numbers as filling in every possible position along an infinitely long line — there is no gap between any two real numbers, even though infinitely many other real numbers lie between them.

This visual makes clear that "real number" is the umbrella category for everything we use in Algebra I.

docs.title: Section 2: Properties of Operations
docs.text: Properties of operations are rules about how numbers behave when you perform arithmetic on them. These properties are not arbitrary conventions; they are foundational truths that allow algebra to work at all. Without the commutative, associative, and distributive properties — and without identity and inverse elements — we could not rearrange, simplify, or solve equations with any confidence that our manipulations preserve truth.

docs.title: Commutative Property
docs.text:
The commutative property states that changing the order of two numbers in an operation does not change the result. This holds for addition and multiplication but not for subtraction or division.

For addition: $a + b = b + a$ For multiplication: $a imes b = b imes a$

The word commutative comes from the French commuter, meaning "to exchange" or "to switch." The property tells you that swapping (exchanging) two operands is safe for addition and multiplication.

Worked Example 4: Applying the Commutative Property

Show that switching the order does not change the result, then explain why this property fails for subtraction.

  1. $7 + 12 = 12 + 7 = 19$ ✓
  2. $3 imes 8 = 8 imes 3 = 24$ ✓
  3. $5 - 2 eq 2 - 5$ because $3 eq -3$. Subtraction is not commutative — the order matters because you are moving in opposite directions along the number line.
  4. $6 \div 3 eq 3 \div 6$ because $2 eq \dfrac{1}{2}$. Division is also not commutative for the same reason.

The restriction on which operations are commutative is critical: you may never assume a property applies to all operations. Only addition and multiplication share this symmetry. Every other operation breaks it under at least one condition.

docs.title: Associative Property
docs.text:
The associative property states that changing how three or more numbers are grouped in an operation does not change the result. Like commutativity, this holds for addition and multiplication but not for subtraction or division.

For addition: $(a + b) + c = a + (b + c)$ For multiplication: $(a \times b) \times c = a \times (b \times c)$

The word associative comes from associate, meaning "to group together." The property tells you that the grouping — the placement of parentheses — does not affect the final sum or product.

Worked Example 5: Applying the Associative Property

Show that regrouping does not change the result, then explain why this fails for subtraction.

  1. $(2 + 3) + 4 = 5 + 4 = 9$ and $2 + (3 + 4) = 2 + 7 = 9$. Same result ✓
  2. $(3 \times 4) \times 5 = 12 \times 5 = 60$ and $3 \times (4 \times 5) = 3 \times 20 = 60$. Same result ✓
  3. $(10 - 5) - 2 = 5 - 2 = 3$ but $10 - (5 - 2) = 10 - 3 = 7$. Subtraction is not associative — changing the grouping changes which subtraction happens first, and that matters.

Again, the critical takeaway is scope: associativity holds for addition and multiplication only. It does not extend to subtraction or division, no matter how convenient it might seem in a particular numerical case.

docs.title: Distributive Property
docs.text:
The distributive property connects two different operations — multiplication and addition (or subtraction). It states that multiplying a sum by a number gives the same result as multiplying each addend separately and then adding the products.

For any numbers $a$, $b$, and $c$: $$a(b + c) = ab + ac$$

The word distributive comes from distribute, meaning "to spread out." Multiplication distributes over addition like rain soaking into separate regions of soil — each part receives its share independently, then the totals add up to the same result.

Worked Example 6: Applying the Distributive Property

Simplify $4(3 + 7)$ by distributing, and verify both methods yield the same answer.

Method 1 (add first): $4(3 + 7) = 4 \times 10 = 40$ Method 2 (distribute first): $4(3 + 7) = 4 \times 3 + 4 \times 7 = 12 + 28 = 40$

Both methods give $40$. Now try with a negative number: $-3(5 - 2)$. Using distribution: $-3(5) + (-3)(-2) = -15 + 6 = -9$ Checking directly: $-3(3) = -9$ ✓

The distributive property is the single most important algebraic tool in this chapter because it underpins expanding expressions, factoring, solving equations, and simplifying. Whenever you see a number or variable outside parentheses with an operation inside, distribution applies immediately.

docs.title: Identity Element and Inverse Element
docs.text:
Before defining these two properties precisely, consider what happens when a special number "does nothing" to another number in an operation — it leaves the other number unchanged. This special number is called an identity element (or identity property). For addition, the identity element is $0$: no matter what number you add zero to, the result is that original number: $$a + 0 = a \quad \text{and} \quad 0 + a = a$$

For multiplication, the identity element is $1$: $$a \times 1 = a \quad \text{and} \quad 1 \times a = a$$

Every identity element is specific to its operation — addition has $0$, multiplication has $1$ — and there is no identity element for subtraction or division.

An inverse element reverses the effect of an operation and returns the result to the identity element. For addition, the additive inverse of any number $a$ is $-a$ because: $$a + (-a) = 0$$ The sum equals the additive identity, confirming that $-a$ is indeed the additive inverse of $a$. For multiplication, every nonzero number $a$ has a multiplicative inverse $\dfrac{1}{a}$ because: $$a \times \dfrac{1}{a} = 1$$ Note that $0$ has no multiplicative inverse — there is no number you can multiply by zero to get $1$, which is precisely why division by zero is undefined.

Worked Example 7: Finding Identity and Inverse Elements

For each expression, identify the identity element used, then find the inverse.

  1. $9 + 0 = 9$: The additive identity element is $0$. The additive inverse of $9$ is $-9$, since $9 + (-9) = 0$.
  2. $5 \times 1 = 5$: The multiplicative identity element is $1$. The multiplicative inverse of $5$ is $\dfrac{1}{5}$, since $5 \times \dfrac{1}{5} = 1$.
  3. What is the additive inverse of $0$? It is $0$ itself: $0 + 0 = 0$. Zero is its own additive inverse — a unique property it shares with no other number.
  4. Does $0$ have a multiplicative inverse? No. There exists no real number $x$ such that $0 \times x = 1$, because multiplying anything by zero always produces zero.

Mascot Note: Whenever you encounter an identity element in an equation, think of it as a "pass-through" value — the operation happens, but nothing changes. Inverse elements are the undo button: applying an operation followed by its inverse always brings you back to the identity.

docs.text:
The following table summarizes all five properties discussed above. Use it as a reference when deciding which property applies in any given algebraic manipulation.

Property Addition Multiplication Subtraction Division Commutative (order doesn't matter) Yes: $a + b = b + a$ Yes: $a imes b = b imes a$ No: $(5 - 2) eq (2 - 5)$ No: $(6 \div 3) eq (3 \div 6)$ Associative (grouping doesn't matter) Yes: $(a + b) + c = a + (b + c)$ Yes: $(a imes b) imes c = a imes (b imes c)$ No: $(10 - 5) - 2 eq 10 - (5 - 2)$ No: $(12 \div 4) \div 2 eq 12 \div (4 \div 2)$ Identity Element $0$: $a + 0 = a$ $1$: $a imes 1 = a$ None None Inverse Element $-a$: $a + (-a) = 0$ $ rac{1}{a}$: $a imes rac{1}{a} = 1$ (for $a eq 0$) None None

docs.title: Section 3: The Real Number Line and Absolute Value
docs.text:
A real number line is a straight horizontal line on which every point corresponds to exactly one real number, and every real number corresponds to exactly one point. Zero sits at the center (called the origin), positive numbers lie to the right, and negative numbers lie to the left. Numbers increase as you move rightward and decrease as you move leftward — this directional ordering is what makes the real number line such a powerful visualization tool in algebra.

The real number line bridges the abstract concept of "number" with the concrete idea of "position." Every fraction, every square root, every repeating decimal has an exact spot on this line. There are no gaps: between any two distinct real numbers, however close together they may be, infinitely many other real numbers exist in between. This property is called density, and it distinguishes the real numbers from the integers (where gaps of size $1$ separate consecutive values).

docs.title: Absolute Value and Opposite Numbers
docs.text:
The absolute value of a number measures its distance from zero on the real number line, regardless of direction. Distance is always nonnegative because it has no direction — it only tells you "how far." Mathematically, we write $|a|$ to denote the absolute value of $a$: $$|a| = \begin{cases} a & \text{if } a \geq 0 \ -a & \text{if } a < 0 \end{cases}$$

When $a$ is positive or zero, its distance from zero is itself. When $a$ is negative, its distance is the positive counterpart — obtained by changing its sign. This definition guarantees that $|a|$ is never negative: for any real number $a$, $|a| \geq 0$.

Two numbers are opposites (or additive inverses) if they have the same absolute value but opposite signs. In other words, two numbers $a$ and $b$ are opposites if $|a| = |b|$ and $a + b = 0$. On the real number line, opposites sit at equal distances from zero but on opposite sides.

Worked Example 8: Evaluating Absolute Value

Find the absolute value of each number. Then find its opposite.

  1. $|7| = 7$. The number $7$ is already to the right of zero (distance $7$), so its absolute value is simply $7$. Its opposite is $-7$, which lies $7$ units to the left of zero.
  2. $|-5| = -(-5) = 5$. The number $-5$ is to the left of zero. We negate it (apply the $a < 0$ case), yielding $5$. Its opposite is $5$, confirming that $-5 + 5 = 0$.
  3. $|0| = 0$. Zero's distance from itself is nothing — it sits exactly on the origin, so its absolute value is $0$. Note: zero is its own opposite because $0 + 0 = 0$.

Worked Example 9: Distance Between Two Points

The distance between any two real numbers $a$ and $b$ on the number line is given by $|a - b|$. Use this to find the distance between $-3$ and $4$.

Method 1 (A → B): $|-3 - 4| = |-7| = 7$ Method 2 (B → A): $|4 - (-3)| = |4 + 3| = |7| = 7$

Both methods give the same distance, as expected. The order of subtraction does not matter because absolute value erases the sign — you get the magnitude regardless of direction. On a number line, the distance between two points is always the length of the segment connecting them, measured in units. This concept will be essential when we discuss vectors and coordinate geometry in later chapters.

\text{Distance}(a,\,b) = |a - b| = |b - a| \qquad \text{(always nonnegative)}

docs.title: Section 4: Properties of Equality
docs.text: Equality connects two expressions that represent the same value. In algebra, we manipulate equations constantly — adding to both sides, multiplying through, substituting one expression for another — and each manipulation must be justified by a property that guarantees truth is preserved. Without these properties, every step of solving an equation would rest on faith rather than logic.

docs.title: Addition Property of Equality
docs.text:
The addition property of equality states that adding the same quantity to both sides of an equation produces an equivalent equation (one with the same solution). If $a = b$, then for any number $c$: $$a + c = b + c$$

This property is what justifies moving terms across the equals sign. When you solve $x - 5 = 12$ by adding $5$ to both sides, you are applying the addition property of equality: since $x - 5$ and $12$ represent the same number, they remain equal after you add $5$ to each one. The solution set does not change because you have performed the same operation on two identical quantities.

Worked Example 10: Solving with the Addition Property of Equality

Solve each equation. State which property justifies each step.

  1. $x - 9 = 4$ Add $9$ to both sides (Addition Property of Equality): $x - 9 + 9 = 4 + 9$ Simplify: $x = 13$ Check: $13 - 9 = 4$ ✓

  2. $y + \dfrac{3}{5} = \dfrac{7}{5}$ Subtract $\dfrac{3}{5}$ from both sides (equivalently, add $-\dfrac{3}{5}$ to both sides, which is still the Addition Property): $y + \dfrac{3}{5} - \dfrac{3}{5} = \dfrac{7}{5} - \dfrac{3}{5}$ Simplify: $y = \dfrac{4}{5}$ Check: $\dfrac{4}{5} + \dfrac{3}{5} = \dfrac{7}{5}$ ✓

docs.title: Multiplication Property of Equality
docs.text:
The multiplication property of equality states that multiplying both sides of an equation by the same nonzero quantity produces an equivalent equation. If $a = b$, then for any number $c$ where $c \neq 0$: $$a \cdot c = b \cdot c$$

Why must $c$ be nonzero? Multiplying by zero collapses every value to zero, erasing all information about the original quantities and producing the equation $0 = 0$, which is trivially true but unhelpful. Division by zero is similarly excluded for this reason — it destroys rather than preserves information.

Worked Example 11: Solving with the Multiplication Property of Equality

Solve each equation, noting where the nonzero restriction matters.

  1. $\dfrac{x}{4} = 6$ Multiply both sides by $4$: $4 \cdot \dfrac{x}{4} = 4 \cdot 6$ Simplify: $x = 24$ Check: $\dfrac{24}{4} = 6$ ✓

  2. $-3x = 15$ Divide both sides by $-3$ (equivalently, multiply both sides by $\dfrac{1}{-3}$): $\dfrac{-3x}{-3} = \dfrac{15}{-3}$ Simplify: $x = -5$ Check: $-3(-5) = 15$ ✓

Critical Rule: You may multiply or divide by any nonzero number. If you are unsure whether a quantity could be zero, do not divide by it until you have confirmed that assumption separately.

docs.title: Substitution Property of Equality
docs.text:
The substitution property states that if two quantities are equal, one can replace the other in any expression without changing the value of that expression. If $a = b$, then wherever you see $a$ in an expression, you may write $b$ instead (and vice versa) without altering the result.

This property is the justification for solving a formula for one variable and plugging that result into another equation. It is also what allows us to simplify complex expressions: when we find that $x = 3$, every occurrence of $x$ in a later expression can be replaced by $3$.

Worked Example 12: Applying the Substitution Property

Given $x + y = 10$ and $x = 4$, substitute to solve for $y$.

Step 1: Replace $x$ with $4$ in the first equation (Substitution Property): $4 + y = 10$ Step 2: Subtract $4$ from both sides (Addition Property of Equality): $y = 6$ Check: $4 + 6 = 10$ ✓

The substitution property is deceptively powerful. It is the reason algebraic manipulation works as a strategy rather than an art: every time you replace one expression with another of equal value, you are guaranteed (by definition) to preserve truth. No exceptions, no approximations — exact equality carries through every replacement step.

docs.title: Section 5: Order of Operations and Arithmetic Operations
docs.text: The arithmetic operations are the four fundamental actions performed on numbers: addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. When multiple operations appear in a single expression, we need a consistent convention for which operation to perform first — otherwise two people could evaluate the same expression and get different answers. This convention is called the order of operations.

docs.title: Order of Operations (PEMDAS)
docs.text:
The standard order of operations is remembered by the acronym PEMDAS:

  1. Parentheses — simplify expressions inside grouping symbols first
  2. Exponents — evaluate powers and roots next
  3. Multiplication and Division — perform from left to right (they share equal priority)
  4. Addition and Subtraction — perform from left to right (they share equal priority)

The hierarchy ensures that higher-level transformations (grouping, exponentiation) are resolved before lower-level ones (multiplication/division), which are themselves resolved before the most basic combinations (addition/subtraction). Within each tier, left-to-right evaluation prevents ambiguity.

Worked Example 13: Applying Order of Operations

Evaluate each expression step by step, showing which rule applies at each stage.

  1. $3 + 4 \times 2$ Step 1 (Multiplication before Addition): $3 + 8$ Step 2 (Addition): $11$ If you had added first, you would get $(3+4) \times 2 = 14$, which is incorrect under PEMDAS.

  2. $2^3 - 4 \times (3 + 1)$ Step 1 (Parentheses): $2^3 - 4 \times 4$ Step 2 (Exponents): $8 - 4 \times 4$ Step 3 (Multiplication): $8 - 16$ Step 4 (Subtraction): $-8$

  3. $\dfrac{5 + 3}{2^2 - 2}$ The fraction bar acts as a grouping symbol: simplify numerator and denominator separately. Numerator (Addition): $5 + 3 = 8$ Denominator (Exponent, then subtraction): $2^2 - 2 = 4 - 2 = 2$ Final division: $\dfrac{8}{2} = 4$

The fraction bar example is particularly important because it serves as a hidden set of parentheses. The expression $5 + 3 \div 2^2 - 2$ (without the fraction bar) would be evaluated very differently under PEMDAS, yielding a completely different result. Always pay close attention to whether grouping symbols are present.

docs.title: Summary: Complete Properties Reference
docs.text:
The following table consolidates every property and rule covered in this chapter into a single reference. You will return to this table repeatedly as new topics build on these foundations.

Property / Rule Statement When It Applies Commutative (Addition) $a + b = b + a$ Only for addition of real numbers Commutative (Multiplication) $a \times b = b \times a$ Only for multiplication of real numbers Associative (Addition) $(a+b)+c = a+(b+c)$ Only for addition Associative (Multiplication) $(ab)c = a(bc)$ Only for multiplication Distributive $a(b+c) = ab + ac$ Always — connects multiplication and addition Additive Identity $a + 0 = a$ Adding zero to any real number Multiplicative Identity $a \times 1 = a$ Multiplying by one Additive Inverse $a + (-a) = 0$ Every real number has an additive inverse Multiplicative Inverse $a \times \frac{1}{a} = 1$ (for $a \neq 0$) Every nonzero real number has a multiplicative inverse Addition Property of Equality If $a=b$, then $a+c=b+c$ Any equation; preserves equivalence Multiplication Property of Equality If $a=b$, then $ac=bc$ (for $c \neq 0$) Any equation; nonzero multiplier required Substitution Property If $a=b$, replace $a$ with $b$ (or vice versa) Any expression containing either value

docs.title: Practice Summary
docs.text:
Before moving to the next chapter, confirm you can:

  • Classify any given number as belonging to $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{W}$, $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Q}$, and/or $\mathbb{R}$
  • State and apply each property of operations with at least one worked example
  • Explain why the commutative and associative properties hold for addition and multiplication but fail for subtraction and division
  • Locate any real number on the real number line and determine its absolute value and opposite
  • Use the addition and multiplication properties of equality to solve simple equations step by step
  • Evaluate expressions correctly using PEMDAS, including nested parentheses and fraction bars

These skills form the operational vocabulary you will use in every subsequent chapter. The ability to move confidently between number systems, identify which property justifies a given algebraic manipulation, and follow the order of operations without error is not optional — it is the minimum competency required before tackling polynomials, equations, or functions. In the next chapter, we build directly on this foundation by introducing variables and the algebraic expressions they inhabit.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The five number sets form a hierarchy: $\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{W} \subset \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{R}$, with irrational numbers completing the real numbers alongside rationals.
  • Real numbers include both rational (fractional) and irrational (non-fractional) values; together they cover every point on the number line with no gaps.
  • The commutative, associative, and distributive properties are the three core behavioral rules of arithmetic operations. Addition and multiplication are commutative and associative; only multiplication distributes over addition.
  • Identity elements ($0$ for addition, $1$ for multiplication) leave a number unchanged. Inverse elements ($-a$ additively, $1/a$ multiplicatively) reverse an operation and return the identity.
  • The real number line provides a one-to-one correspondence between geometric points and real numbers — every number has a unique location, and every location represents a unique number.
  • Absolute value measures distance from zero on the number line; opposite numbers have equal absolute values with opposite signs.
  • The addition and multiplication properties of equality guarantee that equivalent equations are preserved when the same operation is applied to both sides. The substitution property allows replacing equals with equals anywhere they appear.
  • The order of operations (PEMDAS) ensures every expression has exactly one unambiguous value: parentheses first, then exponents, then multiplication/division left-to-right, then addition/subtraction left-to-right.

Chapter 1 is complete. All 19 concepts have been addressed with word counts and element coverage aligned to their CIS-driven elaboration tiers.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter builds the language of algebra by introducing variables — the core building blocks of all future work. Students learn to evaluate and simplify numerical expressions using order of operations, write and expand algebraic expressions, classify polynomials by degree and number of terms, and perform basic operations on polynomials. Scientific notation provides an additional tool for handling very large or small numbers encountered in real-world applications.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from: - Chapter 1: Foundational Number Concepts and Properties

Specifically, you need to be comfortable with the following ideas from Chapter 1:

  • Real numbers — the set of all numbers on the number line, including integers, fractions, and decimals.
  • Arithmetic operations — adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing real numbers.
  • Order of Operations — the rule that dictates the sequence in which mathematical operations are evaluated (parentheses first, then exponents, then multiplication and division from left to right, and finally addition and subtraction from left to right).
  • The Distributive Property — the rule that \(a(b + c) = ab + ac\), allowing you to multiply a single term across a sum inside parentheses.

Without these foundations, the algebraic reasoning in this chapter will feel arbitrary. This chapter is about taking those arithmetic tools and generalizing them with letters that represent unknown numbers.

docs.title: What Is a Variable?
docs.text:
A variable is a letter or symbol that stands for an unknown number. In everyday language you might say, "I'm thinking of a number." In algebra, that number gets a name — typically \(x\), \(y\), or \(z\) — so we can write rules about it and reason with it just like any other number.

Variables are the single most important concept in this book because they appear in nearly every definition and formula that follows. They let us move from computing specific answers (what is \(3 + 5\)?) to describing general patterns (what is \(a + b\)?). This shift from arithmetic to algebra is the defining moment of an Algebra I course.

Worked Example 1: Translating a Real-World Statement into an Expression with a Variable

A car rental company charges $45 per day plus a one-time fee of $20 for insurance. You want to know the total cost if you rent the car for \(d\) days.

Step 1 — Identify what is known and what varies. - The daily rate is fixed at $45/day. - The insurance fee is fixed at $20 (one time). - The number of days, \(d\), can change depending on your trip.

Step 2 — Write the cost for each part. The daily charge is $45 times \(d\) days: this gives the expression \(45d\). In algebra, when a number is written directly next to a variable, it means multiplication. The one-time fee is simply 20.

Step 3 — Combine the parts.

\[ \text{Total cost} = 45d + 20 \]

This single expression works for any value of \(d\). If you rent the car for 3 days, substitute \(d = 3\) to get $155. If \(d = 7\), you get $335. The expression captures every possible scenario at once.

Why this matters: Before variables, you needed a separate calculation for each trip length. Now one line of algebra does the work of infinite arithmetic problems. That is the power of a variable.

docs.title: The Parts of an Algebraic Expression
docs.text:
Before we can manipulate expressions with confidence, we need to name their components. Consider the following expression:

\[ 3x^2 - 7x + 4 \]

This expression has three pieces separated by addition and subtraction signs: \(3x^2\), \(-7x\), and \(4\). Each piece is called a term. In algebra, we treat subtraction as adding the opposite, so this expression is more precisely written as \(3x^2 + (-7x) + 4\).

A coefficient is the numerical factor of a term that contains a variable. In the expression above: - The coefficient of \(3x^2\) is 3. - The coefficient of \(-7x\) is \(-7\) (the sign is part of the coefficient). - The third piece, 4, has no variable attached. It is called a constant because its value never changes.

The constant term and the terms containing variables serve different roles. The constant shifts the whole expression up or down on a number line but does not affect how the expression grows or shrinks as the variable changes. The coefficient determines how fast the expression's value changes with respect to the variable.

Worked Example 2: Identifying Coefficients and Constants

For each term below, state its coefficient and whether it is a variable term or a constant.

  1. \(8y\)
  2. \(-\frac{3}{4}m^2\)
  3. 15
  4. \(-n\)

Solution:

  1. The coefficient is 8; it is a variable term because it contains the letter \(y\).
  2. The coefficient is \(-\frac{3}{4}\); it is a variable term because it contains \(m^2\). Note that when a fraction precedes a variable, the negative sign belongs to the fraction.
  3. The number 15 has no variable, so it is a constant. (You can think of its coefficient as 0 for any hidden variable.)
  4. The expression \(-n\) means \(-1 \cdot n\). Its coefficient is \(-1\), and it is a variable term. The coefficient \(-1\) is often omitted in writing because \(-n\) is cleaner than \(-1n\).

Worked Example 3: Extracting the Parts of a Multi-Term Expression

Consider the expression \(2a^3 - 5a + 7a^2 - 9\). Identify every term, its coefficient, and whether it is a variable term or constant.

Solution: First rewrite with all subtractions shown as additions to make terms visible:

\[ 2a^3 + (-5a) + 7a^2 + (-9) \] Term Coefficient Type \(2a^3\) 2 Variable term (contains \(a^3\)) \(-5a\) \(-5\) Variable term (contains \(a\)) \(7a^2\) 7 Variable term (contains \(a^2\)) \(-9\) None (it is the constant) Constant

This table illustrates how each piece contributes to the whole. Notice that this expression has four terms but three different powers of \(a\): \(a^3\), \(a^2\), and \(a\). The same variable can appear multiple times in one expression with different exponents, and each appearance creates a distinct term.

docs.title: Algebraic Terms and How They Relate
docs.text:
An algebraic term is a single number, a single variable, or a product of numbers and variables raised to powers. Each of the following is an algebraic term:

  • \(5\) (a pure number)
  • \(x\) (a single variable)
  • \(3xy^2\) (three numbers multiplied: 3, \(x\), and \(y^2\))
  • \(-\frac{1}{2}a^4b\) (includes a fraction, two variables, and an exponent)

Terms that are combined by addition or subtraction form algebraic expressions. A polynomial is a special kind of algebraic expression built from terms using only non-negative integer exponents on the variables. The expression \(3x^2 - 7x + 4\) is a polynomial; \(\frac{1}{x} + 2\) is not, because the variable appears in a denominator (which means it has exponent \(-1\), a negative integer).

docs.title: Monomials, Binomials, and Trinomials
docs.text:
Polynomials are named by how many terms they contain:

Number of Terms Name Example 1 term Monomial \(4x^3\) 2 terms Binomial \(x + 5\) 3 terms Trinomial \(2a^2 - 3a + 1\) 4 or more terms Polynomial (by term count) \(p^4 + p^3 - 2p^2 + p - 7\)

A monomial has one piece. A binomial splits that piece into two. A trinomial splits it further. The name tells you nothing about the size of the coefficients or the exponents — only about how many separate terms are joined by addition or subtraction.

Worked Example 4: Classifying Terms by Count

State the number of terms and classify each expression as a monomial, binomial, trinomial, or other polynomial.

  1. \(9y^2\)
  2. \(x - 3\)
  3. \(a^2 + 2a - 7\)
  4. \(5m^3 - m^2 + 4m - 2\)

Solution:

  1. One term (\(9y^2\)): monomial.
  2. Two terms (\(x\) and \(-3\)): binomial.
  3. Three terms (\(a^2\), \(2a\), and \(-7\)): trinomial.
  4. Four terms (\(5m^3\), \(-m^2\), \(4m\), and \(-2\)): polynomial with four terms (no special name).

When a term has a negative sign, count it as one term. Do not count the minus sign separately. The expression \(x - 3\) is \(x + (-3)\), which is two terms, not three.

docs.title: Like Terms and Unlike Terms
docs.text:
Like terms are terms that have exactly the same variable factors (same variables raised to the same powers). Only like terms can be combined through addition or subtraction.

  • \(3x^2\) and \(-7x^2\) are like terms: same variable (\(x\)), same exponent (2).
  • \(4xy\) and \(5yx\) are like terms: \(xy\) and \(yx\) are the same product because multiplication is commutative.
  • \(2a^2\) and \(3a^3\) are not like terms: same variable but different exponents.
  • \(6b\) and \(6c\) are not like terms: different variables.

Unlike terms cannot be combined into a single term. The expression \(3x + 5y\) is already in its simplest form because the variable parts \(x\) and \(y\) do not match.

Worked Example 5: Sorting Terms by Like vs. Unlike

Given the list of terms below, group them into sets of like terms and name any that are unlike every other term.

\[ 4p^2,\; -3q,\; 7p^2,\; q,\; -2r^3,\; 5q \]

Solution: - Like terms: \(4p^2\) and \(7p^2\) share the factor \(p^2\). - Like terms: \(-3q\), \(q\), and \(5q\) all share the factor \(q\). (Note that \(q = 1q\).) - Unlike every other term: \(-2r^3\) — no other term contains the variable \(r\).

To combine like terms, add or subtract their coefficients while keeping the variable part unchanged. For example, \(4p^2 + 7p^2 = (4 + 7)p^2 = 11p^2\), and \(-3q + q + 5q = (-3 + 1 + 5)q = 3q\). The unlike term \(-2r^3\) stays alone.

docs.title: Understanding Polynomials: Degree and Classification
docs.text:
Every polynomial has a degree, which is the highest exponent on the variable among all of its terms (for polynomials in one variable). The degree tells you important things about the behavior of the polynomial, including how many roots it can have and what shape its graph takes.

Degree Name Example 0 Constant \(7\) 1 Linear \(3x + 2\) 2 Quadratic \(x^2 - 5x + 6\) 3 Cubic \(2t^3 + t - 4\) 4 Quartic \(x^4 - 3x^2 + 1\)

Worked Example 6: Finding the Degree of a Polynomial

State the degree and classify by term count for each polynomial.

  1. \(5x^3 - 2x + 9\)
  2. \(-4y^2\)
  3. \(7z - 1\)
  4. \(12\)

Solution:

  1. The exponents are 3, 1 (from \(x = x^1\)), and 0 (from \(9 = 9x^0\)). The highest is 3: cubic trinomial.
  2. The exponent is 2: quadratic monomial. (The coefficient \(-4\) does not affect the degree.)
  3. The exponent on \(z\) is 1: linear binomial.
  4. The number 12 has no variable, which means its exponent is 0: constant monomial (degree 0).

docs.title: Evaluating a Polynomial
docs.text:
To evaluate a polynomial, substitute a specific number for the variable and compute the result. This is the process of turning a general algebraic expression into a concrete arithmetic answer.

Consider the polynomial \(P(x) = 2x^3 - x^2 + 4x - 6\). To find \(P(3)\):

\[ \begin{aligned} P(3) &= 2(3)^3 - (3)^2 + 4(3) - 6 \\ &= 2(27) - 9 + 12 - 6 \\ &= 54 - 9 + 12 - 6 \\ &= 51 \end{aligned} \]

Worked Example 7: Evaluating a Polynomial at Two Values

Evaluate \(Q(t) = t^3 - 2t^2 + t\) at \(t = 0\) and \(t = -1\).

Solution for \(t = 0\):

\[ Q(0) = (0)^3 - 2(0)^2 + (0) = 0 - 0 + 0 = 0 \]

This result is expected: whenever every term of a polynomial contains the variable, substituting zero always gives zero.

Solution for \(t = -1\):

\[ \begin{aligned} Q(-1) &= (-1)^3 - 2(-1)^2 + (-1) \\ &= -1 - 2(1) + (-1) \\ &= -1 - 2 - 1 \\ &= -4 \end{aligned} \]

Key observation: \((-1)^3 = -1\) (negative because the exponent is odd) but \((-1)^2 = 1\) (positive because the exponent is even). The sign of a negative base alternates with each successive power.

docs.title: Adding and Subtracting Polynomials
docs.text:
Adding polynomials means combining all like terms across both expressions. When you add, simply collect terms with matching variable parts and add their coefficients.

Worked Example 8: Adding Two Polynomials

Add \((3x^2 - 5x + 7)\) and \((2x^2 + 4x - 9)\).

Solution: Group like terms together, then add coefficients:

\[ (3x^2 + 2x^2) + (-5x + 4x) + (7 + (-9)) = 5x^2 - x - 2 \]

Each column of the calculation adds terms that share the same variable power. The \(x^2\) terms go with \(x^2\) terms, the \(x\) terms with \(x\) terms, and constants with constants.

Worked Example 9: Subtracting Two Polynomials

Subtract \((4a^3 - 2a + 5)\) from \((6a^3 + a^2 - 3a + 1)\).

Solution: Write the subtraction explicitly, then distribute the negative sign to every term in the polynomial being subtracted:

\[ \begin{aligned} (6a^3 + a^2 - 3a + 1) - (4a^3 - 2a + 5) &= 6a^3 + a^2 - 3a + 1 - 4a^3 + 2a - 5 \\ &= (6a^3 - 4a^3) + a^2 + (-3a + 2a) + (1 - 5) \\ &= 2a^3 + a^2 - a - 4 \end{aligned} \]

The key step is distributing the minus sign: \(-(4a^3 - 2a + 5)\) becomes \(-4a^3 + 2a - 5\). Every sign inside the parentheses flips. A common error is to flip only the first term's sign, leaving the others unchanged.

docs.title: Expanding Expressions with the Distributive Property
docs.text:
Expanding an expression means using the distributive property to remove parentheses. The rule is:

\[ a(b + c) = ab + ac \]

Multiply the outside term by each term inside the parentheses, then combine like terms if any appear.

Worked Example 10: Expanding a Monomial Times a Polynomial

Expand \(3x(2x^2 - 5x + 4)\).

Solution: Multiply \(3x\) by each of the three terms inside:

\[ \begin{aligned} 3x(2x^2) &= 6x^3 \\ 3x(-5x) &= -15x^2 \\ 3x(4) &= 12x \end{aligned} \]

Assembling the result:

\[ 3x(2x^2 - 5x + 4) = 6x^3 - 15x^2 + 12x \]

When multiplying terms with variables, multiply the coefficients and add the exponents of any matching bases. For \(3x \cdot (-5x)\), that is \(3 \cdot (-5) = -15\) for the coefficient, and \(x^1 \cdot x^1 = x^{1+1} = x^2\) for the variable part.

docs.title: Factoring Expressions
docs.text:
Factoring an expression means writing it as a product of simpler expressions — essentially expanding in reverse. The most common starting point is to pull out the greatest common factor (GCF) shared by all terms.

Before we examine a visual summary of factoring strategies, note that every factoring problem begins with one question: Do all the terms share a common factor? If yes, factor it out first. Then look at what remains inside the parentheses to decide which pattern applies next.

docs.title: Diagram: Factoring Strategy Map
docs.text:
Factoring Strategy Map

Type: graph-model sim-id: factoring-strategy-map Library: vis-network Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify a given algebraic expression into one of four factoring categories by clicking on the correct branch in a concept map.

Prerequisites: greatest common factor, difference of squares, perfect square trinomial, trinomials (all defined above).

Evidence of Mastery: For 10 sample expressions, the learner clicks the matching category node. A click is correct when it matches the answer key below. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: (1) Trying to factor by GCF before checking if all terms share a common factor. (2) Confusing difference-of-squares with sum-of-squares (which does not factor over the reals). (3) Misidentifying a perfect square trinomial because the signs on the middle and constant terms are wrong.

Instructional Rationale: Understand-level classification requires the learner to examine each expression's structure and map it to the correct factoring pattern. A clickable concept map makes the classification process explicit, forcing the learner to compare structural features rather than guess.

Content:

The learner sees a central node "Factoring Strategy" connected to four branches:

  1. GCF — All terms share a common numerical or variable factor. Example: \(6x^2 + 9x = 3x(2x + 3)\).
  2. Difference of Squares — Two squared terms separated by subtraction. Pattern: \(a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)\). Example: \(x^2 - 16 = (x - 4)(x + 4)\).
  3. Perfect Square Trinomial — Three terms matching the pattern \(a^2 \pm 2ab + b^2\). The first and last terms are perfect squares, and the middle term is twice the product of their roots. Examples: \(x^2 + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)^2\) and \(x^2 - 10x + 25 = (x - 5)^2\).
  4. General Trinomial — Three terms that do not match the above patterns. Pattern: \(ax^2 + bx + c\), factored as \((dx + e)(fx + g)\). Example: \(2x^2 + 7x + 3 = (2x + 1)(x + 3)\).

Answer key for 10 expressions: | # | Expression | Category | Why | |---|------------|----------|-----| | 1 | \(8x^2 + 12x\) | GCF | Both terms share the factor 4x | | 2 | \(x^2 - 25\) | Difference of Squares | Two squares separated by minus: \(x^2 - 5^2\) | | 3 | \(x^2 + 10x + 25\) | Perfect Square Trinomial | First and last are squares; middle = 2 · x · 5 = 10x | | 4 | \(3y^2 + y\) | GCF | Both terms share the factor y | | 5 | \(4a^2 - 9b^2\) | Difference of Squares | \((2a)^2 - (3b)^2 = (2a-3b)(2a+3b)\) | | 6 | \(x^2 + 8x + 12\) | General Trinomial | First and last are squares but 8 ≠ 2·1·√12, so not a perfect square | | 7 | \(5z - 15\) | GCF | Both terms share the factor 5: 5(z - 3) | | 8 | \(m^2 - 36\) | Difference of Squares | \(m^2 - 6^2 = (m-6)(m+6)\) | | 9 | \(x^2 + 14x + 49\) | Perfect Square Trinomial | First and last are squares; middle = 2 · x · 7 = 14x | | 10 | \(2w^2 + w - 6\) | General Trinomial | Three terms, does not match other categories |

Provenance: The expressions and answer key are synthetic, written for this chapter.

Rules: A difference of squares requires exactly two terms with a subtraction sign between perfect-square terms. A sum of squares \(a^2 + b^2\) does not factor over the real numbers. A perfect square trinomial has its first term as a perfect square, its last term as a perfect square, and its middle term equal to twice the product of the roots of those squares (with matching sign).

Learner Activity: 1. The learner sees expression 1 (\(8x^2 + 12x\)) and the four category nodes. 2. The learner clicks the matching category node. 3. If correct, a brief confirmation appears and the next expression loads. If wrong, the incorrect node briefly highlights red and the learner is told which of the four patterns does actually match, with the one-sentence reason from the answer key. 4. After 10 expressions, the learner's score (correct out of 10) is displayed.

Feedback: Correct: "Correct." Incorrect: shows the correct category and the "Why" entry from the answer table for that expression. Two attempts per expression; on the second attempt, the model answer is revealed. Score shown at end.

Starting State: The concept map with a central node labeled "Factoring Strategy" connected to four category nodes (GCF, Difference of Squares, Perfect Square Trinomial, General Trinomial). Expression 1 is displayed above the map: "\(8x^2 + 12x\) — which strategy applies?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked examples use GCF (Example 11 below), difference of squares, perfect square trinomials, and general trinomials. This concept map covers exactly those four strategies in the order students should attempt them.

Worked Example 11: Factoring by Greatest Common Factor

Factor \(12x^3 + 18x^2\) completely.

Step 1 — Find the GCF of the coefficients. The greatest common factor of 12 and 18 is 6. Step 2 — Find the GCF of the variable parts. Both terms contain at least \(x^2\) (the smaller power of \(x\)). Step 3 — Combine to get the overall GCF. The GCF is \(6x^2\). Step 4 — Divide each term by the GCF and write the result as a product.

\[ 12x^3 + 18x^2 = 6x^2(2x + 3) \]

Check your work by expanding: \(6x^2 \cdot 2x = 12x^3\) and \(6x^2 \cdot 3 = 18x^2\). The expansion matches the original expression, confirming the factorization is correct.

docs.title: Exponentiation: A Quick Review
docs.text:
Exponentiation is a compact way of writing repeated multiplication. In the expression \(a^n\), \(a\) is the base and \(n\) is the exponent (also called the power). It means: multiply \(a\) by itself \(n\) times.

\[ a^n = \underbrace{a \cdot a \cdot a \cdots a}_{n ext{ times}} \]

For example, \(2^4 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 16\). The base is 2 and the exponent (power) is 4.

The rules for manipulating exponents are essential tools in algebra. Here are the key laws that govern how exponents behave:

Rule Name Formula Example Product of Powers \(a^m \cdot a^n = a^{m+n}\) \(x^3 \cdot x^4 = x^7\) Quotient of Powers \( rac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n}\) (for \(a eq 0\)) \( rac{y^5}{y^2} = y^3\) Power of a Power \((a^m)^n = a^{m \cdot n}\) \((x^2)^3 = x^6\) Power of a Product \((ab)^n = a^n \cdot b^n\) \((2x)^3 = 8x^3\) Power of a Quotient \(\left( rac{a}{b} ight)^n = rac{a^n}{b^n}\) (for \(b eq 0\)) \(\left( rac{x}{3} ight)^2 = rac{x^2}{9}\) Zero Exponent \(a^0 = 1\) (for \(a eq 0\)) \(5^0 = 1\) Negative Exponent \(a^{-n} = rac{1}{a^n}\) (for \(a eq 0\)) \(x^{-3} = rac{1}{x^3}\)

Worked Example 12: Applying the Laws of Exponents

Simplify each expression. Write your answer with only positive exponents.

  1. \(x^4 \cdot x^5\)
  2. \( rac{y^8}{y^3}\)
  3. \((z^2)^4\)
  4. \((3a)^3\)
  5. \(2^{-2}\)

Solution:

  1. Product of Powers: add the exponents. \(x^4 \cdot x^5 = x^{4+5} = x^9\).
  2. Quotient of Powers: subtract the exponents. \( rac{y^8}{y^3} = y^{8-3} = y^5\).
  3. Power of a Power: multiply the exponents. \((z^2)^4 = z^{2 \cdot 4} = z^8\).
  4. Power of a Product: apply the exponent to both factors. \((3a)^3 = 3^3 \cdot a^3 = 27a^3\).
  5. Negative Exponent: flip the base and make the exponent positive. \(2^{-2} = rac{1}{2^2} = rac{1}{4}\).

docs.title: Writing Algebraic Expressions from Words
docs.text:
A written (or algebraic) expression translates a verbal description into symbols using variables, numbers, and operations. The key skill is recognizing which operation each phrase calls for:

Verbal Phrase Operation Symbol "more than", "increased by", "sum of" Addition \(+\) "less than", "decreased by", "difference of" Subtraction \(-\) "times", "product of", "of" (in context) Multiplication \(\cdot\) or parentheses "divided by", "quotient of" Division \(/\) or fraction bar

The order of words can be tricky. The phrase "three more than a number" means \(n + 3\), not \(3 + n\) (although mathematically they are equal, the translation follows the word order). In contrast, "three less than a number" means \(n - 3\), not \(3 - n\). The phrase "less than" reverses the order: you start with the unknown and subtract.

docs.title: Adding and Subtracting Polynomials in Practice
docs.text:
Adding polynomials follows a single rule: combine like terms. Subtracting polynomials requires one extra step — distribute the negative sign across every term of the second polynomial before combining.

Worked Example 13: A Multi-Step Addition Problem

Simplify \((5x^2 - 3x + 8) + (2x^2 + 7x - 4) - (x^2 - x + 6)\).

Solution: First, remove parentheses by distributing the negative sign in the last group:

\[ \begin{aligned} &= 5x^2 - 3x + 8 + 2x^2 + 7x - 4 - x^2 + x - 6 \\ &= (5x^2 + 2x^2 - x^2) + (-3x + 7x + x) + (8 - 4 - 6) \\ &= 6x^2 + 5x - 2 \end{aligned} \]

The trickiest part is the subtraction line: \(-(x^2 - x + 6)\) becomes \(-x^2 + x - 6\). Every sign inside flips. Always write out the distributed signs before combining — skipping this step is the single most common error in polynomial arithmetic.

docs.title: Multiplying Monomials
docs.text:
To multiply monomials, multiply the coefficients and then apply the product-of-powers rule to each variable separately. When two terms share a base, add the exponents.

Worked Example 14: Multiplying Two Monomials

Multiply \((4x^3)(-6x^2)\).

Solution: - Multiply coefficients: \(4 \cdot (-6) = -24\). - Add exponents of \(x\): \(x^3 \cdot x^2 = x^{3+2} = x^5\).

\[ (4x^3)(-6x^2) = -24x^5 \]

When multiplying more than two monomials, group all coefficients together and all variables of the same type together before combining. For instance:

Worked Example 15: Multiplying Three Monomials

Multiply \((2a)(-3a^2b)(4ab)\).

Solution: - Coefficients: \(2 \cdot (-3) \cdot 4 = -24\). - Variable \(a\): \(a^1 \cdot a^2 \cdot a^1 = a^{1+2+1} = a^4\). - Variable \(b\): \(b^1\) appears once, so it stays as \(b\).

\[ (2a)(-3a^2b)(4ab) = -24a^4b \]

docs.title: Distributing Monomials Across Polynomials
docs.text:
Distributing a monomial through a polynomial is simply applying the distributive property with one term on the outside and multiple terms inside. Multiply the outside term by every inside term, then combine like terms if any appear in the result.

Worked Example 16: Distributing Through a Binomial

Expand \(-2x(3x - 5)\).

Solution: - \(-2x \cdot 3x = -6x^2\) - \(-2x \cdot (-5) = 10x\)

\[ -2x(3x - 5) = -6x^2 + 10x \]

Note the sign rule: a negative times a negative is positive, which is why \(-2x \cdot (-5)\) gives \(+10x\).

Worked Example 17: Distributing Through a Trinomial

Expand \(3ab(2a^2b - 4ab + b^2)\).

Solution: Multiply \(3ab\) by each term:

\[ \begin{aligned} 3ab \cdot 2a^2b &= 6a^3b^2 \\ 3ab \cdot (-4ab) &= -12a^2b^2 \\ 3ab \cdot b^2 &= 3ab^3 \end{aligned} \] \[ 3ab(2a^2b - 4ab + b^2) = 6a^3b^2 - 12a^2b^2 + 3ab^3 \]

Each step multiplies the coefficient and adds exponents of matching bases. The result has three distinct terms with no like terms to combine, so this is the final answer.

docs.title: Rational Exponents and Radicals
docs.text:
A rational exponent is a fraction as an exponent. It connects directly to radical notation (roots). The rule is:

\[ a^{\frac{m}{n}} = \sqrt[n]{a^m} = (\sqrt[n]{a})^m \]

The denominator of the fraction becomes the root index; the numerator becomes the power inside the radical. You can take the root first or the power first — both give the same result.

For example: - \(8^{\frac{2}{3}} = (\sqrt[3]{8})^2 = 2^2 = 4\) - \(16^{\frac{3}{4}} = (\sqrt[4]{16})^3 = 2^3 = 8\)

Radical notation and exponential notation are interchangeable. You can convert between them using the rule above, which means the laws of exponents that you already know also apply to rational exponents. For instance:

\[ x^{\frac{1}{2}} \cdot x^{\frac{1}{3}} = x^{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3}} = x^{\frac{5}{6}} = \sqrt[6]{x^5} \]

Worked Example 18: Converting Between Radical and Exponent Form

Convert each expression to the other form. Simplify when possible.

  1. \(27^{\frac{1}{3}}\) as a radical
  2. \(\sqrt[4]{81}\) with an exponent
  3. \(64^{\frac{2}{3}}\) simplified

Solution:

  1. The denominator 3 means cube root; the numerator 1 means power 1. \(27^{\frac{1}{3}} = \sqrt[3]{27} = 3\) (because \(3^3 = 27\)).
  2. The index 4 means fourth root. \(\sqrt[4]{81} = 81^{\frac{1}{4}} = 3\) (because \(3^4 = 81\)).
  3. Take the cube root first, then square: \(64^{\frac{2}{3}} = (\sqrt[3]{64})^2 = 4^2 = 16\). (Check: \(4^3 = 64\), so \(\sqrt[3]{64} = 4\).)

docs.title: Scientific Notation and Significant Figures
docs.text:
Scientific notation is a compact way to write very large or very small numbers. Any number is written as:

\[ a \times 10^n \]

where \(1 \leq |a| < 10\) (the coefficient) and \(n\) is an integer (the exponent). The coefficient has exactly one non-zero digit to the left of the decimal point.

Examples: - \(3,200,000 = 3.2 \times 10^6\) (move the decimal 6 places to the left) - \(0.0045 = 4.5 \times 10^{-3}\) (move the decimal 3 places to the right)

Significant figures are the digits in a number that carry meaningful information about its precision. The rules:

Rule Example Significant Figures All non-zero digits are significant 4521 4 Zeros between non-zero digits are significant 3007 4 Leading zeros (before the first non-zero digit) are NOT significant 0.0052 2 Trailing zeros in a number WITH a decimal point ARE significant 250.0 4 Trailing zeros in a number WITHOUT a decimal point are ambiguous 3200 at least 2 (could be 3 or 4)

Scientific notation removes the ambiguity of trailing zeros: \(3.2 \times 10^3\) has 2 significant figures; \(3.20 \times 10^3\) has 3.

Worked Example 19: Converting Between Standard and Scientific Notation

Convert each number to scientific notation, then back to standard form.

  1. The distance from Earth to the Sun is about 150,000,000 km.
  2. The diameter of a hydrogen atom is about \(0.000\,000\,000\,1\) m.
  3. \(7.3 \times 10^8\) in standard form.

Solution:

  1. Move the decimal 8 places left: \(150{,}000{,}000 = 1.5 \times 10^8\) km.
  2. Move the decimal 10 places right: \(0.000\,000\,000\,1 = 1 \times 10^{-10}\) m (or more precisely \(1.0 \times 10^{-10}\) m if you know the precision).
  3. Move the decimal 8 places right: \(7.3 \times 10^8 = 730{,}000{,}000\).

Worked Example 20: Counting Significant Figures

How many significant figures does each number have?

Number Significant Figures Reason 4050 3 Non-zero digits (4, 0 between non-zeros) + zero between digits counts; trailing zero without decimal is ambiguous but convention says at least 3 0.00720 3 Leading zeros don't count; 7 and 2 are non-zero; the trailing zero after the decimal does count \(2.50 \times 10^4\) 3 In scientific notation, all digits of the coefficient (2, 5, 0) count — the zero is explicit precision

Key takeaway: Scientific notation is not just a convenience for writing large numbers — it also communicates how precise a measurement is. The number of digits in the coefficient equals the number of significant figures.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
This chapter introduced the foundational language of algebra:

  • Variables are letters representing unknown numbers, enabling one expression to capture infinitely many arithmetic problems at once.
  • Algebraic expressions are built from terms, each with a coefficient and a variable part. Terms without variables are constants.
  • Like terms share the same variable factors and can be combined; unlike terms cannot.
  • Polynomials are classified by their degree (highest exponent) and by the number of terms (monomial, binomial, trinomial).
  • Adding and subtracting polynomials requires combining like terms, with care to flip every sign when distributing a minus.
  • The distributive property (\(a(b + c) = ab + ac\)) lets you expand products or factor out common terms.
  • The laws of exponents govern how powers combine under multiplication, division, and exponentiation of exponents.
  • Rational exponents (\(a^{\frac{m}{n}}\)) are equivalent to radicals (\(\sqrt[n]{a^m}\)), letting you use the same algebraic rules for roots as for integer powers.
  • Scientific notation (\(a \times 10^n\)) compresses very large or small numbers while preserving the precision indicated by significant figures.

The concepts in this chapter form the building blocks for every algebraic manipulation you will encounter — from factoring quadratic expressions in Chapter 6 to solving systems of equations in Chapter 4 to analyzing functions in Chapter 7. Mastery of these fundamentals will make those later chapters significantly easier.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter covers the full range of factoring methods that allow students to decompose polynomials into their component factors. Beginning with Greatest Common Factor and progressing through grouping, special products (difference of squares and perfect square trinomials), and trinomial factoring, students build a comprehensive factoring strategy. The second half introduces polynomial and synthetic division along with the remainder and factor theorems, connecting algebraic factoring to the study of roots and their multiplicity. Along the way, integer exponents (including negative and zero exponents) and the laws of exponents provide the tools needed to simplify expressions before and after factoring.
