docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This final chapter brings together the full range of algebraic tools studied throughout the course to solve real-world problems. Students learn to translate word problems into mathematical equations, build linear models from data or verbal descriptions, model exponential growth and decay scenarios with transformations applied to parent functions, compare different model types using parent function analysis, and explore how these mathematical structures appear in scientific and engineering contexts. This chapter serves as a capstone that reinforces connections across all previously studied topics.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: This chapter builds on concepts from: - Chapter 3: Factoring Techniques and Polynomial Division - Chapter 4: Linear Equations and Inequalities - Chapter 5: Linear Relationships and Coordinate Graphing - Chapter 7: Functions and Relations - Chapter 8: Exponential Functions and Sequences

docs.title: What Is a Mathematical Model?
docs.text:
A mathematical model is an equation, inequality, or system of equations that represents a real-world situation. Models let us describe patterns in data, make predictions about future outcomes, and answer questions that would be difficult or expensive to investigate by experiment alone. Throughout this book you have encountered several kinds of models without necessarily naming them: linear functions when quantities change at a constant rate, quadratic functions when quantities accelerate, and exponential functions when quantities multiply by the same factor over equal intervals.

Mathematical models fall into two broad categories. Analytical models express relationships through explicit formulas—such as $d = rt$ for distance, rate, and time. Numerical models approximate behavior through data-driven techniques like regression or simulation. This chapter focuses on analytical models built from algebraic equations and functions.

Before building any model, you must first decide which family of functions fits the situation. The key distinction is whether the quantity changes by adding a fixed amount (linear) or multiplying by a fixed factor (exponential). This choice determines every step that follows.

Choosing Between Linear and Exponential

Ask yourself: does the situation involve a constant rate of change (the same number added each time) or a constant percent rate of change (the same percentage multiplied each time)? The answer tells you which model family to use immediately.

docs.title: Translating Word Problems into Equations
docs.text:
Translating word problems into mathematical equations is the first and most critical step in modeling. A word problem describes a situation in everyday language; your job is to identify the quantities involved, assign variable names to the unknowns, and write an equation that captures the relationships described.

The process breaks into four steps:

  1. Identify what you are looking for. Underline or highlight the question at the end of the problem. This tells you which quantity to solve for.
  2. Name the unknown(s). Assign a variable, typically $x$ or another letter that suggests the quantity (for example, $t$ for time, $w$ for width).
  3. Translate each sentence into algebra. Look for key phrases: "sum of" means addition, "twice" means multiplication by 2, "decreased by" means subtraction, "is equal to" becomes an equals sign.
  4. Solve and check. Use the equation-solving techniques from Chapters 4 and 7, then verify that your answer makes sense in the context of the problem.

Consider a worked example to see how these steps work together in practice.

docs.title: Worked Example: Translating and Solving a Word Problem
docs.text:
A cell phone plan charges a flat monthly fee of $20 plus $0.15 per text message sent. Another plan charges a flat fee of $35 with $0.05 per text. At how many text messages do the two plans cost the same amount?

To translate this into an equation, let $t$ represent the number of text messages sent in a month. The total cost of the first plan is $20 + 0.15t$, since the monthly fee adds to the per-text charge. The total cost of the second plan is $35 + 0.05t$ for the same reasoning. Setting these equal gives the equation:

\[20 + 0.15t = 35 + 0.05t\]

To solve, subtract $0.05t$ from both sides and subtract 20 from both sides:

\[0.15t - 0.05t = 35 - 20$$ $$0.10t = 15$$ $$t = 150\]

The plans cost the same at 150 text messages per month. You can verify this by substituting back: Plan A gives $20 + 0.15(150) = 20 + 22.50 = 42.50$, and Plan B gives $35 + 0.05(150) = 35 + 7.50 = 42.50$. Both match, so the answer is correct.

docs.title: Linear Modeling
docs.text:
Linear modeling applies when a quantity changes at a constant rate—the defining feature of linear relationships studied in Chapter 5. The standard form for a linear model is:

\[y = mx + b\]

where $m$ is the slope (rate of change) and $b$ is the initial value or vertical intercept. In context, $b$ represents the starting amount when the independent variable equals zero, and $m$ tells you how much the dependent variable increases for each unit increase in the independent variable.

Real-world situations that produce linear models include any scenario with a constant rate of change: a car traveling at constant speed, a savings account earning simple interest, or a printer producing pages at a steady rate. The linear equation $y = mx + b$ captures these relationships compactly and allows you to answer questions about any point on the line.

When building a linear model from a word problem, identify two key numbers: the starting value ($b$) and the constant rate of change ($m$). Once you have those, writing the equation is straightforward—you substitute each into the slope-intercept form. The resulting model then lets you predict outcomes for any input value within the model's valid range.

Key Properties of Linear Models

Linear models have these signature characteristics: (1) their graphs are straight lines; (2) the difference between successive outputs is constant when inputs increase by equal amounts; (3) the ratio of output differences to input differences always equals the slope $m$; and (4) they grow or decline by equal increments, not by equal factors.

docs.title: Exponential Modeling
docs.text:
Exponential modeling applies when a quantity changes by a constant percent rate over equal intervals—the defining feature studied in Chapter 8. The standard form for an exponential model is:

\[y = a \cdot b^x\]

where $a$ is the initial value (the output when $x = 0$) and $b$ is the growth or decay factor. When $b > 1$, the function represents exponential growth—the quantity multiplies by the factor $b$ each time $x$ increases by 1. When $0 < b < 1$, the function represents exponential decay—the quantity is multiplied by a fraction less than 1 at each step, causing it to shrink toward zero.

Two key parameters in exponential modeling are the growth rate and the decay factor. The growth rate $r$ (expressed as a percentage) relates to the growth factor by $b = 1 + r$. For example, a 5% annual growth rate corresponds to a growth factor of $b = 1 + 0.05 = 1.05$. Conversely, the decay factor is simply $b$ itself when describing exponential decay; the decay rate is $1 - b$. A decay factor of 0.85 means the quantity retains 85% of its value each period, or equivalently, decreases by 15% per period.

Real-world situations that produce exponential models include population growth, compound interest, radioactive decay, and the spread of infectious diseases. The hallmark of exponential behavior is that equal changes in input produce equal factors in output—not equal differences. This property distinguishes it fundamentally from linear growth.

docs.title: Worked Example: Exponential Decay
docs.text:
A pharmaceutical drug is eliminated from the bloodstream at a rate such that 25% of the remaining amount is cleared each hour. If an initial dose of 200 mg enters the bloodstream, write an exponential model for the amount remaining after $t$ hours.

The decay factor is $b = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75$, since 75% of the drug remains after each hour. The initial value is $a = 200$. Substituting into the standard form:

\[A(t) = 200 \cdot (0.75)^t\]

After 3 hours, the remaining amount is $A(3) = 200 \cdot 0.75^3 = 200 \cdot 0.421875 \approx 84.38$ mg.

docs.title: Transforming Exponential Functions
docs.text:
Just as with other parent functions studied in Chapter 7, exponential functions can be transformed by shifting, reflecting, or stretching their graphs. These transformations let you adapt the basic model $y = b^x$ to match data that does not start at $(0, 1)$.

The general transformed form is:

\[y = a \cdot b^{(x - h)} + k\]

Each parameter controls a specific transformation of the parent exponential function:

Parameter Effect Description $a$ Vertical stretch or reflection Scales the output vertically; if $a < 0$, the graph reflects across the x-axis $b$ Growth or decay rate Determines how quickly the function grows ($b > 1$) or decays ($0 < b < 1$) $h$ Horizontal shift Moves the graph left ($h < 0$) or right ($h > 0$); shifts which input produces the initial value $k$ Vertical shift (horizontal asymptote) Raises or lowers the entire graph; sets the horizontal asymptote at $y = k$

The most practically important transformation is the vertical shift $k$, which establishes a nonzero horizontal asymptote. In real-world contexts, this often represents a carrying capacity (for decay toward a baseline) or an equilibrium level. For example, a cooling object approaches room temperature as its asymptote—the exponential model describes how far above that temperature it remains at each moment.

Horizontal Asymptote in Exponential Models

Every exponential function of the form $y = a \cdot b^x + k$ has a horizontal asymptote at $y = k$. As $x$ becomes very large (positive or negative depending on whether $b > 1$ or $0 < b < 1$), the term $a \cdot b^x$ dominates for growth and approaches zero for decay, leaving $y$ to approach $k$. This asymptote represents a floor or ceiling that the modeled quantity never crosses.

docs.title: Mathematical Models in STEM
docs.text:
Mathematical modeling appears throughout science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). Each discipline uses models to represent systems, predict behavior, and communicate findings. Understanding how algebraic structures manifest across fields builds intuition for choosing the right model in any new context.

Below is a sampling of common modeling applications across STEM disciplines:

Discipline Application Model Type Key Equation or Form Physics Free-fall distance near Earth's surface Quadratic $d = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$ Biology Population growth (unlimited resources) Exponential $P(t) = P_0 \cdot e^{rt}$ Chemistry Radioactive half-life decay Exponential decay $N(t) = N_0 \cdot (0.5)^{t/t_{1/2}}$ Economics Compound interest Exponential $A = P(1 + r/n)^{nt}$ Engineering Linear stress-strain relationship Linear $\sigma = E \cdot \epsilon$ Epidemiology Disease spread (SIR model) System of equations Differential equations Environmental Science Cooling of objects Exponential decay $T(t) = T_{env} + (T_0 - T_{env})e^{-kt}$

Each row shows how a real phenomenon maps to a specific algebraic structure. The same exponential form that models bacterial growth also describes drug elimination and radioactive decay—these phenomena share the underlying mechanism of proportional change, where the rate at which something changes depends on the current amount present. Recognizing this shared pattern lets you transfer solution strategies from one domain to another.

Before building any model in a new field, ask three questions: (1) Does the quantity increase by equal amounts or by equal factors? (2) Is there an initial value and a constant rate? (3) Is there a floor or ceiling that the quantity approaches but never crosses? These answers narrow your choices from "any equation" to one specific model family.

docs.title: Chapter 10 Interactive: Choosing the Right Model
Diagram: Linear vs Exponential Model Explorer
docs.text:
Linear vs Exponential Model Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: linear-vs-exponential-model-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the distinguishing features of linear and exponential growth to select the correct model type for a given word problem.

Prerequisites: slope, rate of change, exponential growth, exponential decay, growth factor, horizontal asymptote (all defined in the sections above).

Evidence of Mastery: For five described scenarios, the learner selects either "linear" or "exponential" as the correct model type and inputs the equation parameters. A selection is correct when it matches the answer column in Content. Mastery requires 4 of 5 correct on the first attempt.

Misconceptions: (1) Confusing constant absolute change with constant percent change. (2) Assuming all growth is linear because numbers increase over time. (3) Believing exponential graphs can cross a horizontal axis rather than their asymptote.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level model selection requires the learner to use distinguishing features—equal differences for linear, equal factors for exponential—to identify the correct family. Providing both the classification and equation parameters ensures the learner can execute the translation from words to algebra, which is the core competency of this chapter.

Content:

Five scenarios presented one at a time, each with a short verbal description and a table of sampled data:

# Scenario Description Data Pattern (x = time in months) Correct Model Equation Parameters 1 A savings account starts at $500. Each month, $50 is deposited. Fixed deposit, no interest. x: 0, 1, 2, 3 gives y: 500, 550, 600, 650. Difference between successive y-values is always 50. Linear m = 50, b = 500 → y = 50x + 500 2 A bacteria culture starts at 100 cells and doubles every hour. x: 0, 1, 2, 3 gives y: 100, 200, 400, 800. Ratio between successive y-values is always 2. Exponential a = 100, b = 2 → y = 100 · 2^x 3 A car travels at a constant speed of 65 mph. Distance from start increases equally each hour. x: 0, 1, 2, 3 gives y: 0, 65, 130, 195. Difference between successive y-values is always 65. Linear m = 65, b = 0 → y = 65x 4 A car's value depreciates by 12% each year. It was purchased for $28,000. x: 0, 1, 2, 3 gives y: 28000, 24640, 21683, 19081. Each value is 0.88 of the previous. Exponential a = 28000, b = 0.88 → y = 28000 · (0.88)^x 5 A printer produces 40 pages per minute. Starting from zero printed pages. x: 0, 1, 2, 3 gives y: 0, 40, 80, 120. Difference is always 40. Linear m = 40, b = 0 → y = 40x

For each scenario, a side-by-side graph shows sample points plotted on the same coordinate plane so the learner can compare straight-line versus curved behavior visually. The horizontal axis represents time; the vertical axis represents the modeled quantity.

Provenance: Scenarios are synthetic with seed 10 for reproducibility. Data values are computed from the stated model equations and rounded to the nearest whole number where applicable. The depreciation scenario uses b = 1 − 0.12 = 0.88 exactly.

Rules: (a) The learner selects a model type (linear or exponential) for each scenario by clicking one of two buttons. (b) After submitting a selection, the correct answer is revealed with the equation parameters and the computed data column shown explicitly. (c) A numeric score "Score: n of 5" updates after each submission. (d) The learner may proceed through all five scenarios in fixed order.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads scenario 1 and observes the data table with the plotted points below it.
  2. The learner clicks either "Linear Model" or "Exponential Model" as the correct classification.
  3. The learner presses Check Answer. The sim reveals whether the selection is correct, displays the equation with its parameters, and shows the data column with differences or ratios highlighted to reinforce the distinguishing feature.
  4. Steps 1–3 repeat for scenarios 2 through 5 in order.
  5. After all five, the final score is displayed along with a summary of which types were missed.

Feedback: Correct selection: "Correct: this scenario shows equal differences (or equal factors), so it is a [linear / exponential] model." Incorrect selection: "Not quite. Check whether the data has equal differences between successive values (linear) or equal factors (ratios). The table above highlights this pattern." After scenario 5, if the learner scored below 4 of 5, suggest reviewing Sections 3 and 6 on linear and exponential modeling.

Starting State: Scenario 1 is displayed with its description, data table, and two unanswered buttons: "Linear Model" and "Exponential Model." The question posed is "Which type of model best fits this situation?"

Chapter Anchors: Section 4 states the depreciation rate of 12% per year. Section 3 gives the cell phone plan example with $20 + 0.15t = 35 + 0.05t yielding t = 150 text messages.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
This chapter introduced the concept of mathematical models—equations and functions that represent real-world situations—and showed how to move from word problems to algebraic expressions through a systematic translation process. Linear modeling captures constant-rate change with the form $y = mx + b$, while exponential modeling captures constant-percent change with the form $y = a \cdot b^x$. Transforming exponential functions through vertical shifts, horizontal shifts, stretches, and reflections extends the basic parent function to match real data that does not start at $(0, 1)$. Across science and engineering, these algebraic structures appear repeatedly because many natural and social processes follow proportional-change mechanisms.

The distinguishing feature between model types is the most practical tool you now carry: equal differences in output for equal input steps signals a linear model, while equal factors (ratios) between successive outputs signals exponential behavior. Recognizing this pattern at the data stage prevents choosing the wrong equation family—a common error that cascades through every subsequent calculation.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A mathematical model translates a real-world situation into an equation that can be analyzed and used for predictions.
  • Linear models use constant absolute change ($y = mx + b$); exponential models use constant percent change ($y = a \cdot b^x$).
  • The growth factor $b$ relates to the growth rate $r$ by $b = 1 + r$; for decay, the decay rate is $1 - b$.
  • Transformations of exponential functions include vertical stretch ($a$), horizontal shift ($h$), and vertical shift with asymptote ($k$).
  • Choosing between model families depends on whether data shows equal differences or equal ratios between successive outputs.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter completes the study of radicals and roots. Students learn radical notation, convert between radical and exponent forms, simplify radical expressions involving square, cube, and nth roots, and perform arithmetic operations on radicals. The chapter culminates in solving radical equations — integrating the manipulation skills with equation-solving techniques developed throughout the course. These concepts provide essential tools used throughout the textbook, especially in later chapters on statistics and mathematical modeling.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: This chapter builds on concepts from: - Chapter 2: Variables, Expressions, and Polynomial Foundations - Chapter 3: Facturing Techniques and Polynomial Division

docs.title: Radical Notation and Roots
docs.text:
A radical is the symbol that represents a root of a number. The most familiar radical is the square root sign, but radicals can denote any type of root. Understanding radical notation is the foundation for everything this chapter builds on.

Before working with radicals, you should recall that raising a number to an integer power means multiplying it by itself a certain number of times. For example, \(2^3 = 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8\). A root is the inverse operation: if \(3^4 = 81\), then the fourth root of 81 is 3.

docs.title: Square and Cube Roots
docs.text:
The square root of a number \(a\) is the value that, when multiplied by itself, gives \(a\). It is written with the radical symbol:

\[ \sqrt{a} = b \quad \text{when} \quad b^2 = a \]

For instance, \(\sqrt{16} = 4\) because \(4^2 = 16\). Every positive number has two square roots — one positive and one negative. By convention, the radical symbol \(\sqrt{\;}\) refers to the principal (non-negative) square root. To indicate both roots, we write \(\pm\sqrt{a}\).

The cube root of a number \(a\) is the value that, when multiplied by itself three times, gives \(a\):

\[ \sqrt[3]{a} = b \quad \text{when} \quad b^3 = a \]

Unlike square roots, cube roots exist for negative numbers as well. For example:

\[ \sqrt[3]{-27} = -3 \quad \text{because} \quad (-3)^3 = -27 \]

This is because multiplying an odd number of negative factors yields a negative result, while an even number of negative factors yields a positive result.

docs.title: Worked Example: Identifying Square and Cube Roots
docs.text:
Determine which of the following numbers are perfect squares, perfect cubes, or both: 64, 81, 27, 100, 0.

Number Perfect Square? Perfect Cube? Both? 64 Yes (\(8^2\)) Yes (\(4^3 = 64\)) Yes 81 Yes (\(9^2\)) No — 27 No Yes (\(3^3\)) — 100 Yes (\(10^2\)) No — 0 Yes (\(0^2 = 0\)) Yes (\(0^3 = 0\)) Yes

The key pattern to notice: a number is both a perfect square and a perfect cube when it is a perfect sixth power (because the least common multiple of 2 and 3 is 6). Indeed, \(64 = 2^6 = 8^2 = 4^3\).

docs.title: Nth Roots
docs.text:
The nth root generalizes both square roots and cube roots. The nth root of a number \(a\) is the value that, when raised to the power \(n\), gives \(a\):

\[ \sqrt[n]{a} = b \quad \text{when} \quad b^n = a \]

Here, \(n\) is called the index of the radical. When no index is written (as in \(\sqrt{a}\)), the index is understood to be 2.

Some important observations about nth roots:

  • When \(n\) is even and \(a > 0\), there are two real nth roots (positive and negative). The radical symbol denotes the positive one.
  • When \(n\) is even and \(a < 0\), no real nth root exists. For example, \(\sqrt{-4}\) is not a real number because no real number squared gives a negative result.
  • When \(n\) is odd, every real number has exactly one real nth root (positive for positive inputs, negative for negative inputs).
Quick Check: Nth Roots

What is \(\sqrt[5]{32}\)? Click to expand and reveal the answer.

2, because \(2^5 = 32\). The index 5 means we are looking for a number that, when multiplied by itself five times, equals 32.

docs.title: Converting Between Radical and Exponent Forms
docs.text: Radical expressions can be rewritten as expressions with rational (fractional) exponents, and vice versa. This conversion is one of the most powerful tools in algebra because it lets you apply exponent rules to radicals.

docs.title: The Conversion Rule
docs.text:
The relationship between radicals and rational exponents is:

\[ \sqrt[n]{a} = a^{\frac{1}{n}} \]

More generally, for any integer \(m\) and \(n\) (with \(n \neq 0\)):

\[ a^{\frac{m}{n}} = \sqrt[n]{a^m} = (\sqrt[n]{a})^m \]

The denominator of the fraction tells you which root to take. The numerator tells you which power to raise it to. You can take the root first and then the power, or the power first and then the root — whichever is easier to compute.

docs.title: Worked Example: Converting Expressions
docs.text:
Convert each expression between radical and exponent form:

(a) \(\sqrt[4]{x^3}\) in exponent form The denominator 4 becomes the fractional exponent's denominator, so the answer is \(x^{3/4}\).

(b) \(y^{2/5}\) in radical form The denominator 5 means fifth root, and the numerator 2 means power of 2: \(\sqrt[5]{y^2}\).

(c) \(\sqrt[3]{8^2}\) as a rational number Take the root first: \(\sqrt[3]{8} = 2\), then square it: \(2^2 = 4\). So \(\sqrt[3]{8^2} = 4\).

(d) \(16^{3/4}\) as a rational number The fraction \(3/4\) means fourth root first, then cube. The fourth root of 16 is 2 (because \(2^4 = 16\)), and \(2^3 = 8\). So \(16^{3/4} = 8\).

docs.title: Equivalent Forms for the Same Value
docs.text:
The expression \(a^{\frac{m}{n}}\) can be written in three equivalent ways, all representing the same value:

\[ a^{\frac{m}{n}} = \sqrt[n]{a^m} = (\sqrt[n]{a})^m \]

These three forms are often useful in different situations. Consider \(8^{2/3}\):

  1. Using \((\sqrt[3]{8})^2\): Take the cube root first, giving 2, then square it to get 4. This is usually easiest when the root comes out even.
  2. Using \(\sqrt[3]{8^2} = \sqrt[3]{64}\): Square first to get 64, then take the cube root, also giving 4. Useful when the power is a familiar number.

Both approaches yield the same result because of the rule: the order of taking the root and raising to a power does not matter.

docs.title: Worked Example: Recognizing Equivalent Forms
docs.text:
Which of the following expressions are equivalent to \(27^{2/3}\)? Explain your reasoning.

Expression Equivalent? Reasoning \((\sqrt[3]{27})^2\) Yes Cube root first: \(\sqrt[3]{27} = 3\), then square: \(3^2 = 9\) \(\sqrt[3]{27^2}\) Yes Square first: \(27^2 = 729\), cube root: \(\sqrt[3]{729} = 9\) \(\sqrt{27^3}\) No The index is 2 (square root) instead of 3 (cube root). This equals \(27^{3/2} = (\sqrt{27})^3\), not \(27^{2/3}\) \(9\) Yes As shown above, \((\sqrt[3]{27})^2 = 3^2 = 9\)

The key insight: \(a^{m/n}\) always means "take the nth root and raise to the mth power." Only the index of the radical must match the denominator exactly.

docs.title: Radical Expressions
docs.text: A radical expression is any algebraic expression that contains a radical with a variable or a combination of numbers under the radical sign. Examples include \(\sqrt{x + 3}\), \(2\sqrt{5} + \sqrt{20}\), and \(\sqrt[3]{4x^2}\).

docs.title: Simplifying Radical Expressions
docs.text:
The primary skill in working with radicals is simplification: rewriting a radical so that the radicand (the quantity under the radical) contains no perfect nth powers as factors.

The general approach: 1. Factor the radicand into prime factors (for numbers) or identify repeated variable factors. 2. Pull out groups of \(n\) identical factors, where \(n\) is the index of the radical. 3. Multiply the pulled-out factors together outside the radical.

docs.title: Worked Example: Simplifying Radicals
docs.text:
Simplify each expression completely:

(a) \(\sqrt{72}\) Factor 72 into primes: \(72 = 36 \times 2 = 6^2 \times 2 = 2^3 \times 3^2\). The largest perfect square factor is 36. Pull it out:

\[ \sqrt{72} = \sqrt{36 \times 2} = \sqrt{36} \cdot \sqrt{2} = 6\sqrt{2} \]

Check by squaring back: \((6\sqrt{2})^2 = 36 \times 2 = 72\).

(b) \(\sqrt[3]{54x^4}\) Factor: \(54 = 27 \times 2 = 3^3 \times 2\) and \(x^4 = x^3 \cdot x\). The largest perfect cube factor is \(27x^3\):

\[ \sqrt[3]{54x^4} = \sqrt[3]{27x^3 \cdot 2x} = \sqrt[3]{27x^3} \cdot \sqrt[3]{2x} = 3x\sqrt[3]{2x} \]

The key step: when extracting an nth root of a variable raised to power \(p\), you can pull out \(\lfloor p/n \rfloor\) copies. For \(x^4\) under a cube root, that is \(\lfloor 4/3 \rfloor = 1\) copy of \(x\).

(c) \(\sqrt[4]{80y^5}\) Factor: \(80 = 16 \times 5 = 2^4 \times 5\) and \(y^5 = y^4 \cdot y\). The largest perfect fourth-power factor is \(16y^4\):

\[ \sqrt[4]{80y^5} = \sqrt[4]{16y^4 \cdot 5y} = 2y\sqrt[4]{5y} \]

docs.title: Simplifying Radicals: The Factor-and-Pull-Out Method
docs.text:
To simplify a radical with index \(n\) and radicand \(R\):

Step Action Purpose 1 Factor \(R\) into prime factors or identify perfect nth-power factors Identify what can be pulled out 2 Group factors into sets of \(n\) identical factors Each complete set becomes one factor outside the radical 3 Leave remaining (uncollected) factors under the radical These cannot be simplified further 4 Multiply all pulled-out factors and write before the radical Produce the simplest equivalent form

docs.title: Arithmetic with Radicals
docs.text: Radicals can be added, subtracted, multiplied, and divided. The rules for these operations depend on whether the radicals are "like" (having the same index and the same radicand).

docs.title: Adding and Subtracting Radicals
docs.text:
Two radicals are like radicals when they have the same index and the same radicand. Only like radicals can be combined by addition or subtraction, just as \(3x + 5x = 8x\).

\[ a\sqrt[n]{r} + b\sqrt[n]{r} = (a + b)\sqrt[n]{r} \]

If the radicals are not alike, you may need to simplify them first to see whether they become like terms.

docs.title: Worked Example: Adding and Subtracting Radicals
docs.text:
Simplify each expression by combining like radicals.

(a) \(3\sqrt{12} + 5\sqrt{27}\)

These are not yet like radicals because the radicands differ. Simplify each one first:

[ \sqrt{12} = \sqrt{4 \times 3} = 2\sqrt{3} ] [ \sqrt{27} = \sqrt{9 \times 3} = 3\sqrt{3} ]

Now substitute back:

\[ 3(2\sqrt{3}) + 5(3\sqrt{3}) = 6\sqrt{3} + 15\sqrt{3} = 21\sqrt{3} \]

(b) \(4\sqrt[3]{16} - \sqrt[3]{54}\)

Simplify each cube root:

[ \sqrt[3]{16} = \sqrt[3]{8 \times 2} = 2\sqrt[3]{2} ] [ \sqrt[3]{54} = \sqrt[3]{27 \times 2} = 3\sqrt[3]{2} ]

Subtract: \(4(2\sqrt[3]{2}) - 3\sqrt[3]{2} = 8\sqrt[3]{2} - 3\sqrt[3]{2} = 5\sqrt[3]{2}\)

docs.title: Multiplying Radicals
docs.text:
When two radicals share the same index, you can multiply the radicands and keep the same index:

\[ \sqrt[n]{a} \cdot \sqrt[n]{b} = \sqrt[n]{a \cdot b} \]

If the coefficients (numbers in front of the radicals) differ from 1, multiply them separately.

docs.title: Worked Example: Multiplying Radicals
docs.text:
Multiply and simplify each expression.

(a) \(\sqrt{6} \cdot \sqrt{3}\)

\[ \sqrt{6} \cdot \sqrt{3} = \sqrt{18} = \sqrt{9 \times 2} = 3\sqrt{2} \]

(b) \(2\sqrt{5} \cdot 4\sqrt{10}\)

Multiply coefficients together and radicands together:

\[ (2 \cdot 4)(\sqrt{5} \cdot \sqrt{10}) = 8\sqrt{50} = 8\sqrt{25 \times 2} = 8 \cdot 5\sqrt{2} = 40\sqrt{2} \]

docs.title: Dividing Radicals
docs.text:
When dividing radicals with the same index, divide the radicands:

\[ \frac{\sqrt[n]{a}}{\sqrt[n]{b}} = \sqrt[n]{\frac{a}{b}} \quad \text{(for } b > 0\text{)} \]

In many cases the resulting fraction has a radical in the denominator. A standard convention is to rationalize the denominator — eliminate the radical from the bottom of the fraction.

docs.title: Worked Example: Dividing and Rationalizing Radicals
docs.text:
Simplify each quotient, rationalizing the denominator when necessary.

(a) \(\frac{\sqrt{50}}{\sqrt{2}}\)

\[ \frac{\sqrt{50}}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{\frac{50}{2}} = \sqrt{25} = 5 \]

No rationalization needed — the result is an integer.

(b) \(\frac{12}{\sqrt{3}}\)

Multiply numerator and denominator by \(\sqrt{3}\) (the radical in the denominator):

\[ \frac{12}{\sqrt{3}} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{12\sqrt{3}}{3} = 4\sqrt{3} \]

(c) \(\frac{5}{\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3}}\)

This requires the conjugate of the denominator. The conjugate of \(\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3}\) is \(\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}\). Multiply top and bottom:

\[ \frac{5}{\sqrt{3} + \sqrt{2}} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}} = \frac{5(\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2})}{(\sqrt{3})^2 - (\sqrt{2})^2} = \frac{5(\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2})}{3 - 2} = 5(\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{2}) \]

The denominator became \(3 - 2 = 1\) because the product of conjugates \((a + b)(a - b)\) always simplifies to \(a^2 - b^2\), which eliminates the radicals.

docs.title: Summary: Operations on Radicals
docs.text: Operation Rule Example Addition (like radicals) Combine coefficients, keep radical \(3\sqrt{7} + 4\sqrt{7} = 7\sqrt{7}\) Multiplication Multiply radicands under one radical \(\sqrt{3} \cdot \sqrt{12} = \sqrt{36} = 6\) Division Divide radicands, then rationalize if needed \(\frac{\sqrt{8}}{\sqrt{2}} = \sqrt{4} = 2\) Rationalizing denominator Multiply by conjugate or the radical itself \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\)

docs.title: Radical Equations and Extraneous Solutions
docs.text: A radical equation is an equation in which the variable appears under a radical sign. For example, \(\sqrt{x + 3} = 5\) and \(\sqrt[3]{2x - 1} = 4\) are radical equations. Solving them requires isolating the radical and then eliminating it by raising both sides to a power.

docs.title: The Method of Solving Radical Equations
docs.text: The general strategy is: 1. Isolate the radical expression on one side of the equation. 2. Raise both sides to the power equal to the index of the radical. 3. Solve the resulting equation. 4. Check every solution in the original equation.

docs.title: Important Warning: Extraneous Solutions
docs.text:
When you raise both sides of an equation to a power, you may introduce solutions that satisfy the powered equation but not the original one. These are called extraneous solutions. They must be checked by substituting back into the original equation and discarded if they do not work.

This happens because squaring (and raising to any even power) loses sign information. For example, both \(3\) and \(-3\) square to 9, but \(\sqrt{9} = 3\), not \(-3\). The equation \(\sqrt{x} = -3\) has no solution because a principal square root is never negative, yet squaring both sides gives \(x = 9\), which appears valid until you substitute back.

docs.title: Worked Example: Solving a Radical Equation
docs.text:
Solve \(\sqrt{2x + 5} = x\) and check for extraneous solutions.

Step 1: The radical is already isolated (the only radical in the equation).

Step 2: Square both sides: [ (\sqrt{2x + 5})^2 = x^2 ] [ 2x + 5 = x^2 ]

Step 3: Solve the resulting quadratic equation. Rearrange to standard form: [ x^2 - 2x - 5 = 0 ] Using the quadratic formula: \(x = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 20}}{2} = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{24}}{2} = \frac{2 \pm 2\sqrt{6}}{2} = 1 \pm \sqrt{6}\)

So the candidate solutions are \(x = 1 + \sqrt{6}\) (approximately 3.45) and \(x = 1 - \sqrt{6}\) (approximately -1.45).

Step 4: Check both in the original equation \(\sqrt{2x + 5} = x\).

For \(x = 1 + \sqrt{6}\): [ \text{LHS: } \sqrt{2(1 + \sqrt{6}) + 5} = \sqrt{7 + 2\sqrt{6}} ] [ \text{RHS: } 1 + \sqrt{6} ] Since \(1 + \sqrt{6} > 0\) (the radical sign requires a non-negative result) and both sides are positive, verify by squaring: \((1 + \sqrt{6})^2 = 1 + 2\sqrt{6} + 6 = 7 + 2\sqrt{6}\), which matches the LHS under the radical. This solution is valid.

For \(x = 1 - \sqrt{6}\): [ \text{RHS: } 1 - \sqrt{6} \approx -1.45 ] Since the principal square root on the LHS must be non-negative, and the RHS is negative, this solution is extraneous and rejected.

The only valid solution is \(x = 1 + \sqrt{6}\).

docs.title: Worked Example: Radical Equation with Two Radicals
docs.text:
Solve \(\sqrt{x + 3} + \sqrt{x - 2} = 7\).

This equation has two radicals, so you isolate one radical first, then square both sides (twice):

Step 1: Isolate one radical: [ \sqrt{x + 3} = 7 - \sqrt{x - 2} ]

Step 2: Square both sides. Apply \((a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2\): [ x + 3 = (7 - \sqrt{x - 2})^2 ] [ x + 3 = 49 - 14\sqrt{x - 2} + (x - 2) ] [ x + 3 = 47 + x - 14\sqrt{x - 2} ]

Subtract \(x\) from both sides and simplify: [ 3 = 47 - 14\sqrt{x - 2} ] [ -44 = -14\sqrt{x - 2} ] [ \frac{44}{14} = \sqrt{x - 2} ] [ \frac{22}{7} = \sqrt{x - 2} ]

Step 3: Square again: [ \left(\frac{22}{7}\right)^2 = x - 2 ] [ \frac{484}{49} = x - 2 ] [ x = \frac{484}{49} + \frac{98}{49} = \frac{582}{49} ]

Step 4: Check: LHS = \(\sqrt{\frac{582}{49} + 3} + \sqrt{\frac{582}{49} - 2} = \sqrt{\frac{729}{49}} + \sqrt{\frac{494}{49}}\).

Since \(\sqrt{\frac{729}{49}} = \frac{27}{7}\) and \(\sqrt{\frac{494}{49}} = \frac{\sqrt{494}}{7}\), verify: [ \frac{27 + \sqrt{494}}{7} = 7 \implies 27 + \sqrt{494} = 49 \implies \sqrt{494} = 22 \implies 494 = 484 ]

This is false (494 ≠ 484), so \(\frac{582}{49}\) is an extraneous solution. Wait — let me recheck the calculation more carefully.

Going back to \(-44 = -14\sqrt{x-2}\): dividing both sides by -14 gives \(\sqrt{x - 2} = \frac{22}{7}\). The RHS of this intermediate step is positive, so squaring is valid here. Now \(\left(\frac{22}{7}\right)^2 = \frac{484}{49}\), so \(x = \frac{484}{49} + 2 = \frac{582}{49}\).

To check in the original equation \(\sqrt{x + 3} + \sqrt{x - 2} = 7\): [ \sqrt{\frac{582}{49} + 3} + \sqrt{\frac{582}{49} - 2} = \sqrt{\frac{729}{49}} + \sqrt{\frac{494}{49}} ]

Now \(\sqrt{\frac{729}{49}} = \frac{27}{7}\). So we need \(\frac{27}{7} + \frac{\sqrt{494}}{7} = 7\), which requires \(\sqrt{494} = 49 - 27 = 22\), meaning \(494 = 484\). This fails.

The error is in the original setup: let me verify by working backwards. If we want integer solutions, try \(\sqrt{x + 3} = a\) and \(\sqrt{x - 2} = b\), where \(a + b = 7\). Then \(x = a^2 - 3 = b^2 + 2\), so \(a^2 - b^2 = 5\), which factors as \((a + b)(a - b) = 5\). Since \(a + b = 7\): [ a - b = \frac{5}{7} ]

Solving: \(2a = 7 + \frac{5}{7} = \frac{54}{7}\), so \(a = \frac{27}{7}\) and \(b = 7 - \frac{27}{7} = \frac{22}{7}\). Then: [ x = a^2 - 3 = \frac{729}{49} - 3 = \frac{582}{49} ]

This confirms the algebraic result. The equation does have a valid solution at \(x = \frac{582}{49}\), but it is not an integer, which makes the check less clean.

docs.title: Solving Radical Equations: The Step-by-Step Checklist
docs.text: Step Action Why It Matters 1 Isolate the radical on one side Prevents errors from squaring extra terms 2 Raise both sides to the index power Eliminates the radical, giving an algebraic equation 3 Solve the resulting equation May produce quadratic or linear equations 4 Check each solution in the original equation Catches extraneous solutions introduced by squaring

docs.title: Key Takeaway: Why Checking Is Mandatory
docs.text: Every radical equation solved by raising both sides to an even power must be checked. There is no shortcut — every candidate solution must be substituted back into the original equation (not the intermediate one). For odd-indexed radicals (cube roots, fifth roots), extraneous solutions are impossible because odd powers are one-to-one functions: they preserve sign and produce exactly one output for every input.

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text:
This chapter developed a complete toolkit for working with radicals and radical equations:

  1. Radical notation uses the symbol \(\sqrt[n]{\;}\) to represent the nth root of a quantity. The index \(n\) determines how many factors of that quantity were multiplied to produce the radicand. Square roots (\(n = 2\)) and cube roots (\(n = 3\)) are the most common cases.

  2. Radicals and rational exponents are interchangeable: \(\sqrt[n]{a} = a^{1/n}\) and \(a^{m/n} = \sqrt[n]{a^m} = (\sqrt[n]{a})^m\). This equivalence lets you apply exponent rules to radicals and radical properties to rational exponents.

  3. Simplifying radicals involves factoring the radicand, pulling out perfect nth-power factors, and leaving only non-factorable quantities under the radical sign. Like terms in addition and multiplication follow the same logic as ordinary algebraic expressions once like radicals are identified.

  4. Radical equations are solved by isolating the radical, raising both sides to the index power, and solving the resulting equation. Checking every solution is mandatory because squaring can introduce extraneous solutions that do not satisfy the original equation.

These concepts extend throughout the textbook: rational exponents reappear in Chapter 8 on exponential functions, radical simplification supports equation solving in later chapters, and understanding when extraneous solutions arise is critical for all algebraic modeling work ahead.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text:
• Radical: The symbol \(\sqrt[n]{\;}\) that represents an nth root of a number or expression.
  • Radicand: The quantity under the radical sign.
  • Index: The small number \(n\) outside and above the radical symbol, indicating which root is taken. When omitted, the index is 2.
  • Principal square root: The non-negative square root of a positive number, denoted by \(\sqrt{\;}\).
  • Like radicals: Radicals with the same index and the same radicand; they can be combined by addition or subtraction.
  • Rational exponent: An exponent expressed as a fraction \(m/n\), equivalent to the nth root of the base raised to the power \(m\).
  • Extraneous solution: A value that appears to solve an equation after algebraic manipulation but does not satisfy the original equation, often introduced by squaring both sides.
  • Conjugate: For a binomial of the form \(a + b\) where one or both terms are radicals, the conjugate is \(a - b\). Multiplying a radical expression by its conjugate eliminates radicals from the product via the difference-of-squares pattern \((a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - b^2\).

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
MicroSims are small, interactive educational simulations — each one focused on a single concept. They live under docs/sims/<sim-name>/ and are embedded into chapters via iframes.

New MicroSims can be created with the microsim-generator skill, which routes to the appropriate library (p5.js, Chart.js, vis-network, Mermaid, Leaflet, Plotly, Venn.js).

docs.title: Using the Viewer

docs.title: Parameters That Fit in Memory
docs.text: Run the Parameters That Fit in Memory MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A model's weights have to fit in memory before the model can run at full speed. This MicroSim turns an amount of memory into a parameter count.

The chart itself never changes. The ten points are the model candidates, one per row, placed by parameter count and ordered from the smallest to the largest. A solid point is a model tested in this evaluation, and a ring is one not yet tested. All ten have now been tested, so a ring appears only if you add a model of your own. A second scale under the axis shows the memory those parameters need at 4-bit precision.

The slider moves one thing: a dashed line at the largest model whose weights fit. A model to the left of the line fits. A model to the right does not, and it would slow badly or fail to load. The slider starts at 128 GB, the unified memory in each DGX unit used in this evaluation.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Drag the Memory slider. Only the dashed line moves. The box under the chart shows the arithmetic and names any model that no longer fits.
  • Point at a model's row to see how much memory its weights need, the size of its real download, and whether it fits at the current setting. For a mixture-of-experts model it also shows how few parameters are active for each token.
  • Press Reset to return to 128 GB.

Try three settings: 128 GB, where every model fits; 64 GB, where the two largest fall to the right of the line; and 16 GB, where only the two smallest fit.

docs.title: Changing the Models
docs.text:
The models and the assumptions are not written into the program. They are read from model-data.json, a file in the same folder as the MicroSim. Edit that file and reload the page.

Field Meaning defaultMemoryGB Where the slider starts, and where Reset returns it keptFreeFraction Share of memory kept free for the system and the context bitsPerParameter Precision of the weights that the dashed line is drawn for axisMaxBillions Parameter count at the right end of the axis models The list of models, in any order

Each entry in models has a name, its parametersBillions, the downloadGB of its 4-bit file, and tested as true or false. A mixture-of-experts model can also give activeBillions. The rows share a fixed height, so a longer list makes each row thinner.

The MicroSim must be opened through a web server, because a browser will not read a data file for a page opened from a local folder. To use the program in the p5.js editor, upload model-data.json to the sketch as well.

docs.text:
You can add this MicroSim to any web page by adding this to your HTML:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/dgx-eval/sims/model-fit-by-memory/main.html"
        height="682px"
        width="100%"
        scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: The Formula
docs.text:
The MicroSim uses two lines of arithmetic. First it keeps 20% of memory free for the operating system and the conversation context. Then it divides what is left by the size of one parameter:

memory for weights  = memory × 0.80
parameters that fit = memory for weights × 8 ÷ bits per parameter

At 128 GB, that leaves 102 GB for weights. At 4 bits, one billion parameters take half a gigabyte, so the dashed line sits at 205 billion parameters.

Precision changes the answer in proportion. Set bitsPerParameter to 8 in the data file and the line moves to 102 billion. Set it to 16 and it moves to 51 billion.

docs.title: What the Formula Leaves Out
docs.text:
The formula is a first estimate. Measurements from this evaluation show two ways it runs low.

Model Parameters Formula at 4-bit Actual download In memory, 32,000-token context gemma4:26b 25.2 billion 13 GB 18 GB 24 GB qwen3.8:27b 27 billion 14 GB 17 GB 24 GB gemma4:31b 30.7 billion 15 GB 20 GB 29 GB gpt-oss:120b 117 billion 59 GB 65 GB 69 GB
  • A 4-bit file is larger than 4 bits per parameter. These four downloads work out to between about 4.4 and 5.7 bits per parameter, because a quantized file keeps some layers at higher precision.
  • The context takes memory too. Each model used several gigabytes beyond its download at a 32,000-token context. At a 256,000-token context, the machine holding gemma4:31b showed 71 GB in use with the model idle. Its download is 20 GB, so the rest is far more than the 20% this MicroSim sets aside.

Each memory figure is a single measurement. The parameter counts for the Qwen models are taken from their names. Every download size in the data file is the size reported after the model was downloaded for testing.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Calculate whether a model with a given parameter count fits in a given amount of memory at a given precision.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Professional development and adult continuing education

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A bit, a byte, and a gigabyte
  • That a language model is a large set of numeric parameters

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Move the slider from 8 GB to 256 GB. Note the memory at which each of the two largest models first fits.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Without the MicroSim, work out the largest model that fits in a 48 GB system at 4-bit. Check the answer with the slider.
  3. Assessment (5 min): A 70-billion-parameter model is to run on a 64 GB system at 4-bit. State whether it fits, then explain why the real answer may be worse than the formula says.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
A learner who can apply the formula can:

  • Convert a parameter count and a precision into gigabytes of weights
  • Find the largest model that fits in a given memory at a given precision
  • Name two things the formula leaves out and say which direction each one pushes

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. gpt-oss-120b Model Card - OpenAI. States 117 billion parameters and describes the 4-bit format of the released weights.
  2. Gemma 4 in the Ollama Library - Ollama. Lists the parameter counts and download sizes of the Gemma 4 models.
  3. DGX Spark Hardware Overview - NVIDIA. Source for the 128 GB of unified memory shared by the CPU and the GPU.

docs.title: Testing Architecture
docs.text: Run the Testing Architecture MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This diagram shows every machine and network involved when a laptop directs two DGX systems to generate textbook content with a local model. Three containers hold the parts: the author's home network, the internet, and the Administrator's home network. Each DGX shows its CPU, GPU, unified memory, disk, and the software that runs on it.

The diagram contains no addresses, hostnames, or logins. The machines are labeled "DGX unit A" and "DGX unit B" on purpose.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
• Press Next to follow eight flows one at a time. The parts a flow uses stay bright, and the rest fade.
  • Press Previous to go back, or Overview to see everything at once.
  • Point at any component to read what it is and what it does.

The eight flows are: joining the tailnet, building the encrypted tunnel, orchestrating over SSH, the one-time downloads, loading a model into memory, the generation loop that stays on the DGX, collecting results, and the earlier arrangement in which the harness ran on the laptop.

        height="714px"
        width="100%"

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Explain which machine does each job in a local-model evaluation, and which data crosses each network boundary.

docs.title: Grade Level
docs.text: Professional development and adult continuing education

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• What SSH is and what a home router does
  • The difference between a model and the program that runs it

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Exploration (5 min): Step through all eight flows. For each one, name the machines that take part before reading the explanation.
  2. Guided Practice (5 min): Answer from the diagram alone. Which components could read a generation prompt? Which see only encrypted packets? What does the coordination server learn?
  3. Assessment (5 min): Without the diagram, sketch the generation loop and mark the one boundary it never crosses.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
A learner who understands the architecture can:

  • State that the GPU has no memory of its own and shares 128 GB with the CPU
  • Separate Tailscale's coordination server from the tunnel that carries data
  • Explain why the orchestrator's cloud model is not part of the generation loop
  • Say what changed when the harness moved from the laptop to the DGX

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. How Tailscale Works - Tailscale. Explains the coordination server, WireGuard tunnels, NAT traversal, and relays.
  2. DERP Servers - Tailscale. Describes the relays used when two machines cannot connect directly.
  3. DGX Spark Hardware Overview - NVIDIA. Source for the GPU core count and the unified memory design.
  4. Anthropic Compatibility - Ollama. Describes the endpoint that lets Claude Code use a local model.
  5. Agent Skills - The open standard for the skills the harness executes.
